wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the planned treatment was done. But risk management never ends; a new threat can make a treated risk unacceptable again.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a technical control may help later. But choosing a fix before reassessing skips the step that shows what the risk now is.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reviews run on a schedule. But major changes and new threats also trigger reassessment, not only the calendar.

tips: Eliminate: B treats the cycle as finished once a risk is treated, and D waits for the calendar, though new threats trigger reassessment.
Final two: A beats C because assessment comes before treatment; a tool bought first may not fit the risk as it now stands.
Exam cue: a new threat, a big change or an incident sends a risk back to assessment. Assess, then treat, then monitor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 2.1 (Components of Risk Management: frame, assess, respond and monitor); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'risk management repeats: new threats, changes and incidents send risks back to assessment' (notes 1.2.2 The Risk Management Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A home-care agency rated laptop theft high in likelihood and impact, as laptops hold client records, and has since turned on full-disk encryption. How should the risk team update the rating MOST accurately?

options.A: Lower the likelihood, since encrypted laptops are less likely to be stolen
options.B: Lower the impact, since data on stolen laptops would stay unreadable
options.C: Remove the risk, since encryption leaves no remaining risk
options.D: Keep both ratings as they are until the next yearly review

questions.key_concept: Match each control to the factor it changes: encryption leaves theft just as likely but lowers the harm when it happens.
questions.pre_read: Separate the two factors: does the control make theft less likely, or make a theft do less harm?
questions.correct_explanation: Encryption does not deter thieves, who cannot see it, so the chance of a laptop being stolen is unchanged. What changes is the harm: without the key, client records stay unreadable, so a theft costs a device, not a data breach. The impact rating drops and the residual risk is recorded. Lowering likelihood, the runner-up, credits the control with an effect it does not have.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the overall risk does fall. But thieves cannot see encryption, so theft is no less likely; the control works by cutting the harm.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the data is now protected. But controls rarely remove risk entirely; lost devices and their cost remain as residual risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reviews follow a schedule. But a register should reflect a major control change when it happens, not months later.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a control as removing every risk, and D waits for the yearly review although the controls just changed.
Final two: B beats A because encryption changes what a theft costs, not whether a theft happens.
Exam cue: ask which factor a control moves. Locks and guards cut likelihood; encryption and backups cut impact.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'rate likelihood and impact separately; inherent risk before controls, residual risk after' (notes 1.2.3 Assessing Likelihood and Impact). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A junior analyst at a museum finds its donation page loads a script from an expired domain anyone could buy, and the marketing director owns the website. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Remove the live page's script today, then tell the marketing director
options.B: Rate the risk as low, since no attack has happened yet
options.C: Add the finding to the next quarterly project report
options.D: Log the risk in the register and alert the marketing director today

questions.key_concept: Anyone can raise a risk, but its owner decides the treatment; record it through the agreed channel instead of fixing it quietly.
questions.pre_read: Note who owns the website and what the analyst's role is. Ask who should decide how this risk is treated.
questions.correct_explanation: The analyst found a live risk on a system they do not own. Logging it in the register and alerting the marketing director today lets the owner decide the fix quickly and track it. Removing the script themselves, the runner-up, feels quicker, but a live change outside the owner's process could break donations and leaves no record of the risk or the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: removing the script would cut the risk. But it changes a live system the analyst does not own, outside change control and the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing has happened yet. But anyone could buy the domain today, and the analyst does not set ratings alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because findings belong in reports. But a quarterly report delays a live risk that its owner should see now.

tips: Eliminate: B rates the risk down alone, though anyone could buy the domain, and C delays a live risk to a later report.
Final two: D beats A because the owner decides and tracks the fix; a quiet change bypasses them and could break a live page.
Exam cue: you can raise any risk, but its owner decides what happens to it. Record it through the agreed channel; don't quietly fix someone else's system.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-01 (vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated and recorded); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'anyone can raise a risk; the owner decides; record it through the agreed channel' (notes 1.2.7 Risk Register, Ownership and Reporting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): key now alerts the owner today as well as logging the risk (blind test); neutral subtopic.

questions.question: After a risk review, a city council's leaders drop a plan to let an AI chatbot approve parking-fine refunds, and staff keep handling refunds. Which risk treatment is this MOST accurately?

options.A: Mitigation, because staff checks reduce the chance of errors
options.B: Transfer, because responsibility passes back to council staff
options.C: Avoidance, because the activity that created the risk will not happen
options.D: Acceptance, because leaders have formally decided on the outcome

questions.key_concept: Avoidance removes the activity that creates a risk; mitigation keeps the activity but adds controls that reduce the risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the council still does the risky activity in some form, or has stopped it.
questions.correct_explanation: Avoidance means not doing the activity that creates the risk. The council dropped the AI refund plan, so the risks it would have brought, such as wrong or manipulated approvals, never arise. Mitigation, the runner-up, would keep the chatbot approving refunds but add controls, such as staff checking each one. Staff carrying on as before adds no control to the AI; the AI is simply not used.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: staff handling refunds does limit errors. But mitigation keeps the risky activity and adds controls; here the AI plan was dropped.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the work stays with people. But transfer shifts financial impact to another party, such as an insurer; nobody outside takes anything on.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because leaders made a formal decision. But acceptance means going ahead and living with the risk; here the plan was stopped.

tips: Eliminate: B needs an outside party, such as an insurer, to take on impact, and D would mean going ahead with the plan and living with the risk.
Final two: C beats A because the AI plan was dropped; mitigation would keep the chatbot and add controls around it.
Exam cue: stopped or never started means avoid; kept with added controls means mitigate; shifted to an insurer means transfer; knowingly kept means accept.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-7 (Risk Response)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept: match the treatment to what happens to the risky activity' (notes 1.2.5 Risk Treatment Options). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A hospital board says it will take very little risk with patient safety, and the IT director sets a 30-minute monthly downtime limit for the patient-monitoring network. What is this limit MOST accurately?

options.A: A risk appetite statement
options.B: A risk tolerance level
options.C: A residual risk rating
options.D: A risk acceptance decision

questions.key_concept: Risk appetite is leaders' broad stance; risk tolerance is a measurable limit that puts appetite into practice for one objective.
questions.pre_read: Compare the board's statement with the IT director's figure. Which one is broad, and which one can be measured?
questions.correct_explanation: The board's statement of very little risk with patient safety is the risk appetite: broad and set by leaders. The 30-minute limit turns that stance into a measurable boundary for one system, which makes it a risk tolerance. Calling it appetite, the runner-up, misses the difference in level: appetite sets direction for the organization, while a tolerance is a number someone can check against.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the limit flows from the board's appetite. But appetite is the broad stance; a measurable limit for one network is a tolerance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the limit sits beside risk ratings. But residual risk is what remains after controls, not a limit leaders set in advance.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a limit sounds like a decision about risk. But acceptance is a risk owner's documented decision to keep a specific risk.

tips: Eliminate: C is the risk left after controls, and D is a risk owner's decision to keep a specific risk; neither is a limit set in advance.
Final two: B beats A because a measurable limit for one system is a tolerance; appetite is the board's broad stance above it.
Exam cue: appetite is broad words from leaders; tolerance is a number for a specific objective. If you can measure against it, it is tolerance.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'appetite is the broad stance leaders set; tolerance is the measurable limit for one objective' (notes 1.2.6 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and Acceptance). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A university's governing council is deciding what part it should play in cybersecurity. Which task BEST belongs to the council rather than to management?

options.A: Approving each new user's access to the student records system
options.B: Carrying out the yearly security risk assessment
options.C: Setting how much security risk the institution will accept
options.D: Writing the step-by-step procedure for nightly backups

questions.key_concept: Governance sets direction and oversees results; management runs daily security work, including individual access decisions.
questions.pre_read: Sort the tasks into direction and oversight versus day-to-day operations. Then ask which level each belongs to.
questions.correct_explanation: Governance sets direction and checks results: the council decides how much risk the university will accept, and management works within that limit. Approving each user's access to student records, the runner-up, feels like protecting what the council cares about, but it is daily operational work for data owners and managers. Pulling it up to the council would slow access without improving oversight.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the council is accountable for student data. But approving individual access requests is daily work for data owners and managers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because risk is the council's concern. But carrying out assessments is management's work; the council uses the results to set direction.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because backups protect the university. But step-by-step procedures are written and maintained by the teams that do the work.

tips: Eliminate: B and D are management's work, carrying out assessments and writing procedures, done within the direction the council sets.
Final two: C beats A because governing bodies set direction, such as risk appetite; approving each access request is operational work.
Exam cue: governance asks where we are going and whether we are getting there. If a task is daily, technical or step by step, management owns it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'governance sets direction and oversees; management runs daily security work' (notes 1.3.1 Security Governance and Its Roles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): re-angled away from the notes 1.3.1 worked example and its firewall-change trap.

questions.subtopic: 1.3 Governance. Laws, regulations and industry rules
questions.question: A coffee chain's IT team hears that the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) is a government law. Which description of PCI DSS is MOST accurate?

options.A: A government law that applies to every business that takes card payments
options.B: An optional guideline the chain may follow if it chooses
options.C: An industry standard the chain must meet under its card agreements
options.D: An ISO standard that binds a company once it is certified

questions.key_concept: PCI DSS is an industry standard, not a law; it binds merchants through their contracts with card brands and banks.
questions.pre_read: Ask who writes PCI DSS and how a business becomes bound by it. Law, contract and choice bind in different ways.
questions.correct_explanation: PCI DSS comes from the payment card industry's own standards council, not from a government. It binds merchants through their agreements with banks and card brands, so a chain that takes cards must meet it even though it is not legislation. Calling it optional, the runner-up, confuses 'not a law' with 'not mandatory': contracts can make a standard compulsory, with penalties for failing it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because PCI DSS is strict and widely required. But it is written by the card industry, not a legislature; contracts make it binding.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: PCI DSS is not a law. But the chain's card agreements require it, so meeting it is not a matter of choice.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ISO publishes well-known standards. But PCI DSS comes from the card industry's own council and binds through card agreements.

tips: Eliminate: A treats PCI DSS as legislation, and D credits it to ISO, but it is the card industry's own standard.
Final two: C beats B because contracts can make a standard mandatory; not being a law does not make it optional.
Exam cue: ask where a rule's force comes from. Laws bind by legislation, industry standards often by contract, frameworks by choice.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.31 (Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'industry rules such as PCI DSS bind through contracts, not legislation' (notes 1.3.2 Laws and Regulations). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from D to C (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A regional library service's security team has drafted a new remote-work security policy. Whose approval does the policy MOST need before it takes effect?

options.A: The security team that drafted the policy
options.B: The senior management team of the organization
options.C: The legal adviser who reviewed its wording
options.D: Each remote worker who must follow the new policy

questions.key_concept: Policies are drafted by the security team but approved by senior management, which gives them authority across the organization.
questions.pre_read: Separate who writes the policy from who gives it authority over the whole organization.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy is a mandatory statement for the whole organization, so it needs the authority of senior management, who approve it and stand behind it. The security team, the runner-up, is right to draft and maintain the policy because it has the expertise. But a team approving its own draft gives it no authority over other departments, and leaders have not accepted the duties it creates.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the security team writes and maintains the policy. But approving its own draft gives it no organization-wide authority.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because legal review checks a policy's wording. But reviewing a draft is advice; it does not give the policy authority over staff.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because remote workers must follow it. But staff acknowledge a policy rather than approve it, or anyone could veto a rule.

tips: Eliminate: C reviewed the wording and D must follow the policy; neither gives a policy authority over the whole library service.
Final two: B beats A because the security team drafts policy, but senior management approves it and gives it authority.
Exam cue: drafting and approving are different roles. Policies come from leadership; the security team writes, maintains and explains them.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.1 (Policies for information security); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (cybersecurity policy is established, communicated and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'policies are drafted by the security team and approved by senior management' (notes 1.3.4 Security Policies). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): strawman help-desk option replaced; key no longer alone echoes the stem.

questions.question: A law firm's IT manager owns a backup procedure keeping copies 7 days, though the standard every procedure must meet requires 30, and operators may set retention. Which action by the backup technician is BEST?

options.A: Follow the 7-day procedure and tell the IT manager
options.B: Keep copies for 30 days and tell the IT manager
options.C: Edit the procedure to say 30 days and carry on
options.D: Treat the 30-day rule as advice the procedure overrides

questions.key_concept: A procedure carries out its standard and cannot lower it; follow the higher document and report the conflict to the procedure's owner.
questions.pre_read: Place the two documents in the hierarchy, then ask who may change the lower one.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards are mandatory, and a procedure only sets out steps for meeting them, so it cannot lower the 30-day requirement. Operators may set retention, so the technician keeps 30 days of copies and tells the IT manager, who owns the procedure. Following the 7-day procedure and reporting it, the runner-up, sounds in role, but it breaks the standard, and copies deleted early cannot be brought back.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: following the procedure and telling its owner sounds in role. But a procedure cannot lower its standard, and copies deleted after 7 days cannot be recovered.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 30 days is the right figure. But the IT manager owns the procedure; the technician should report the conflict, not rewrite it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the procedure is more detailed. But standards are mandatory; only guidelines are advice, and detail does not outrank a standard.

tips: Eliminate: C rewrites a document the technician does not own, and D treats a mandatory standard as optional advice, which describes a guideline.
Final two: B beats A because a procedure cannot lower the standard above it; operators may set retention, so the technician meets 30 days and reports the gap.
Exam cue: when documents conflict, follow the higher one and report the gap to the owner of the lower one. Policy, then standard, then procedure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Standards, Guidelines, and Procedures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each document must agree with the one above it; if they conflict, follow the higher one where your role allows and report the conflict to the lower document's owner' (notes 1.3.5 Standards, Procedures and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): replaced a repeat of 035's lesson with the document hierarchy (procedure versus standard). Blind re-test fix (30 Oct 2026): stem states operators may set retention; A is the runner-up. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): concept quote corrected to the rule the item tests (notes test); relabeled analysis, since it weighs the standard, the procedure and the operator's latitude (CD-21).

questions.subtopic: 1.4 Security controls. What a control is
questions.question: A firm installed a data-loss prevention tool two years ago; its rules still date from installation, and nobody is responsible for it. What should the security team do FIRST?

options.A: Assign an owner to test and tune the tool regularly
options.B: Run a single test of the tool's rules this month
options.C: Ask management to replace it with a newer product
options.D: Remove the tool, since it has reported no incidents

questions.key_concept: A control keeps reducing risk only if someone owns it, tests it and updates it; an unowned control quietly stops working.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the tool may no longer be reducing risk, and what would keep it working from now on.
questions.correct_explanation: Controls need an owner who tests and updates them, or they drift out of step with the data and threats they were bought for. Assigning an owner with a regular test-and-tune duty fixes the cause. A single test this month, the runner-up, shows how far the rules have drifted, but with nobody responsible afterward nothing keeps them current, and the same gap returns.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: testing shows whether the rules still work. But one test with nobody responsible afterward leaves the tool to drift again.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because newer products sound stronger. But a new tool without upkeep would decay the same way; the gap is ownership.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool reports nothing. But outdated rules may be missing leaks, so silence proves nothing about the risk.

tips: Eliminate: C buys a product that would decay the same way without upkeep, and D reads silence from outdated rules as safety.
Final two: A beats B because ongoing ownership keeps the control working; a one-time test finds the drift but does not stop it returning.
Exam cue: a control is only as good as its upkeep. Look for an owner, regular testing and monitoring, not a new purchase.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'controls need owners, testing and monitoring, or they quietly stop working' (notes 1.4.1 What a Security Control Is). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A charity gives new volunteers donor database access on day one, but nobody explains how donor data may be used. What should the volunteer manager add as the BEST administrative control?

options.A: Rules for using donor data, signed by each volunteer before first use
options.B: Encryption of the donor database on the charity's server
options.C: A locked office for the computer that holds donor data
options.D: A donor-data session in each volunteer's yearly awareness training

questions.key_concept: Administrative controls set expectations: people should know and acknowledge the rules for data before they can use it.
questions.pre_read: Note when volunteers get access and when they learn the rules. Look for the control that closes that gap in time.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules of behavior are an administrative control: they tell people how data may be used, and a signed acknowledgment before access means nobody starts without knowing them. The yearly awareness session, the runner-up, is also administrative and worthwhile, but volunteers who join after it would use donor data for months without guidance. Encryption and a locked office teach nobody the rules.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects the database. But it is a technical control, and it cannot tell volunteers which uses are allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because physical security matters. But a locked office is a physical control, and volunteers would still not know the rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: training is an administrative control. But a yearly session can leave new volunteers using donor data for months first.

tips: Eliminate: B is a technical control and C a physical one; neither tells volunteers how donor data may be used.
Final two: A beats D because the rules are acknowledged before access; a yearly session can come months after volunteers start.
Exam cue: administrative controls shape what people know and do. Check timing too: rules should be acknowledged before access is granted.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'administrative controls are the policies, procedures and people practices that direct how security is handled' (notes 1.4.3 Administrative Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.4 Security controls. Controls for AI tools
questions.question: A parcel carrier's AI assistant drafts damage-claim replies for staff to approve, but nobody can tell how a disputed reply was produced. Which control should the security analyst propose to BEST close this gap?

options.A: Log each reply's model version, prompt and approver
options.B: Save each approved reply with its claim number
options.C: Filter each prompt to remove customers' account numbers
options.D: Test each new model version on past claims before use

questions.key_concept: To trace what an AI did, record which model version and prompt produced each output, and who approved it, not just the output.
questions.pre_read: Picture a customer disputing one reply months from now. Ask what each option would let staff find out about that reply.
questions.correct_explanation: Tracing what an AI did means recording what produced each output, not just the output. Logging the model version, the prompt and the approving staff member for every reply lets the carrier explain a disputed reply and find a faulty version or prompt. Saving each approved reply with its claim number, the runner-up, shows what each customer received, but not which version or prompt wrote it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the saved reply and claim number show what each customer received. But they show the result, not the model version or prompt that produced it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because filtering prompts is a real AI safeguard. But it keeps personal data out of the model; it records nothing about how a reply was made.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing each version catches errors before use. But it checks quality in advance; it cannot show which version wrote a reply already sent.

tips: Eliminate: C filters prompts to protect privacy, and D tests versions before use; neither records how a given reply was produced.
Final two: A beats B because tracing needs the model version and prompt behind each reply; a saved reply with its claim number keeps the output but not its source.
Exam cue: to trace what an AI did, record which model, prompt and person produced each output, not just the output itself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 3.4 (Accountable and Transparent); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-3 (Content of Audit Records)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'log prompts with the model version used' and 'limit and log what AI agents can do' (notes 1.4.7 Controls for AI Tools), with 'make every action traceable' (notes 1.1.9 AI and the Core Security Concepts). Original parcel carrier scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review re-angle (31 Oct 2026, CD-09): the earlier human-review lesson duplicated cc_d3_019, so the item now tests tracing what an AI did (a blueprint D1 AI angle with no item); key stays A, the stem says 'propose', and no option uses encryption. Kept under 1.4.7, the notes home of logging AI tools, so that sub-topic keeps an item and section 1.1 does not grow further. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026): the setting moved from a water utility to a parcel carrier, since Domain 2 notes 2.4.7 now use a water utility's billing assistant (rule 8), and the stem asks what to propose 'to BEST close this gap'. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026, blind test): option B now keeps each reply with its claim number, so the runner-up also records context and only the key records how a reply was produced; this removes the plain-English shortcut from 'how it was produced'.

questions.question: After ransomware locks a school's file server, the IT team wipes it and restores last night's offline backup. Which control function does the restore MOST accurately serve?

options.A: A preventive control
options.B: A detective control
options.C: A recovery control
options.D: A deterrent control

questions.key_concept: Recovery controls restore normal operations after an incident; backups do not stop an attack, they let you return from one.
questions.pre_read: Look at when the restore happens compared with the attack, and what it achieves for the school.
questions.correct_explanation: The restore happens after the attack and brings the file server back to normal service, which is what recovery controls do; recovery is a kind of corrective control. Preventive, the runner-up, is tempting because backups feel like protection, but the restore did nothing to stop the ransomware running. Prevention blocks an incident; recovery limits how long its damage lasts.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: backups are planned in advance, which feels preventive. But the ransomware still ran; the restore acts afterward to bring service back.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the team knew the server was locked. But detective controls find incidents, such as alarms; a restore finds nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because good backups can make ransom demands pointless. But deterrent controls discourage attempts in advance, such as warning signs.

tips: Eliminate: B finds incidents and D discourages attempts; a restore does neither.
Final two: C beats A because the restore acts after the attack to bring service back; preventive controls stop the attack itself.
Exam cue: place a control on the timeline. Before: deter or prevent. During: detect. After: correct and recover.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-10 (System Recovery and Reconstitution); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'control function is what a control does: prevent, detect, correct, deter, recover or compensate' (notes 1.4.5 Control Functions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: Small amounts of medicine keep vanishing from a pharmacy's locked cabinet, and all three pharmacists hold keys. Which addition should the pharmacy manager make to BEST layer the cabinet's protection?

options.A: Fit a second key lock and give the pharmacists its keys
options.B: Replace the lock with a high-security, pick-resistant model
options.C: Post a sign warning that theft of medicine is a crime
options.D: Require a signed log of each opening, matched to stock

questions.key_concept: Layering adds controls of different types and functions; when the people holding keys are the risk, more locks add nothing.
questions.pre_read: Notice who can already open the cabinet. Then ask which option still works against those people.
questions.correct_explanation: Everyone who could be taking medicine already holds a key, so any extra or stronger lock fails the same way. A signed log checked against stock counts adds an administrative, detective layer: missing stock is spotted and tied to the openings around it. The warning sign, the runner-up, does add a new function, deterrence, but pharmacists already know theft is a crime.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because two locks sound twice as strong. But the same pharmacists hold both keys, so the second lock stops nobody who matters here.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a better lock resists picking. But nobody is picking the lock; whoever takes the medicine opens it with their own key.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a sign adds deterrence, a different function from the lock. But insiders already know the rules, and a sign cannot trace a loss.

tips: Eliminate: A and B add more of the same preventive control, and the people with keys pass through any lock.
Final two: D beats C because a reconciled log detects losses and links them to openings; a sign only discourages, and insiders know the rules.
Exam cue: layering means different types and functions aimed at the actual threat. If insiders hold the keys, add detection and accountability, not more locks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Appendix A Glossary (defense in depth)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'layering mixes control types and functions so one failure does not leave the asset unprotected' (notes 1.4.6 Layering and Compensating Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A client asks a consulting firm's certified tester to include its payroll provider's web portal in a penetration test, but the provider has not given permission. What is the tester's BEST response?

options.A: Test the portal, since the client is paying for the work
options.B: Test the portal lightly so the provider does not notice
options.C: Decline the whole engagement so that no unlawful testing happens
options.D: Exclude the portal unless the provider authorizes testing in writing

questions.key_concept: Diligent service never extends to unlawful acts: testing needs the system owner's permission, but the authorized work can go ahead.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the portal and who can authorize testing it. Then ask what the client can still lawfully receive.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing a system without its owner's permission can be illegal, whoever is paying, so the portal stays out unless the provider agrees in writing. The client's own systems can still be tested, which is diligent, competent service. Declining the whole engagement, the runner-up, is lawful but gives up work that can be done properly; the canons point to the lawful course that still serves the client.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because serving the client is a professional duty. But a client cannot authorize testing a system it does not own.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a light test seems low risk. But unauthorized testing is unauthorized however light, and hiding it is dishonest.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: refusing avoids any unlawful testing. But the client's own systems can be tested lawfully, so walking away fails the service owed.

tips: Eliminate: A and B test a system its owner has not authorized, which is unlawful however the client pays or the test is run.
Final two: D beats C because it keeps the work lawful and still serves the client; declining everything gives up work that is authorized.
Exam cue: when part of a request would be unlawful, do the lawful part and get written authorization for the rest. Serving the principal never requires breaking the law.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'stay within your authority: test only with the system owner's written permission, whoever is paying' (notes 1.5.4 Applying the Canons to Dilemmas), with acting legally and serving principals from notes 1.5.3 The ISC2 Code of Ethics. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): 1.5.4 cited first, as it holds the deciding rule (notes test); relabeled application, since one authorization rule decides it (CD-21).

questions.question: A bakery owner who hired a certified consultant files a sworn written complaint naming the canon on competent service, but attaches no supporting evidence. What will the ethics committee MOST likely do?

options.A: Investigate the consultant's work to find the missing evidence
options.B: Suspend the consultant's certification until the facts are settled
options.C: Close the complaint unless it makes a solid initial case
options.D: Reject the complaint because clients lack standing under that canon

questions.key_concept: The ethics committee does not investigate; it weighs the sworn evidence submitted and closes complaints that make no solid initial case.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the committee can and cannot do with a complaint, and what it relies on to act.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee is not an investigative body and cannot compel testimony; it considers only what complainants submit in writing. If the submission does not make a solid initial (prima facie) case, it closes the complaint without prejudice. Investigating, the runner-up, is what many expect of a disciplinary body, but this committee has no investigative resources, so gathering evidence is the complainant's job.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many oversight bodies investigate. But this committee has no investigative role or resources; it weighs only the evidence it is sent.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the concern is serious. But the committee only recommends; the board decides discipline, and doubt about the facts favors the respondent.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because standing rules vary by canon. But clients are principals, and principals may complain about the canon on competent service.

tips: Eliminate: B skips the respondent's rights and the board's decision, and D overlooks that clients are principals with standing under that canon.
Final two: C beats A because the committee does not investigate; without enough submitted evidence, it closes the complaint.
Exam cue: the ethics committee weighs sworn, written evidence it is given. It does not investigate, and it closes complaints that make no prima facie case.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (standing of complainant and form of complaints)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'complaints are sworn, written, name the canon and need standing; the committee does not investigate' (notes 1.5.5 Ethics Complaints and Enforcement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): re-angled from the notes 1.5.5 worked example (standing) to the committee's role; key moves to B. Key letter moved from B to C (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.subtopic: 1.5 Professional conduct. Due care and due diligence
questions.question: An architecture firm patched known flaws promptly, kept tested offline backups and trained staff, yet ransomware entered through a flaw its software vendor had not yet found. Which statement about the firm is MOST accurate?

options.A: It failed due care, since the attack still succeeded
options.B: It failed due diligence, since the flaw went undiscovered
options.C: It met due care, since it took reasonable precautions
options.D: It met due care, since the vendor is responsible for the flaw

questions.key_concept: Due care is judged by an organization's own conduct, not by the outcome or by who caused the flaw.
questions.pre_read: List what the firm did before the attack, then what happened. Check each option against both lists.
questions.correct_explanation: Due care asks whether an organization acted as a prudent one would, judged by its conduct, not the outcome. Prompt patching, offline backups and staff training were due care, and testing the backups was diligence; no one can patch a flaw the vendor has not found. Blaming the vendor, the runner-up, gets the verdict right for the wrong reason: without those precautions the firm would fail due care, whoever wrote the flaw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a successful attack feels like proof that something was missed. But due care is judged by conduct, and prompt patching, offline backups and staff training are prudent conduct.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because diligence means finding out about risks. But diligence cannot require finding a flaw the vendor itself had not found, and the firm did test its backups.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the verdict is right. But due care rests on the firm's own conduct; a firm that skipped patching and backups would fail it, whoever wrote the flaw.

tips: Eliminate: A judges due care by the outcome instead of the firm's conduct, and B expects diligence to find a flaw even the vendor had not found.
Final two: C beats D because due care rests on the firm's own precautions; whose flaw it was would not excuse a firm that skipped patching or backups.
Exam cue: judge due care by the organization's own conduct, not by the outcome or by who caused the flaw. Ask what a prudent organization would have done beforehand.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the test is what a reasonable, informed professional would have done, judged by conduct, not by whether an attack still succeeded' (notes 1.5.2 Due Care and Due Diligence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review re-angle (31 Oct 2026, CD-10): the earlier 'knowing without acting fails due care' lesson repeated cc_d1_017, so the item now tests judging due care by conduct, not outcome (two facts that pull apart: prudent conduct and a successful attack); key stays C. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): option D is now a second 'met due care' option with a wrong reason (the vendor's responsibility), so the key is no longer the odd one out and the final two differ only by the reason; the key no longer uses the definition word 'prudent'; wrong_explanations.B no longer says an unknown flaw cannot be found (the attacker found it); the runner-up is now D. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026, audit): the explanations no longer count backup testing as due care; testing the backups is diligence, as notes 1.5.2 teach.

questions.question: A help desk analyst, whose procedure covers fixing over-broad permissions, finds the accounts manager's Confidential folder of landlords' bank details open to all staff on an encrypted file server. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Relabel the folder Internal and record the change in a ticket
options.B: Leave the access as is, since the server encrypts stored files
options.C: Restrict the folder to approved users and record it in a ticket
options.D: Copy the bank details to a restricted drive the help desk controls

questions.key_concept: Encryption at rest protects data on stolen disks; against users the system lets in, confidentiality depends on access limited to need to know.
questions.pre_read: Note who owns the folder, what the help desk procedure covers and who can open the folder now.
questions.correct_explanation: Restricting the folder to approved users ends the exposure, and the procedure lets the help desk do it, with a ticket that keeps the change traceable for the accounts manager. Leaving the access, the runner-up, trusts encryption to do access control's job: encryption at rest protects files if a disk or backup is stolen, but the server decrypts them for every user it lets in, so all staff could still read the bank details.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the label would match the access and the ticket records it. But only the data owner sets classification; lowering it to fit a mistake hides the exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: encryption does protect stored files. But the server decrypts them for anyone it lets in, so it cannot stop staff who were wrongly given access.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it moves the data somewhere locked. But it copies bank details to people with no need to know and leaves the original folder open.

tips: Eliminate: A lowers a classification only the data owner may set, and D copies bank details to staff with no need to know.
Final two: C beats B because the server decrypts files for every user it lets in; only narrowing access keeps the bank details from staff with no need to know.
Exam cue: encryption at rest guards against stolen disks and backups. Against people the system lets in, confidentiality depends on access control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability)
related_concepts: Encryption at rest versus access control
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'access control, guided by need to know and least privilege, keeps the reader list short' (notes 1.1.2 Confidentiality). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, audit): re-angled from 'the procedure assigns the fix, so do it' (a lesson cc_d4_044 already teaches) to a confidentiality point, that encryption at rest does not replace access control; the audit's suggested preventive-versus-detective runner-up was not used because cc_d3_038 already teaches it. Cross-domain gate (31 Oct 2026): option A now also records its change in a ticket, so the record clause is no longer on the key alone.

questions.question: An intruder replaced a thermostat maker's firmware download and its posted hash with a malicious file and matching hash. Which change should the product security team propose as BEST so customers can spot a swap?

options.A: Digitally sign each firmware file with the maker's private key
options.B: Post each file's hash on a second page of the same site
options.C: Serve the maker's download page over HTTPS with a valid certificate
options.D: Encrypt each firmware file before posting it for download

questions.key_concept: When many people must check a file's source, use a digital signature: only the maker can sign, and anyone can verify with the public key.
questions.pre_read: Consider what an intruder who controls the download page can change, and what each protection needs to work.
questions.correct_explanation: A digital signature is made with the maker's private key, which the intruder does not hold, and customers check it with the maker's public key from a certificate or built into the thermostat, not from the download page, so a swapped file fails. HTTPS, the runner-up, protects the download in transit and shows which server sent it; it cannot tell a genuine file from a fake sitting on a server the intruder controls.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it separates the hash from the file. But an intruder who can change one page can change another, and anyone can recompute a plain hash.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: HTTPS shows the file came from the maker's server. But the intruder controls that server, so HTTPS delivers the fake as safely as the real file.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects files. But it hides content without proving who made a file, and customers would need the key to open it anyway.

tips: Eliminate: B posts a plain hash on the same site the intruder already controls, and D hides content without proving who made the file.
Final two: A beats C because only the maker's private key makes a valid signature; HTTPS only protects the trip from a server the intruder already controls.
Exam cue: HTTPS protects data in transit, not the file sitting on the server. To prove who made a file, look for a digital signature checked with a trusted public key.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.3.2 (Public Key Electronic Signatures: anyone can verify with the signer's public key)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a digital signature uses the signer's private key, which only they hold; anyone can check it with the public key' (notes 1.1.7 Non-Repudiation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): explanation now says the public key must come from a trusted source, not the page the intruder controls. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): explanation now says where a trustworthy public key comes from (a certificate or the device), not the page the intruder controls. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): runner-up C changed from a shared keyed hash, which repeated cc_d1_002 and cc_d1_050, to HTTPS on the compromised server; 'maker' now appears in C as well as the key, and the key is no longer the shortest option.

questions.question: A city's tax help chat crashes every filing-deadline week, when genuine visits from taxpayers triple. What should the IT manager propose to BEST protect the chat's availability?

options.A: Encrypt every chat session between taxpayers and staff
options.B: Filter out traffic above normal daily levels that week
options.C: Add server capacity sized for the deadline-week peak
options.D: Back up the chat server's data every hour that week

questions.key_concept: Availability needs enough capacity for known peaks; filtering suits attack traffic, not genuine demand.
questions.pre_read: Note what causes the outages and who is sending the extra traffic.
questions.correct_explanation: The outages come from genuine demand that outgrows the service, so the fix is enough capacity for the known peak, planned and tested before deadline week. Filtering, the runner-up, is a denial-of-service defense: here the extra traffic is real taxpayers, so capping it at normal levels would turn away the very people the chat exists to serve.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because chats may hold tax details worth protecting. But encryption serves confidentiality; it adds no capacity and may add load.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: filtering protects availability against floods of bogus requests. But these visitors are genuine taxpayers, so dropping traffic above normal levels would deny them service.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because backups protect availability after data loss. But the chat crashes from overload; restoring data does not keep it answering during the peak.

tips: Eliminate: D restores lost data and A protects secrecy; neither keeps an overloaded service running.
Final two: C beats B because the surge is genuine demand; filtering suits attack traffic and here would turn real taxpayers away.
Exam cue: match the availability control to the cause. Predictable genuine peaks need capacity; floods of bogus traffic need filtering.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-04 (adequate resource capacity to ensure availability is maintained); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability)
related_concepts: Denial of service versus genuine demand
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'patching and capacity planning prevent faults and overload' (notes 1.1.4 Availability). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from D to C (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: role sweep: 'IT lead' became 'IT manager'.

questions.question: A support line caller gives a bike-share member's name and the account number printed on every receipt, then asks to change the account's email. How should the support agent MOST accurately treat these details?

options.A: As two separate factors, so no further check is needed
options.B: As identification only, with no authentication yet
options.C: As proof of something the member knows
options.D: As authorization to change the account's details

questions.key_concept: Identifiers such as names and account numbers only claim an identity; authentication needs proof the claimant controls.
questions.pre_read: Separate identification, authentication and authorization, then place what the caller has done so far.
questions.correct_explanation: A name and account number identify which account the caller means, but neither is a secret only the member holds; both appear on every receipt. They are a claim, and the agent still needs proof, such as a code sent to contact details already on file. Treating them as a knowledge factor, the runner-up, confuses an identifier with a secret.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because two details were given. But factors are counted by type, not number, and identifiers are not authentication factors.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the caller does know these details. But a knowledge factor must be secret; names and account numbers are identifiers, and both appear on every receipt.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the caller gave the right details. But authorization comes only after identity is proven, and nothing has been proven yet.

tips: Eliminate: D grants rights before identity is proven, and A counts details instead of factor types.
Final two: B beats C because a name and an account number printed on every receipt are identifiers; a knowledge factor must be a secret.
Exam cue: identification claims, authentication proves, authorization grants. Anything printed on a receipt or bill is an identifier, not a secret.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-4 (Identifier Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-8 (Identification and Authentication (Non-organizational Users))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'identification comes first: the user claims an identity, such as a username' (notes 1.1.5 Authentication). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): key B reworded so it no longer reads as the only cautious option. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): A now carries a rival negation, so key B is not the only negated option.

questions.question: A bakery cooperative's purchasing lead signs stock write-offs with a private key stored in a folder the whole office can open; one large write-off looks fraudulent. What should the security analyst MOST accurately conclude?

options.A: The purchasing lead cannot deny it, since their private key made it
options.B: The write-off is genuine, since the signed record is unchanged
options.C: The signature cannot show the purchasing lead signed the write-off
options.D: Encrypting write-offs with a shared key would have named the signer

questions.key_concept: Non-repudiation holds only while the private key stays under its owner's sole control; a key others can copy proves nothing about who signed.
questions.pre_read: Ask who could have used the signing key, then what a valid signature can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: Non-repudiation needs a signing key that only one person controls. Here the key sits in a folder anyone in the office could copy, so a valid signature proves the write-off was signed with that key but not that the purchasing lead signed it. The runner-up is right that a private key made the signature, but a key anyone in the office could copy cannot tie the action to one person.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a digital signature normally stops the signer denying it. But only while one person controls the private key; anyone in the office could copy this one.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because an intact record shows nothing was altered. But integrity says the write-off was not changed after signing; it cannot show it was honest or who made it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption feels like proof of the sender. But a shared key is held by several people, so any of them could have encrypted the write-off.

tips: Eliminate: B treats an unchanged record as proof the write-off is genuine, and D relies on a shared key, which any holder could use.
Final two: C beats A because a key anyone in the office could copy cannot tie the signature to the purchasing lead.
Exam cue: for non-repudiation, ask who else could reach the private key. If others could copy it, the signature names no one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-10 (Non-repudiation); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.3.2 (Public Key Electronic Signatures: anyone can verify with the signer's public key)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'non-repudiation needs something only one person controls, plus a record nobody can quietly change' (notes 1.1.7 Non-Repudiation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): re-angled from five shift leads sharing one certificate (the shape of cc_d1_003) to a private key left where the whole office can copy it; A now names the purchasing lead too, so the stem's role is not echoed in the key alone.

questions.question: A dairy cooperative's operations manager deployed an AI agent, built on a vendor's model and hosted by IT, that wrongly canceled a farmer's contract; the manager says it decided alone. Who is MOST accurately accountable?

options.A: The operations manager who deployed the agent
options.B: Nobody, since no human made the decision
options.C: The AI vendor that built the agent's model
options.D: The IT team that runs the agent's servers

questions.key_concept: Accountability for an AI agent's actions stays with the organization and the named human owner who deployed it.
questions.pre_read: List who built, hosts, deployed and uses the agent, then ask who answers for its decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Accountability for an AI agent's actions stays with people: the organization that runs it, through the named owner who deployed it and set its permissions. The vendor, the runner-up, may owe the cooperative under contract for a faulty model, but the cooperative chose to let the agent cancel contracts, and it answers to the farmer for that decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because no person clicked cancel. But accountability does not pass to software; every agent needs a named human owner who answers for it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a faulty model may give the cooperative a claim against its vendor. But the cooperative chose to deploy the agent with this power, so it stays accountable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IT team keeps the agent running. But hosting is a custodian's job; custodians run systems for owners and do not answer for business decisions.

tips: Eliminate: D confuses the custodian who hosts the agent with its owner, and B lets accountability pass to software.
Final two: A beats C because the cooperative deployed the agent with power to cancel contracts; a vendor's contract duties do not move that accountability.
Exam cue: an AI agent never owns its actions. Look for the named human owner; vendors and hosts do not take the accountability away.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 3.4 (Accountable and Transparent); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each AI agent needs its own identity, limited permissions and logs, tied to an accountable human owner' (notes 1.1.9 AI and the Core Security Concepts). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, audit): the stem now states the named owner and the IT hosting, so the deciding fact and every option's role appear in the stem. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): the stem no longer calls the operations manager the named owner, which answered the question; each option's party (deployed, built, hosts) now appears in the stem evenly.

questions.question: A seed bank keeps its freezer controllers in a basement beside a river that floods most springs. Which item MOST accurately describes the vulnerability the risk analyst should record?

options.A: The chance that a flood reaches the basement this year
options.B: The river that floods the area most springs
options.C: The loss of stored seeds if the controllers fail
options.D: The controllers' basement location below the flood line

questions.key_concept: A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can exploit; natural events such as floods are threats, not vulnerabilities.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option into threat, vulnerability, likelihood or impact before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use. The weakness here is where the controllers sit: low, in a basement the river can reach. The river, the runner-up, is the threat, the thing that causes harm; nobody can stop it flooding, so risk is lowered by moving or raising the controllers. The yearly chance is likelihood, and lost seeds are the impact.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it describes the risk in numbers. But a yearly chance is the likelihood, one part of rating the risk, not the weakness.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the flood is what would do the damage. But that makes it the threat; the weakness it exploits is the controllers' low location.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is what the seed bank fears most. But lost seeds are the impact, the harm if the threat succeeds.

tips: Eliminate: A is the likelihood and C is the impact; both rate the risk rather than name a weakness.
Final two: D beats B because the river is the threat that causes harm; the weakness it exploits is where the controllers sit.
Exam cue: sort each risk statement into four boxes: threat (the cause, including floods and fire), vulnerability (the weakness), likelihood (the chance) and impact (the harm).
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix D Table D-2 (Taxonomy of Threat Sources: adversarial, accidental, structural and environmental)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use, such as unpatched software' (notes 1.2.1 Threats, Vulnerabilities and Risk). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): stem ends on the priority word plainly; C now also says 'controllers', so the stem noun is not echoed in key D alone.

questions.question: Working within the risk appetite its leaders set, a boat-hire company's risk team has listed its risks and rated each for likelihood and impact. Which lifecycle step MOST logically comes next?

options.A: Monitor each rated risk for changes in threats and systems
options.B: Frame the context by setting the company's risk appetite
options.C: Close the register, since rating the risks completes the cycle
options.D: Treat each rated risk by choosing how to respond to it

questions.key_concept: After risks are identified and assessed, the next lifecycle step is treatment; monitoring follows and the cycle repeats.
questions.pre_read: Place what the team has already done on the risk lifecycle before choosing the step that follows.
questions.correct_explanation: The lifecycle runs frame, identify, assess, treat and monitor. The team has identified and assessed, so the next step is treatment: deciding for each risk whether to avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept it, within the appetite already set. Monitoring, the runner-up, is a real and ongoing step, but it watches risks after a response is chosen; there is nothing yet to track.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: monitoring is part of the cycle and never stops. But it follows treatment; without a chosen response there is no plan to track.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because framing comes before everything else. But the stem says leaders already set the appetite, so this step is done.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rating feels like the finish line. But a rated risk with no response is unmanaged, and the cycle keeps repeating.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats framing that leaders already finished, and C stops the cycle before any risk has a response.
Final two: D beats A because treatment comes straight after assessment; monitoring tracks responses that do not exist yet.
Exam cue: learn the order frame, identify, assess, treat, monitor, then repeat. Place the stem's facts on that loop to find the next step.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 2.1 (Components of Risk Management: frame, assess, respond and monitor); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'treat each risk: avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept' (notes 1.2.2 The Risk Management Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): key B lengthened so it is no longer clearly the shortest option. Key letter moved from B to D (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A regional newspaper's remote-access gateway has a known, unpatched flaw, and a national cyber agency now warns that attackers have begun exploiting it. Which rating should the newspaper's analyst change MOST directly?

options.A: Likelihood rises, since attackers are now going after the flaw
options.B: Neither changes until the flaw is exploited at the newspaper
options.C: Impact rises, since attacks now make any breach more serious
options.D: The asset's value rises, since attackers now target it

questions.key_concept: New threat activity raises likelihood; impact changes only when the harm an attack would cause changes.
questions.pre_read: Separate the chance of an attack from the harm it would cause, then test the new fact against each.
questions.correct_explanation: Likelihood weighs threat activity, how easy a weakness is to use and the controls in place. Active exploitation means capable attackers now target this exact flaw, so an attack on the newspaper is more likely. Impact, the runner-up, measures the harm if an attack succeeds; a break-in through the gateway would hurt just as much as before, so that rating stays.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing has happened here yet. But ratings describe what could happen; waiting for an attack at the newspaper means rating too late.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: active attacks feel more serious. But impact is the harm if an attack succeeds, and that harm is the same as before; only the chance has grown.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because attackers' interest feels like value. But asset value is what the gateway is worth to the newspaper, which has not changed.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for harm before rating it, and D mixes attacker interest with what the asset is worth to the newspaper.
Final two: A beats C because active exploitation raises the chance of an attack; the harm one would cause is unchanged.
Exam cue: threat activity, exposure and weak controls move likelihood. Harm to people, money and operations moves impact. Change only the factor the new fact touches.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'likelihood weighs threat activity, how easy the weakness is to use and existing controls' (notes 1.2.3 Assessing Likelihood and Impact). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, audit and blind test): the new threat fact is now a national agency's warning rather than attacks 'at other' organizations, which retold cc_d1_005; the key is no longer the longest option.

questions.subtopic: 1.2 Risk management. Choosing an analysis method
questions.question: A chain of garden centers must rank 40 newly found risks for its leaders by Friday and has almost no loss history. Which approach is BEST for its risk analyst to use?

options.A: Rank each risk by its impact alone, from highest down
options.B: Calculate the annualized loss expectancy for each of the 40 risks
options.C: Rate each risk's likelihood and impact as high, medium or low
options.D: Rank the risks by how much each fix would cost

questions.key_concept: Qualitative analysis ranks many risks quickly with judgment; quantitative analysis needs reliable data and suits specific spending decisions.
questions.pre_read: Note how many risks there are, how much time the team has and what data exists.
questions.correct_explanation: Qualitative rating is fast, needs only informed judgment and helps leaders compare many risks, which suits 40 risks, a Friday deadline and almost no loss data. Annualized loss expectancy, the runner-up, needs reliable values and frequencies; without loss history the figures would be guesses that look precise. Numbers suit a later decision on funding one specific control.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because impact is what leaders fear most. But ranking needs likelihood too; a severe but very rare risk would outrank a likely, moderate one.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: dollar figures can justify spending. But they need reliable data and time; guessed inputs for 40 risks would look precise while being wrong.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cost matters later. But fix cost is a treatment question; ranking needs each risk's likelihood and impact first.

tips: Eliminate: D ranks by the price of fixes and A by impact alone; ranking a risk needs both likelihood and impact.
Final two: C beats B because quantitative figures need data and time the team lacks; qualitative levels rank many risks quickly.
Exam cue: many risks, little data and a short deadline point to qualitative. One investment decision with good data points to quantitative.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: quantitative assessments support cost-benefit analysis of risk responses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'use numbers when a spending decision needs them and levels when speed matters' (notes 1.2.4 Qualitative and Quantitative Analysis). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, audit): option A, ranking by discovery order, was a strawman; it now ranks by impact alone, a real beginner shortcut. Cross-domain gate (31 Oct 2026): setting moved from a city parks department to a garden-center chain to cut repeated local-government settings.

questions.question: An auction house's junior analyst sees that the fix for a risk the head of sales owns is installed; the register lets only risk owners close entries. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Mark the entry closed and note the evidence in the register
options.B: Delete the entry, since the risk no longer needs tracking
options.C: Lower the entry's rating until the head of sales reviews it
options.D: Send the evidence to the head of sales and request closure

questions.key_concept: Closing a risk entry is the risk owner's decision: the analyst supplies evidence the fix works, and the owner signs off closure and residual risk.
questions.pre_read: Note who owns the risk and what the register says about closing entries.
questions.correct_explanation: The register gives closure to the risk owner, so the analyst's job is to give the head of sales the evidence that the fix works and let them close it. Marking it closed, the runner-up, looks efficient and keeps a record, but it takes a decision the register reserves for the owner, who may want the fix tested first or residual risk recorded.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the evidence would be recorded. But the register lets only risk owners close entries, and the owner may want testing or residual risk noted first.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the fix is in. But deleting erases the history of the risk and its treatment, which later reviews and reports rely on.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the risk does look smaller. But the risk owner signs off ratings; a junior analyst re-rating before the owner reviews it bypasses them.

tips: Eliminate: B erases the record that reviews rely on, and C changes a rating the risk owner must sign off.
Final two: D beats A because the register reserves closure for the risk owner; the analyst supplies evidence, not the decision.
Exam cue: closing a risk is the owner's decision, like accepting one. Bring evidence the fix works; the owner records closure and any residual risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'anyone can raise a risk; the owner decides what happens to it' (notes 1.2.7 Risk Register, Ownership and Reporting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): key_concept and Exam cue now teach closure as the risk owner's decision, distinct from cc_d1_031 (raising a risk); C names the head of sales too, and D is no longer the shortest option.

questions.question: A county records office has run unsupported scanning software for two years; no manager has ever reviewed the risk or decided how to handle it. How should the risk analyst MOST accurately describe this risk?

options.A: Avoided, since no incident has happened in two years
options.B: Unmanaged, since no response to it has been chosen yet
options.C: Accepted, since the office has kept using the software
options.D: Transferred, since the vendor ended support for the software

questions.key_concept: Acceptance is a documented decision by someone with authority; a risk left alone by default is unmanaged, not accepted.
questions.pre_read: Check what decision, if any, someone with authority has made about this risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance is a deliberate, documented decision by whoever holds the authority: the risk owner within tolerance, senior management beyond it. No one has reviewed this risk, so no one has decided on it; it is unmanaged, and the analyst should raise it for an owner's decision. The runner-up mistakes drift for a choice: acceptance can mean taking no further action, but only as a recorded decision, and carrying on by default is not one.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing has gone wrong yet. But avoidance means stopping the risky activity, and the office still runs the software.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: accepting a risk can mean taking no further action. But only after someone with authority decides that and records it; here no one has even reviewed the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor caused the support gap. But transfer shifts financial impact to another party, such as an insurer; an ended contract shifts nothing.

tips: Eliminate: D calls a vendor's exit a transfer, and A calls continued use avoidance; neither fits what the office did.
Final two: B beats C because acceptance is a documented decision by someone with authority; carrying on by default is not one.
Exam cue: a risk nobody has decided on is unmanaged, not accepted. Look for a named approver and a record before calling any risk accepted.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ignoring a risk is not acceptance; acceptance is a documented decision by whoever holds the authority' (notes 1.2.5 Risk Treatment Options). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.
