Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, blind test): the stem no longer negates the runner-up directly ('no acceptance'); it states only that no one has reviewed the risk. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): key B no longer carries the key-only word 'authorized'. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): the stem states plainly that no manager has decided how to handle the risk; C's explanation and the correct explanation now meet the 'acceptance means taking no action' reading head on.

questions.question: A fitness center chain's board hands daily security work to its new security manager and says security is now that manager's responsibility alone. Which reply from the security manager is MOST accurate?

options.A: Accountability rests with the staff who follow security rules
options.B: Accountability rests with the security manager who does the work
options.C: Accountability rests with the board, which delegated the work
options.D: Accountability rests with the auditors who test the controls

questions.key_concept: Senior leaders can delegate security work to management but remain accountable for cybersecurity risk.
questions.pre_read: Separate who does the security work from who answers for the outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaders can delegate security work but not their accountability for it: the board sets direction, approves the risk appetite and oversees results, while management runs daily operations. The runner-up describes responsibility, which the security manager does take on for the delegated work; answering in the end for how well the organization manages cyber risk stays with the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because everyone must follow security rules. But staff are responsible for their own conduct; they do not answer for the organization's security.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the manager becomes responsible for doing the work well. But accountability, answering for the outcome, stays with the board that delegated it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditors check and report on security. But they give independent assurance on the controls; they do not answer for how the organization manages its risk.

tips: Eliminate: A makes staff answer for the organization, and D hands accountability to auditors, who only check and report on controls.
Final two: C beats B because responsibility can be delegated but accountability cannot; the board still answers for security.
Exam cue: responsible means doing the work; accountable means answering for the outcome. Leaders delegate work but stay accountable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'senior management is accountable; owners decide for their assets; custodians and users follow the rules' (notes 1.3.1 Security Governance and Its Roles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, blind test): 'now' and 'still' removed from all options, as only the key said 'still'. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): distractor D now names auditors, a real confusion, instead of a vendor the stem never mentions.

questions.question: A US craft-supply shop with no office abroad starts shipping orders to customers in France and Germany. Which statement about the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) should its IT manager accept as MOST accurate?

options.A: It applies once the shop offers goods to people in the EU
options.B: It exempts the shop as a small craft business
options.C: It applies only once the shop opens an office inside the EU
options.D: It is satisfied once the shop complies with US privacy law

questions.key_concept: Privacy laws such as GDPR can apply to organizations abroad that offer goods or services to people in their region.
questions.pre_read: Ask what links the shop to the EU now, and what GDPR uses to decide who it covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy laws can reach a business through where its customers are. GDPR reaches organizations outside the EU that offer goods or services to people in the EU, so shipping orders to France and Germany brings the shop within it, and its IT manager should raise this with legal counsel to confirm its duties. The runner-up reflects how many local laws work, but GDPR's reach does not depend on having an office there.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because some laws exempt small firms. But GDPR's reach turns on offering goods or services to people in the EU, not on business size.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: many laws apply only where a business is based. But GDPR also reaches businesses abroad that offer goods or services to people in the EU.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the shop follows privacy law at home. But meeting US law does not meet GDPR's separate duties, which apply once it offers goods to people in the EU.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes GDPR's reach depends on business size, which it does not, and D assumes that following US law meets GDPR's separate duties.
Final two: A beats C because GDPR covers offering goods to people in the EU, with or without an office there.
Exam cue: privacy laws can reach a business through where its customers are, not only where it is based. When customers are in a new region, ask legal counsel which of its laws now apply.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'privacy laws, such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), can reach organizations outside the EU' (notes 1.3.2 Laws and Regulations). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): D is now a wrong 'it can apply' option, so the key is no longer the only positive statement. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): B now tests business size, not the same 'where it is based' idea as runner-up C; D lengthened so the key is not the longest. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): key A no longer hedges ('can apply') or carries a reason clause; A, C and D now all say 'It applies' with a condition, leaving B as the single denial; explanation and cue say GDPR turns on offering goods to people in the EU, not on citizenship. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): B and D no longer carry restricting words ('cannot', 'only'), so the key is not the lone unrestricted option; D now tests the belief that home-country law meets GDPR's duties. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: role sweep: 'IT lead' became 'IT manager'.

questions.question: A sports club's new security manager is mapping the board's work on risk strategy, roles and policy to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0. Which function does this work MOST accurately fit?

options.A: The Respond function
options.B: The Identify function
options.C: The Protect function
options.D: The Govern function

questions.key_concept: CSF 2.0's Govern function covers risk management strategy, roles and responsibilities, policy and oversight.
questions.pre_read: Recall the six CSF 2.0 functions and what each one covers.
questions.correct_explanation: CSF 2.0 added Govern, which covers the organization's risk management strategy, expectations and policy, plus roles, responsibilities and oversight; the board's work fits it directly. Identify, the runner-up, is close because it deals with understanding current risks and assets, but it works within the strategy Govern sets rather than setting it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because boards step in during major incidents. But Respond covers actions taken once an incident is detected.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Identify is about understanding risk, which sounds strategic. But it covers assets and current risks; setting strategy, roles and policy is Govern.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because policy often leads to safeguards. But Protect covers safeguards in use, such as access control and training, not setting strategy.

tips: Eliminate: C covers safeguards in use and A covers incident actions; neither sets strategy or roles.
Final two: D beats B because Govern sets risk strategy, roles and policy; Identify understands assets and current risks within that strategy.
Exam cue: CSF 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Strategy, roles, policy and oversight point to Govern.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 2 (Introduction to the CSF Core: GOVERN covers risk management strategy, roles and responsibilities, and policy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 [...] groups outcomes into six functions' (notes 1.3.3 Security Frameworks and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): 'security lead' changed to the canonical 'security manager'.

questions.question: A supermarket chain's AI screening tool rejects far more job applicants over 50 than younger ones. Besides privacy law, which legal concern should the security analyst flag to legal counsel as MOST pressing?

options.A: Consumer protection law on the fair treatment of shoppers
options.B: Employment law that bans age discrimination in hiring
options.C: Disability law on making the application site accessible
options.D: Pension law on retirement benefits for staff over 50

questions.key_concept: Existing laws, such as employment anti-discrimination law, apply to AI decisions about people just as to human ones.
questions.pre_read: Ask what decision the tool makes about people, and which existing law governs that kind of decision.
questions.correct_explanation: AI decisions about people stay under the laws that already govern those decisions. Rejecting older applicants at a far higher rate points to possible age discrimination, which employment law covers whether a person or a tool made the call. Consumer protection, the runner-up, also reaches AI, but it guards customers in their dealings with a business; job applicants here are being judged for work.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: consumer law does reach some AI decisions. But it protects customers buying goods or services; this tool judges people applying for jobs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because job sites must be usable by disabled applicants. But nothing in the pattern points to access barriers; it shows older applicants being rejected.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it also concerns people over 50. But pension law governs benefits for staff already employed; this tool screens applicants before hiring.

tips: Eliminate: C concerns site access for disabled users and D concerns benefits for current staff; the pattern here is the rejection of older applicants.
Final two: B beats A because the tool judges job applicants, which employment law covers; consumer law protects buyers.
Exam cue: name the decision the AI makes, such as hiring, lending or housing, then ask which existing law already governs that decision.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.1 (legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed and documented); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 3.7 (Fair – with Harmful Bias Managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'employment and consumer laws also reach AI decisions about people' (notes 1.3.6 Laws and Rules That Apply to AI). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): C and D replaced with near-misses about people (site accessibility, pension benefits for over-50s) instead of payment card rules and copyright.

questions.question: A small design studio's leaders adopted selected ISO/IEC 27002 controls as its security standard, and a designer calls them optional because no law requires them. Which reply from the IT coordinator is MOST accurate?

options.A: They are optional, since no law or contract requires them
options.B: They bind staff as internal rules, with or without a law
options.C: They bind each person once they finish training on them
options.D: They become binding once the studio is certified to ISO/IEC 27001

questions.key_concept: An external standard is voluntary until adopted or required; once leaders adopt it, it binds staff like any internal standard.
questions.pre_read: Note what the studio's leaders did with the standard, and what the designer is relying on.
questions.correct_explanation: An external standard is voluntary until an organization adopts it, or until a law or contract requires it. Here the studio's leaders adopted the controls as its own standard, so they are now mandatory internal requirements. The runner-up states the rule for a standard nobody has adopted; at the studio, adoption, not law, is what binds staff.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an external standard nobody has adopted is voluntary unless a law or contract requires it. But the studio's leaders adopted these controls, which makes them its own standard.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because training explains the rules. But a standard applies to everyone in its scope once approved, not person by person after training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because certification is a visible milestone. But an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate is outside proof about the studio's management system; leaders' adoption already made these controls binding.

tips: Eliminate: C ties the rules to training and D to certification; neither is what makes an adopted standard binding on staff.
Final two: B beats A because leadership adoption makes the controls the studio's own standard; a law or contract is only one way a standard becomes binding.
Exam cue: ask whether a standard has been adopted or required. Once leaders adopt it, it binds staff like any internal standard.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Standards, Guidelines, and Procedures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'it is voluntary until adopted, or until a law or contract requires it' (notes 1.3.5 Standards, Procedures and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): re-angled from 'is the studio legally required' to whether an adopted standard binds staff; the key no longer echoes the stem's 'adopted'. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): key B no longer repeats the stem's wording about the studio's leaders. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): D names ISO/IEC 27001, the standard organizations certify to, so the distractor no longer implies certification to 27002. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: stem says 'small', since IT coordinator is kept only for small offices with no specialists.

questions.question: A tutoring firm's acceptable use policy, owned by the operations director, has technicians remove and log unapproved software. A tutor's unapproved music app has a team leader's emailed OK; what should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Uninstall and log the app, and explain the policy exception process
options.B: Log the app under the team leader's email as a policy exception
options.C: Reimage the tutor's laptop to clear any other unapproved software
options.D: Block the app's download site for all staff on the firewall

questions.key_concept: Only the policy owner grants exceptions, through the formal process; an informal OK from anyone else does not change what the policy requires.
questions.pre_read: Note what the policy assigns to technicians and who owns the policy.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy assigns removal and logging to technicians, and only its owner can approve an exception, through the formal process. A team leader's email is not an exception, so the technician removes and logs the app and explains how the tutor can request one. Logging the app as an exception under the team leader's email, the runner-up, treats an informal OK as if anyone could set a policy aside.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the email shows a manager backs the tutor. But a team leader does not own the policy; only the owner approves exceptions, through the formal process.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would catch any other unapproved software. But wiping a whole laptop goes far beyond the step the policy assigns and risks the tutor's work.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it stops other installs. But a firewall change for all staff goes through the change process and is outside the removal task the policy assigns.

tips: Eliminate: C wipes a whole laptop when the policy asks only that the app be removed, and D makes a firewall change for all staff, which goes beyond the assigned task and needs change approval.
Final two: A beats B because only the policy owner grants exceptions, through the formal process; a team leader's email does not set the policy aside.
Exam cue: an informal OK from someone who does not own the policy is not an exception. Follow the policy and point the requester to the exception process.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-11 (User-installed Software); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior)

Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): wrong explanation D no longer mentions a help desk the stem does not name. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): B now also logs the app, so the stem's procedure verbs are not echoed in the key alone; the Eliminate tip now describes option D as written; the key uses the glossary term 'policy exception' and is no longer the shortest option. questions.question: A seafood wholesaler's risk assessment ranks fake supplier invoices as its top risk, and the IT team proposes a new perimeter firewall as its main control. What is the MOST important problem with the proposal?

options.A: A firewall detects attacks but cannot block any traffic
options.B: A firewall is a physical control, not a technical one
options.C: It has not yet been tested against the firm's current traffic
options.D: It does nothing to stop the way this fraud happens

questions.key_concept: A control must treat the assessed risk; a strong control aimed at the wrong risk leaves the top risk open.
questions.pre_read: Recall how controls are chosen, then weigh how serious each problem the options name would be.
questions.correct_explanation: Controls are chosen to treat assessed risks. Fake invoices trick staff into paying, which a perimeter firewall does nothing to stop; controls such as verifying bank-detail changes by phone and payment approval rules would. The runner-up names good practice for any new control, but testing cannot fix the mismatch: a well-tested control aimed at the wrong risk still leaves the top risk open.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because some tools only alert. But blocking traffic by rule is a firewall's main job; detection-only tools are intrusion detection systems.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because firewalls are often physical boxes. But a firewall enforces rules in software and firmware, which makes it a technical control.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: new controls should be tested before relying on them. But even a well-tested firewall would leave the top risk, fake invoices, untreated.

tips: Eliminate: B misplaces a firewall among physical controls, and A confuses it with a detection-only tool.
Final two: D beats C because a control must fit the assessed risk; testing improves a control but cannot point it at the right risk.
Exam cue: trace each proposed control back to the risk it treats. A strong control aimed at the wrong risk does nothing for the top one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'pick the control that directly addresses the assessed risk at a sensible cost. A strong control aimed at the wrong risk does nothing' (notes 1.4.1 What a Security Control Is). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, audit): the key no longer echoes the stem's 'risk assessment ranks ... top risk'. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): 'actually' removed from the key. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): pre_read no longer paraphrases the key.

questions.question: A payroll bureau sends weekly backup drives holding clients' salary and bank details to an offsite vault by courier. Which technical control BEST keeps the data confidential if a drive goes missing?

options.A: Ship each drive in a locked, tamper-evident transport case
options.B: Encrypt the data on each drive before it is shipped
options.C: Have the courier sign a receipt at every handover
options.D: Record a hash of the data on each drive before shipping

questions.key_concept: Encryption is the technical control that keeps data on lost or stolen media confidential; hashing only detects changes.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options by control type, then ask which one keeps a lost drive's data from being read.
questions.correct_explanation: Encryption is a technical control that keeps stored data unreadable without the key, so a lost or stolen drive exposes nothing as long as the key is kept separately. A hash, the runner-up, is also technical and protects integrity: it can show whether a drive's contents changed, but anyone who finds the drive can still read every salary and bank detail.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because locked cases do protect media in transit. But a case is a physical control, and it can be forced open once lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because receipts show who held a drive and when. But they are an administrative record; they do not stop anyone reading a lost drive.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a hash is a technical control too. But it detects changes; it leaves the data fully readable to whoever finds a missing drive.

tips: Eliminate: A is a physical control and C an administrative one; the stem asks for a technical control.
Final two: B beats D because encryption keeps a lost drive unreadable; a hash only shows whether its contents changed.
Exam cue: match the tool to the goal. Encryption serves confidentiality; hashing serves integrity. Keep the key away from the media.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MP-5 (Media Transport); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.1 (Data Encryption)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'some protect data directly, such as encryption' (notes 1.4.2 Technical Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): key B no longer echoes the stem's 'backup' and 'bureau'; D also says 'data'.

questions.question: A casino's new cash-cage cashiers will have access to the vault room. Which administrative control should the security manager propose to BEST lower the risk of hiring someone with a theft record?

options.A: Cameras recording everyone who enters the vault room
options.B: A signed code of conduct from each cashier on their first day
options.C: A badge-and-PIN lock on the vault room door
options.D: Background checks on candidates before their first day

questions.key_concept: Personnel screening is an administrative control that lowers people risk before access is granted.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options by control type, then ask which one targets the specific risk the stem names.
questions.correct_explanation: Personnel screening, such as a background check completed before a new cashier starts, is an administrative control that works before access is granted, so someone with a relevant theft record never reaches the vault room. A signed code of conduct, the runner-up, is also administrative and sets expectations, but it comes after hiring and reveals nothing about a candidate's past.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because cameras deter and record theft. But they are physical controls that act after someone is already hired and inside.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a code of conduct is a real administrative control. But it is signed after hiring and tells the casino nothing about a candidate's history.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it limits who enters the vault. But it is a physical access control, and a newly hired cashier would hold a badge anyway.

tips: Eliminate: A and C are physical controls, and both act only after the person is already hired.
Final two: D beats B because screening works before a cashier starts; a code of conduct sets rules but reveals nothing about a candidate's past.
Exam cue: for people risks, look at hiring practices first. Screening keeps risk out; training and codes shape people already inside.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-3 (Personnel Screening); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'hiring practices include background checks and prompt access removal when people leave' (notes 1.4.3 Administrative Controls). questions.question: Staff at a recording studio often hold the equipment room's badge-entry door for people behind them, and gear has gone missing. Which proposal by the security analyst would BEST stop this?

options.A: An access control vestibule that admits one person per badge
options.B: A door sign asking staff not to hold it for others
options.C: A camera recording everyone who walks into the equipment room
options.D: A badge reader on the inside so people must badge to leave

questions.key_concept: An access control vestibule admitting one person per badge stops followers, with or without consent; a camera deters and records but cannot physically stop anyone.
questions.pre_read: Name what staff are doing at the door, then ask what each option changes for the person walking in behind a badge holder.
questions.correct_explanation: Holding the door for someone is piggybacking (tailgating when the badge holder does not notice). An access control vestibule, once called a mantrap, has two doors that open one at a time; set to admit one person per badge, it stops a follower at the door instead of relying on staff habits. A camera, the runner-up, deters and shows who followed whom, which helps an investigation, but it stops nobody at the door.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it reminds staff of the rule. But staff already hold the door for others, and a sign depends on those same people changing their habit.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a camera deters and records who followed whom. But it only shows the problem afterward; it does not stop anyone walking in.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it adds another badge check. But it controls leaving, not the entry being abused, and it can trap people in an emergency.

tips: Eliminate: B depends on the very staff habit causing the losses, and D controls leaving rather than the entry being abused, and can trap people in an emergency.
Final two: A beats C because a camera records the follower but stops nobody; a vestibule physically admits one person per badge.
Exam cue: to stop people following others in, with or without consent, pick a control that physically admits one person at a time.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-6 (Monitoring Physical Access)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Entry controls, such as badge readers and access control vestibules, admit authorized people only.' (notes 1.4.4 Physical Controls). questions.subtopic: 1.4 Security controls. Controls for AI tools
questions.question: A city housing office's AI tool, which tested 98% accurate, drafts benefit eligibility decisions, and the office manager wants them sent automatically. Which control should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: The server running the AI tool sits in a locked room
options.B: The model is retested on a larger sample before launch
options.C: Each resident is told the decision was drafted by AI
options.D: A caseworker approves each decision before it goes out

questions.key_concept: A model's accuracy score measures it but controls nothing; high-impact AI decisions need a review step that can stop each wrong one.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the impact of a wrong decision on residents against the model's test score.
questions.correct_explanation: Benefit decisions have high impact on people, so a person must stay accountable for each one. Even at 98%, about one decision in fifty is wrong, and models drift or meet crafted input after testing; review before sending catches those. Retesting on a larger sample, the runner-up, gives a more reliable score but still lets each wrong decision reach a resident.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI hardware does need physical protection. But a locked room does nothing about wrong decisions the tool drafts.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a larger test gives a more trustworthy accuracy figure. But no score removes every error, and each wrong decision would still reach a resident unreviewed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because being open about AI's role is good practice. But telling residents does not stop a wrong decision from affecting them.

tips: Eliminate: A protects hardware rather than decisions, and C tells residents about the AI but stops no wrong decision reaching them.
Final two: D beats B because even a better test score leaves some wrong decisions; only review of each one stops them reaching residents.
Exam cue: a score describes a model, not any single decision. When AI makes high-impact decisions about people, pick the control that lets a person stop a wrong one before it takes effect.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 4.1 (post-deployment monitoring plans, including capturing user input, appeal and override)

Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): key_concept is one sentence.

questions.question: A system administrator at a courier firm thinks their own paycheck is wrong and could check it through the payroll console they manage. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Ask a teammate to look the record up in the console
options.B: Ask the payroll team to look into the suspected pay error
options.C: View only their own record in the console, changing nothing
options.D: Correct the record in the console and tell payroll afterward

questions.key_concept: Privileged access is for assigned work only; personal matters, even about your own data, go through normal channels.
questions.pre_read: Separate the administrator's job duties from their personal interest in the record.
questions.correct_explanation: Administrator access exists for assigned work, such as keeping the payroll system running, not for personal business, even about one's own pay. Raising it with the payroll team, like any employee, keeps the conflict of interest out and leaves the right people to fix it. Viewing only their own record, the runner-up, changes nothing, but it still uses privileged access for a personal purpose.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the administrator is not touching the record personally. But it is still privileged access used for a personal purpose, now by two people.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it is their own data and nothing changes. But admin access is for assigned work; using it for personal matters breaches the code of conduct.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the fix seems obvious. But changing one's own pay record is a clear conflict of interest, whatever the error, and bypasses payroll's checks.

tips: Eliminate: D changes their own pay record, a conflict of interest, and A has a colleague misuse the same access for them.
Final two: B beats C because privileged access is for assigned work; personal questions go through the normal channel, even about your own data.
Exam cue: having access is not having a reason. Use privileged access only for assigned work, and handle personal matters like any other employee.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)

questions.question: A newly certified analyst at a stock photo agency hears a colleague call their certification's code of ethics friendly advice. Which statement about the code is MOST accurate?

options.A: Breaching it requires conduct that also breaks the law
options.B: It applies only while certified members work on client projects
options.C: Following it is a condition of keeping the certification
options.D: The employer's code of conduct replaces it at work

questions.key_concept: The code of ethics is a mandatory condition of certification, and it asks more of members than the law does.
questions.pre_read: Recall who the code covers, when it applies and how it relates to other rules members follow.
questions.correct_explanation: Members agree to the code as a condition of certification, and a proven breach can cost the credential, so it is mandatory, not friendly advice. The runner-up rightly notes that acting legally is part of the code, but the canons ask for more than the law: honesty, diligent and competent service and care for the public, so a dishonest act can breach the code without any crime.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: acting legally is one of its duties. But the code also asks for honesty and diligent service, so a member can breach it without breaking any law.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because client work is where many dilemmas arise. But the code covers certified members' professional conduct generally, including work for their own employer.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because employers set their own rules. But both codes apply at once, and any conflict between them is raised, not settled by dropping one.

tips: Eliminate: B limits the code to client projects, and D lets an employer's code replace it; both codes apply at once.
Final two: C beats A because following the code is a condition of certification, and it asks more than the law; a dishonest act can breach it without any crime.
Exam cue: a certification's code of ethics is mandatory for members, applies wherever they work and asks more than the law: honesty, diligence and care for the public.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Preamble and Canons
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'following it is a condition of holding ISC2 certification. A proven breach can cost the credential' (notes 1.5.3 The ISC2 Code of Ethics). questions.question: A certified freelance analyst is hired by a theater company to review its ticketing system. Under the canon on diligent and competent service, who is MOST accurately the analyst's principal?

options.A: The theater company paying the analyst for this work
options.B: The certifying body that issued the analyst's credential
options.C: The theater's audience, whose data the system holds
options.D: Fellow certified professionals working in the same field

questions.key_concept: Principals are the employers and clients a member serves professionally; duties to the public and the profession sit under other canons.
questions.pre_read: List everyone the analyst's work affects, then match each one to the canon that covers duties toward them.
questions.correct_explanation: Principals are those a member serves professionally under an employment or contract relationship, such as employers and clients; here that is the theater company that hired the analyst. The audience, the runner-up, matters a great deal, but protecting the public falls under the canon on society and public trust, not the canon on service to principals.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the certifying body sets the code. But it is not a client; duties toward the profession sit under the canon on advancing the profession.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the analyst's work does protect audience data. But duties to the public sit under the canon on protecting society; principals are those who engage the analyst.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because members owe each other support. But that duty belongs to the canon on advancing and protecting the profession, not service to principals.

tips: Eliminate: B and D point to the profession and its certifying body, which the canon on advancing the profession covers.
Final two: A beats C because principals are those who employ or engage the member; duties to the public sit under the canon on protecting society.
Exam cue: match each party to its canon: society and the public, honest and legal conduct, principals who employ or engage you, and the profession.

questions.question: Renewing a book online, a certified analyst sees their borrower number in the city library's page address and suspects changing it would show other borrowers' records. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Change the number just once to confirm the flaw before reporting it
options.B: Report the suspicion privately to the library without testing it
options.C: Do nothing, since the analyst has no contract with the library
options.D: Post the suspected flaw online so the library acts quickly

questions.key_concept: A flaw found by chance is reported privately to the owner; testing it without permission is unauthorized access.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the analyst is authorized to do on this site, and who can fix the flaw.
questions.correct_explanation: Reporting privately to the system owner protects borrowers and gives the library a chance to fix the flaw, while staying within the law. The runner-up feels responsible, since a confirmed report is more useful, but changing the number would open other people's records without authorization; the analyst has no permission to test, and the library can confirm the flaw itself.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a confirmed flaw makes a stronger report. But opening others' records without permission is unauthorized access, whatever the motive; the library can verify it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst owes the library no service. But the duty to protect society covers everyone's data, and a private report costs little.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because public pressure can speed fixes. But publishing before a fix shows attackers exactly how to reach borrowers' records.

tips: Eliminate: D shows attackers the flaw before any fix, and C leaves borrowers' data exposed when a private report costs little.
Final two: B beats A because testing without permission is unauthorized access; report the suspicion and let the owner confirm it.
Exam cue: when you stumble on a flaw, report it privately to the owner. Never test without written permission, and never publish before a fix.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons; NIST SP 800-115 Section 6.5 (Assessment Plan Development: the plan states the type and level of testing permitted)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'report flaws to the owner first; publishing before a fix hands attackers a way in' (notes 1.5.4 Applying the Canons to Dilemmas). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An analyst can prove a coworker with the same credential sold client scan results; the firm fired the coworker and calls it closed. What does the code of ethics MOST clearly expect of the analyst?

options.A: Post the evidence online to warn the coworker's future employers
options.B: Treat the matter as closed, since the employer has acted
options.C: File a complaint with the certifying body's ethics committee
options.D: Leave any ethics complaint to the client, who was the one harmed

questions.key_concept: Members who observe another member breach the code are expected to file a complaint; employer discipline does not replace it.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the employer has done from what only the certifying body can do.
questions.correct_explanation: Members who see another member breach the code are expected to use the complaint procedure, and staying silent may itself breach the canon on protecting the profession. Firing the coworker settles the employment matter, but the runner-up misses that the certification is separate: only the certifying body can act on it, and only if a sworn complaint with evidence reaches its committee.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because future employers could be harmed. But public accusations bypass the formal process and may expose the client's confidential results.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the firm has dealt with the employment side. But the certification is separate; the coworker keeps it unless a complaint reaches the certifying body.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the client was harmed. But members of the public may complain under canons one and two, and certified peers under canon four, so the analyst has standing.

tips: Eliminate: A goes public instead of using the formal process, and D misreads who has standing to complain.
Final two: C beats B because an employer's action does not touch the certification; members who see a breach are expected to report it.
Exam cue: a member's breach goes to the certifying body through a sworn, evidenced complaint. Silence can itself breach the duty to the profession.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics (members who observe a breach by another member must follow the complaint procedure); ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (standing of complainant and form of complaints)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'members who see another member breach the code are expected to report it; staying silent may breach canon 4' (notes 1.5.5 Ethics Complaints and Enforcement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, audit): wrong_explanations.D now states the published standing rule exactly. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): the stem now says the coworker holds the same credential, the fact the duty to complain depends on, and no longer repeats 'certified'. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): D now says 'ethics complaint', so the stem's 'ethics' is not echoed in the key alone.

questions.question: A certified analyst drafted a client's risk report with an approved AI assistant and verified every finding; the client's contract requires disclosing AI use. Which step is BEST before sending the report?

options.A: Name the AI vendor as responsible for any errors in the report
options.B: Have the assistant reword the draft so it reads as human-written
options.C: State in the report that every finding was checked by hand
options.D: State in the report that an AI assistant helped draft it

questions.key_concept: Professionals stay honest about AI's role in their work, especially when a principal requires it, and stay accountable for the result.
questions.pre_read: Note what the client's contract asks for and what the analyst has already done.
questions.correct_explanation: Honesty about how work was produced matters most where a principal asks for it, and this contract requires disclosure of AI use. Stating the assistant's role meets that duty while the analyst stays accountable for the content. Saying every finding was checked, the runner-up, describes good practice, but it leaves out the very fact the client asked to know.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor built the tool. But the professional who relies on AI output stays accountable for the report, whoever made the tool.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it avoids awkward questions. But disguising AI's role is deception, the opposite of what the contract and honest service require.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: verification is what competent service requires. But the contract asks about AI use, and describing the checks without naming the assistant leaves that out.

tips: Eliminate: A shifts accountability to a vendor, and B disguises the AI's role, which is deception.
Final two: D beats C because the contract asks about AI use; describing checks without naming the assistant leaves out what the client asked to know.
Exam cue: with AI at work, verify output, protect principals' data, stay accountable and be open about AI's role where it matters.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 3.4 (Accountable and Transparent); ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons (service to principals)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'be honest about AI's role where it matters, such as in reports' (notes 1.5.6 Ethical Use of AI at Work). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.5 Professional conduct. Due care and due diligence
questions.question: Each quarter, a marina's IT manager verifies that encryption is switched on in every backup job and reports any gaps to the system owner. How should this verification MOST accurately be described?

options.A: Due diligence, because it checks that a safeguard is in place
options.B: Due care, because it switches encryption back on where it is off
options.C: Risk avoidance, because it removes the risk of data exposure
options.D: Risk transfer, because it moves backup risk to the IT manager

questions.key_concept: A routine check that an existing safeguard still works is due diligence, however often it repeats; due care is acting on what it finds.
questions.pre_read: Recall what due care and due diligence each involve, then place the quarterly check against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Due diligence is finding out and verifying: researching, assessing and testing whether safeguards work. A quarterly check that backup encryption is on, with gaps reported to the owner, is verification, so it is diligence however often it repeats. Due care, the runner-up, is acting on what is known, such as switching encryption back on; this IT manager only checks and reports. Sources word these terms differently; this course uses: diligence checks, care acts.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: switching encryption back on would be due care. But this IT manager only checks and reports gaps; the owner who fixes them acts with due care.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption lowers exposure. But avoidance means stopping the activity that creates the risk; the marina still makes backups.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IT manager now carries the task. But transfer shifts financial impact to another party, such as an insurer; assigning work is not transfer.

tips: Eliminate: D mistakes assigning work for risk transfer, and C calls a check avoidance though the backups continue.
Final two: A beats B because the IT manager only verifies and reports; switching encryption back on is the owner's act of due care, not part of this check.
Exam cue: a check stays due diligence however often it repeats. It turns into due care only when someone acts on what the check found, such as re-enabling a control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'due diligence investigates: researching a vendor, assessing risks, testing controls' (notes 1.5.2 Due Care and Due Diligence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026, blind test): the stem now calls the activity verification, the key no longer echoes it, and the explanation addresses texts that count all upkeep as due care. Fix-up round 2, second pass (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): key A no longer mirrors the stem's 'actually switched on'. Final pass (31 Oct 2026, audit merge): B now states the 'ongoing duty' reading some texts give due care, a stronger runner-up than 'keeps encryption running'. Batch 3 fix-up (31 Oct 2026, blind test and audit): the stem says the IT manager reports gaps to the owner, and B's reason (switching encryption back on) is false for this check under either common wording of the terms; key_concept, pre_read and Exam cue re-angled to 'a repeated check is still diligence', distinct from cc_d1_017; the explanation notes that sources word the terms differently. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: role sweep: 'IT lead' became 'IT manager'.

questions.question: A city radio station airs a storm-warning recording exactly as it was received, but a prankster posing as the weather service sent it. Which property does the recording MOST clearly lack?

options.A: Integrity, because the station aired a recording it should have refused
options.B: Availability, because the real service's warning could not get through
options.C: Authenticity, because it did not come from the service it claims
options.D: Confidentiality, because an outsider slipped a recording in

questions.key_concept: Data can arrive complete and unchanged yet be fake; confirming it came from its claimed source is authenticity, a separate question from integrity.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions about any data: has it changed, and did it come from where it claims?
questions.correct_explanation: Authenticity means data truly comes from its claimed source. The recording aired exactly as received, so nothing was altered, but a prankster made it, not the weather service. Integrity, the runner-up, asks whether data was changed without authorization; NIST's broad definition folds authenticity in, but asked as two separate questions, the answer to 'has it changed?' is no here.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: airing a fake warning is a real failure. But the recording was not altered; the problem is who made it, which is an authenticity question.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a fake warning can drown out a real one. But nothing in the stem says the weather service's own warnings were blocked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because an outsider reached the station. But sending a recording in is not reading data out; nothing was disclosed.

tips: Eliminate: B needs the real warnings to be blocked, and D mistakes slipping a recording in for disclosure; confidentiality is about data going out.
Final two: C beats A because the recording aired unchanged, so integrity held; what failed is proof that it came from the weather service.
Exam cue: when data is intact but its sender is fake, name authenticity; keep integrity for data changed after it was created or sent.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Appendix A Glossary (authenticity); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'authenticity means data truly comes from its claimed source' (notes 1.1.3 Integrity and Authenticity). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Final fix round (4 Nov 2026): neutral subtopic; D rewritten as the real confidentiality misconception.

questions.question: A couple's seating plan vanished from a wedding planning firm's shared system, and the office manager needs to know which planner deleted it. Which AAA function MOST directly answers this?

options.A: Authentication, which proved each planner's identity at sign-in
options.B: Authorization, which records which planners may delete plans
options.C: Accounting, which recorded each planner's actions after sign-in
options.D: Availability, which keeps each couple's plans reachable when needed

questions.key_concept: Accounting records what each identity did; authentication proves who signed in, and authorization sets what each may do.
questions.pre_read: Recall the question each part of AAA answers, then match it to what the office manager needs to know.
questions.correct_explanation: Accounting records what each authenticated identity actually did, such as deleting a file, so an action can be traced to one person. The manager needs to know who carried out this deletion, which only an activity record can show. Authentication, the runner-up, proved who signed in, but it records nothing about what each planner did afterward, so it cannot name who deleted the plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: knowing who signed in is part of the trail. But proof at sign-in says nothing about which planner later deleted the plan; only the activity record does.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because permissions show who could delete plans. But several planners may hold that right; a list of who may act does not show who did.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the plan is now missing. But availability is a security goal, not part of AAA, and it does not identify who deleted anything.

tips: Eliminate: D names a CIA goal rather than an AAA function, and B shows only who was allowed to delete, not who did.
Final two: C beats A because authentication proves identity at sign-in, while accounting records each later action, such as this deletion, against that identity.
Exam cue: who are you is authentication, what may you do is authorization, and what did you do is accounting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-3 (Content of Audit Records)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'accounting records what it actually did, so actions can be traced to a person or process' (notes 1.1.6 Authorization and Accounting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A yoga studio chain's members agreed to research use of anonymized attendance data, and the export drops names but keeps birth date, home postal code and gender. Which concern should the security analyst raise FIRST?

options.A: Whether the export file is encrypted before it is sent
options.B: Whether the fields kept still identify members in combination
options.C: Whether the partner will delete members' data once the study ends
options.D: Whether the attendance counts are accurate enough for research

questions.key_concept: Removing names does not make data anonymous; fields such as birth date and postal code can identify people in combination.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the members agreed to, then whether the export really matches that description.
questions.correct_explanation: Members agreed to anonymized data, but birth date, postal code and gender together can single out many people, so the export may still be personal data. That comes first, because it decides whether this sharing fits what members agreed to at all. Retention, the runner-up, is a real privacy principle, but a promise to delete the data later does not fix data that already identifies people.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the file holds personal details. But encryption protects it in transit; the partner still receives data that can identify members.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: limiting how long data is kept is a real privacy principle. But it comes after confirming the data is truly anonymized, as members were told.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because research needs good data. But accuracy is an integrity concern; the privacy question is whether members can be identified.

tips: Eliminate: A protects the file in transit but not the members' identities, and D is about data accuracy rather than privacy.
Final two: B beats C because deleting the data later does not help if the export already identifies members, contrary to what they agreed.
Exam cue: anonymized means nobody can be picked out. Check combinations of fields such as birth date, postal code and gender, not just names.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-188 Section 4.3 (De-Identification by Removing Identifiers and Transforming Quasi-Identifiers: quasi-identifiers can be used to triangulate a specific individual)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'personally identifiable information (PII) identifies a person, alone or combined with other data' (notes 1.1.8 Privacy and Personal Data). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A tour operator's AI itinerary assistant stops answering customers whenever one automated client sends it thousands of long requests an hour. Which control should the security team propose as BEST?

options.A: Filter each request for hidden instructions before the model reads it
options.B: Add servers so the assistant can serve every client's requests
options.C: Cap how many requests each client can send in a set time
options.D: Encrypt every chat between customers and the assistant

questions.key_concept: Flooding an AI service attacks availability; a per-client rate limit stops one source from using up shared capacity.
questions.pre_read: Name the security goal under attack first, then pick the control built for that kind of traffic.
questions.correct_explanation: One client flooding the assistant attacks availability: real customers cannot get answers. A per-client rate limit stops any single source from using up the shared capacity, while normal customers stay well within it. Adding servers, the runner-up, suits genuine growth in demand, but an automated client can simply send more requests and use up the new capacity too.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI assistants face prompt injection. But nothing suggests hidden instructions; the harm comes from the volume of requests, not their content.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: more capacity does help availability. But it serves abusive traffic as readily as customers, and the automated client can scale up its requests.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because chats can hold travel details. But encryption protects confidentiality and does nothing to stop a flood of requests.

tips: Eliminate: A targets malicious content in prompts and D protects secrecy; neither limits the volume that is crowding out customers.
Final two: C beats B because extra servers serve the flood as well, while a per-client cap stops one source from using up shared capacity.
Exam cue: one source overloading a service calls for rate limiting; genuine demand peaks call for capacity. Match the fix to who is sending the load.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-5 (Denial-of-service Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI service flooded with requests: availability; rate limits and spare capacity' (notes 1.1.9 AI and the Core Security Concepts). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A golf club's booking clerk mistakenly overwrites this month's tee times with last year's schedule, and members arrive for slots that do not exist. Which security goal was MOST directly harmed?

options.A: Integrity, because the booking data is no longer accurate
options.B: Availability, because members could not use the slots they booked
options.C: Non-repudiation, because the clerk could deny making the change
options.D: None, because an authorized clerk made the change by mistake

questions.key_concept: Integrity covers accidental changes as well as attacks: data overwritten by mistake is no longer accurate, which is an integrity failure.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the data became unreachable, exposed or wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Integrity means data stays accurate and complete. The tee times were replaced with wrong ones, so the data is no longer correct; mistakes by authorized staff harm integrity just as attacks do. Availability, the runner-up, fails when authorized users cannot reach a system or its data; here the booking system worked, but the data it served was wrong, which is why members turned up for missing slots.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: members could not play the slots they booked. But the system stayed reachable; the cause was wrong data, so the harm is to integrity.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because changes need tracing. But the stem already says the clerk made it, and nobody denies anything; the problem is the data itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no attacker was involved. But security goals cover errors too; an authorized user's mistake can still break integrity.

tips: Eliminate: C needs someone denying an action, which the stem does not describe, and D wrongly treats honest mistakes as outside security.
Final two: A beats B because the system stayed reachable; members were misled by wrong data, and wrong data is an integrity failure.
Exam cue: if the system works but the data is wrong, think integrity. Availability fails only when authorized people cannot reach what they need.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Integrity fails through alteration: data or a system changes without authorization' (notes 1.1.1 The CIA Triad). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A researcher publishes working code that takes control of a door controller model still used at a perfume maker's warehouse. What is the published code MOST accurately?

options.A: An exploit, because it is the means of using the weakness
options.B: A vulnerability, because it shows the controller is weak
options.C: A threat, because it can be used to harm the warehouse
options.D: A risk, because it is the chance that harm will happen

questions.key_concept: A vulnerability is the weakness, an exploit is the code or technique that uses it, and a threat is who or what might use it.
questions.pre_read: Recall the separate meanings of threat, vulnerability, exploit and risk.
questions.correct_explanation: An exploit is the technique or code that takes advantage of a vulnerability. The weakness sits in the door controller; the published code is the means of using it. A threat, the runner-up, is the person or event that could cause harm, such as an attacker who downloads and runs the code. Publishing the exploit makes that threat more capable, which raises likelihood.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the code proves the controller is weak. But the vulnerability is the flaw in the controller itself; the code is how someone uses it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the code can certainly help cause harm. But a threat is the actor or event, such as an attacker; the code is the tool they would use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the code makes harm more likely. But risk is the combined likelihood and impact of harm, not the code that raises it.

tips: Eliminate: B puts the weakness in the code rather than the controller, and D names the overall likelihood and impact rather than one part.
Final two: A beats C because a threat is who or what might cause harm, such as an attacker; the code is the means they would use.
Exam cue: the weakness is the vulnerability, the tool that uses it is the exploit, whoever might use it is the threat, and the chance and cost of harm is the risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'An exploit is the technique or code that takes advantage of a weakness' (notes 1.2.1 Threats, Vulnerabilities and Risk). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A water park treated a ticket-fraud risk by adding a daily sales reconciliation. In the monitoring step of the risk lifecycle, what should its risk team check MOST?

options.A: Whether the reconciliation works and the risk stays within tolerance
options.B: Whether the original assessment used the correct rating scale
options.C: Whether a cheaper control could now replace the reconciliation
options.D: Whether the risk's register entry can be closed, as a control exists

questions.key_concept: Monitoring checks that chosen responses work and that each risk stays within tolerance as things change; then the cycle repeats.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each lifecycle step produces, and what monitoring adds after treatment.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring follows treatment: it checks that the chosen response is in place and working, and that the risk stays within tolerance as threats and the business change. A reconciliation nobody checks may quietly stop catching fraud. Finding a cheaper control, the runner-up, is a treatment decision for the risk owner; monitoring may prompt one, but its job is to confirm effectiveness first.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because ratings matter. But checking the rating scale belongs to assessment, which already happened; monitoring looks at the treated risk now.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: monitoring results can lead to a better treatment. But choosing a cheaper control is a treatment decision; monitoring first checks that this one works.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a control is now in place. But a risk stays open while it exists; a control lowers it, and only the risk owner closes an entry.

tips: Eliminate: B belongs to the assessment step, and D wrongly treats adding a control as the end of the cycle.
Final two: A beats C because monitoring confirms the response works and the risk stays within limits; picking a new control is a later treatment choice.
Exam cue: after treatment comes monitoring. Ask whether the control works and whether the risk has changed, then loop back if needed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Monitor, and repeat on a schedule and after major changes or incidents' (notes 1.2.2 The Risk Management Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A chocolate maker has the same unpatched flaw on its internet-facing ordering server holding customer accounts and on an internal test server with dummy data. Which conclusion should the risk analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Equal risk, since the same flaw is present on each
options.B: Higher for the test server, as lax patching raises likelihood
options.C: Higher for the ordering server, on likelihood and impact
options.D: No rating yet, until the flaw is exploited somewhere

questions.key_concept: The same vulnerability carries different risk on different systems: exposure drives likelihood and the asset's value drives impact.
questions.pre_read: Rate each server's likelihood and impact separately, using what the stem says about each one.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk depends on the asset, not only the flaw. The ordering server faces the internet, so attackers can reach the flaw more easily (higher likelihood), and it holds customer accounts, so a breach would cost far more (higher impact). Equal risk, the runner-up, treats the shared flaw as the whole story; the same vulnerability carries different risk on systems with different exposure and value.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the flaw is identical on both. But risk also depends on who can reach the system and what it holds, and the two servers differ on both.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because test systems are often neglected. But the stem gives no patching difference, and a server with dummy data has little to lose.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because active exploitation raises likelihood. But risks are rated before attacks happen; waiting for one leaves customer accounts exposed.

tips: Eliminate: B rests on a patching difference the stem never gives, and D waits for an attack before rating a risk.
Final two: C beats A because the flaw is shared but the context is not: the ordering server is reachable from the internet and holds customer accounts.
Exam cue: rate risk per asset. The same flaw scores higher likelihood where it is exposed and higher impact where the data is valuable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Likelihood weighs threat activity, how easy the weakness is to use and existing controls' (notes 1.2.3 Assessing Likelihood and Impact). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Final fix round (4 Nov 2026): canonical role name.

questions.question: A festival organizer's ticket-scanning tablets are worth $800 each, each theft is a total loss, and about 15 are stolen a year. Which annualized loss expectancy (ALE) should the risk analyst report as MOST accurate?

options.A: $12,000 a year
options.B: $800 a year
options.C: $53 a year
options.D: $120 a year

questions.key_concept: ALE is SLE times ARO, and ARO can exceed 1: an event that happens 15 times a year has an ARO of 15.
questions.pre_read: Work out the cost of one theft first, then multiply by how often thefts happen each year.
questions.correct_explanation: A stolen tablet is a total loss, so the exposure factor is 100% and the single loss expectancy (SLE) is $800. About 15 thefts a year is an annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) of 15, so ALE = $800 × 15 = $12,000 a year. The runner-up, $800, is the SLE: the cost of one theft, not the expected loss per year.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: $800 is a correct figure, but for one theft. That is the SLE; the yearly figure multiplies it by the 15 thefts expected each year.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it uses both numbers. But it divides by 15 as if one theft happened every 15 years; 15 a year is an ARO of 15.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because 15 can look like a percentage. But 15 is how many thefts happen a year, not an exposure factor; each theft loses the whole tablet.

tips: Eliminate: C treats 15 thefts a year as one every 15 years, and D reads the yearly count as a 15% exposure factor.
Final two: A beats B because $800 is the cost of one theft (the SLE); ALE multiplies it by the 15 thefts expected each year.
Exam cue: ALE = SLE × ARO. 'Once every N years' gives an ARO of 1/N, but 'N times a year' gives an ARO of N.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: quantitative assessments support cost-benefit analysis of risk responses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Step 5: annualized loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE × ARO, the expected loss per year' (notes 1.2.4 Qualitative and Quantitative Analysis). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Final fix round (4 Nov 2026): canonical role name.

questions.question: A campground operator keeps its online booking site but adds a web application firewall and weekly patching to cut its breach risk. Which risk treatment is this MOST accurately?

options.A: Avoidance, because a breach becomes far less likely to happen
options.B: Transfer, because the firewall vendor now carries the risk
options.C: Acceptance, because some breach risk still remains after the changes
options.D: Mitigation, because controls reduce the risk of the activity

questions.key_concept: Mitigation keeps the activity and adds controls to reduce its risk; the residual risk that remains does not make it acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the activity continues, and what the new controls change.
questions.correct_explanation: Mitigation keeps the risky activity and adds controls that lower likelihood or impact; the firewall and patching do exactly that while bookings continue. Acceptance, the runner-up, is a deliberate decision to take a risk without further action. Every mitigated risk leaves some residual risk, which its owner may then accept, but the response chosen here is to reduce the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a breach becomes less likely. But avoidance means stopping the activity; the site keeps taking bookings, so the risk is reduced, not avoided.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a vendor supplies the firewall. But buying a product moves no risk; transfer shifts financial impact to another party, such as an insurer.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: residual risk does remain. But acceptance means choosing not to act further; here the operator acted to reduce the risk, which is mitigation.

tips: Eliminate: A would mean shutting the booking site down, and B confuses buying a security product with shifting financial impact to another party.
Final two: D beats C because adding controls is mitigation; residual risk remains after any treatment and is accepted separately by its owner.
Exam cue: every treatment leaves some residual risk, so 'risk remains' never alone means acceptance. Ask what the organization chose to do about the risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk treatment is choosing how to respond to an assessed risk: avoid, mitigate, transfer (share) or accept it' (notes 1.2.5 Risk Treatment Options). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A surf school's booking-kiosk risk is within tolerance, yet its risk owner wants a cheap card-reader cover, and a colleague says tolerable risks must be accepted. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree, since within tolerance means the risk must be accepted
options.B: Agree, unless the owner gets senior management to approve treating it
options.C: Disagree, since every risk must be treated until it is gone
options.D: Disagree, as the owner chooses whether to accept or treat it

questions.key_concept: Tolerance caps the risk that may be accepted but does not force acceptance; within it, the risk owner may accept or treat the risk.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a tolerance limit allows, and who decides about a risk that sits within it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk tolerance sets the most risk the organization will accept; it is a ceiling, not an instruction. Within it, the risk owner chooses the response, and a cheap control that lowers the risk further is a valid choice. Senior management approval, the runner-up, applies to risks beyond tolerance; this one is within it, so the owner decides.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tolerable risks are often accepted. But tolerance is the most risk that may be accepted, not a rule that it must be; owners can still treat it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: senior management does decide some risks. But they decide those beyond tolerance; within it, the risk owner chooses the response.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds safest. But no control removes all risk, and treating every risk to zero would cost more than the harm it prevents.

tips: Eliminate: A turns a ceiling into a duty to accept, and C demands zero risk, which no set of controls can reach.
Final two: D beats B because the risk is within tolerance, so its owner may accept it or treat it; senior management decides beyond tolerance.
Exam cue: tolerance marks how much risk may be accepted, not how much must be. Below that line, the risk owner picks the response.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Residual risk within tolerance can be formally accepted by its owner; anything beyond goes to senior leaders' (notes 1.2.6 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and Acceptance). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A publisher rated the risk of editors pasting manuscripts into public AI tools as High, then rated it Medium after adding an approved AI tool and upload filters. What is the Medium rating MOST accurately?

options.A: The inherent risk, before any controls are counted
options.B: The risk tolerance the publisher's leaders have set
options.C: The residual risk that remains after the controls
options.D: The risk appetite for the use of AI writing tools

questions.key_concept: Inherent risk is rated before controls; residual risk is what remains after them. Tolerance and appetite are limits, not ratings.
questions.pre_read: Separate ratings of a risk from the limits leaders set on how much risk is acceptable.
questions.correct_explanation: Residual risk is the risk that remains after controls are applied. High was the inherent rating, made before the approved tool and filters; Medium is what is left with them in place. Risk tolerance, the runner-up, is a limit leaders set: if Medium is within it, the risk owner may accept the risk; if it is beyond it, senior management decides whether to accept it or require more treatment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is one of the two ratings. But inherent risk is the High rating, made before the approved tool and filters were counted.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: tolerance is the yardstick for this rating. But tolerance is a limit leaders set; the Medium rating is the risk measured against it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because appetite concerns how much risk to take. But appetite is the leaders' broad stance, not a rating of one risk after controls.

tips: Eliminate: A is the High rating made before controls, and D is the leaders' broad stance on risk rather than a rating.
Final two: C beats B because Medium measures the risk left after controls; tolerance is the limit that rating is compared with.
Exam cue: inherent comes before controls, residual comes after them, and tolerance is the line residual risk is checked against.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix B Glossary (residual risk); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Inherent risk is rated before controls; residual risk is what remains after them' (notes 1.2.3 Assessing Likelihood and Impact). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.
