questions.question: A gym's procedure says whoever finds a risk logs it. A help desk technician finds unsupported booking software, whose owner asks them not to log it before an upgrade; what should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Hold off logging the risk until the owner's upgrade is done
options.B: Upgrade the booking system to a supported version tonight
options.C: Log the risk, noting the owner's planned upgrade in the entry
options.D: Move the booking system behind a stricter firewall rule

questions.key_concept: When procedure gives logging to the finder, an owner's request cannot keep a risk off the register; record the owner's plan in the entry.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the procedure requires of the finder from what the owner gets to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure makes logging the finder's duty, and the register is how risks stay visible to the people who oversee them. The owner decides the treatment, here the upgrade, so the technician logs the risk and records the planned fix in the entry. Holding off logging it, the runner-up, defers to the owner, but owners decide what to do about a risk, not whether it is recorded.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner does decide about the system. But the procedure requires logging, and an unlogged risk is hidden from oversight even if a fix is planned.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because upgrading removes the weakness. But it changes a system the technician does not own, outside change control, and takes over the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to lower exposure quickly. But a firewall change is a treatment decision for the owner, made through change control.

tips: Eliminate: B and D both change a system the technician does not own and pick a treatment that is the owner's decision.
Final two: C beats A because owners decide how a risk is treated, not whether it is recorded; the procedure still requires the finder to log it.
Exam cue: a planned fix is no reason to keep a risk off the register. Record it, note the plan, and let the owner treat it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-01 (vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated and recorded); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Anyone can raise a risk; the owner decides what happens to it' (notes 1.2.7 Risk Register, Ownership and Reporting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Final fix round (4 Nov 2026): key concept re-angled away from cc_d1_031.

questions.question: At a piano maker, the sales director decides who may see customer contracts, and a system administrator configures and backs up the contract database. Which role is the administrator MOST accurately performing?

options.A: Data owner, because they control the contract database's access settings
options.B: Data custodian, because they apply and maintain the owner's rules
options.C: Risk owner, because they manage the contract system's risks
options.D: Data user, because they handle the contracts in their work

questions.key_concept: The data owner decides who may access data; the custodian, often IT, applies those decisions and maintains the systems that hold it.
questions.pre_read: Separate who decides about the data from who looks after the systems that hold it.
questions.correct_explanation: A data custodian looks after data on the owner's behalf: configuring access as the owner decides, running backups and maintaining the system. The sales director decides who may see contracts, which makes them the data owner. Data owner, the runner-up, is tempting because the administrator holds the technical controls, but holding the settings is not the same as deciding who may have access.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the administrator controls the settings. But the sales director decides who may see contracts; carrying out those decisions is the custodian's job.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because administrators deal with system risks. But a risk owner is accountable for deciding how a risk is treated, which the stem does not describe.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the administrator handles the data. But users work with data for business tasks; this role configures and protects the system holding it.

tips: Eliminate: C names an accountable decision-maker for risks, which the stem does not describe, and D describes people who use data for business work.
Final two: B beats A because the sales director decides access; the administrator carries out those decisions and keeps the database running and backed up.
Exam cue: owners decide, custodians carry out. The person with technical control is often the custodian, not the owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The custodian applies access settings; the data owner decides who gets access' (notes 1.3.1 Security Governance and Its Roles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: During a file-share cleanup at a ferry company, a network technician finds a folder of crew passport scans that no department will claim. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the folder, since no department will claim it
options.B: Tell the security manager about the unowned folder
options.C: Record the human resources director as the folder's owner
options.D: Leave the folder in place until a department claims it

questions.key_concept: Every data set needs an owner who decides about it; practitioners report unowned data to the security manager rather than assign or delete it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who has the authority to decide about data, and what to do when nobody holds it.
questions.correct_explanation: Owners decide about their data: who may see it, how long it is kept and when it is deleted. Unowned data has nobody to make those decisions, so the technician reports the folder to the security manager, who arranges an owner. Recording the human resources director as owner, the runner-up, guesses at a business decision the technician has no authority to make.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because unclaimed data seems unneeded. But deletion is the owner's decision, the scans may have to be kept by law, and deleting cannot be undone.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: human resources may well be the right owner. But assigning ownership is a management decision, not the technician's, so the folder goes to the security manager.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it changes nothing. But sensitive scans stay unmanaged, possibly open to many staff, with nobody deciding who may see them.

tips: Eliminate: A deletes data that only an owner may decide to delete, and D leaves sensitive scans unmanaged with nobody deciding about them.
Final two: B beats C because assigning an owner is a management decision; the technician reports the gap instead of choosing an owner themselves.
Exam cue: every asset needs an owner. When you find data nobody owns, report it to the security manager rather than deciding for it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Send ownership questions to the named owner, and report unowned data to the security manager' (notes 1.3.1 Security Governance and Its Roles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A tax-preparation firm's retention policy says to delete client files after 2 years, and an accountant warns that national tax law requires 6. What should the system administrator who runs deletions do FIRST?

options.A: Run the deletion job as the approved retention policy requires
options.B: Edit the retention policy to six years, then run the job
options.C: Pause the deletion job and refer the conflict to legal counsel
options.D: Change the job to keep files six years, as the accountant advises

questions.key_concept: Laws outrank internal policy. When they seem to conflict, stop irreversible steps and bring in legal counsel rather than interpreting the law alone.
questions.pre_read: Rank the two rules by authority, and note which action could not be undone.
questions.correct_explanation: Laws outrank internal policy, and deleted files cannot be recovered, so the administrator pauses the deletions and refers the conflict to legal counsel, who confirm what the law requires and how the policy must change. Changing the job as the accountant advises, the runner-up, also keeps the files, but it acts on an informal reading of the law and changes an approved setting without legal advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because staff must follow approved policy. But a law outranks internal policy, and deleting files the law may require cannot be undone.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the policy may be what is wrong. But a practitioner cannot rewrite an approved policy; its owner changes it after legal advice.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it keeps the files safe. But it acts on an accountant's informal reading of the law and changes an approved setting; legal counsel confirms what applies first.

tips: Eliminate: A follows a policy that may break the law, and B has the administrator rewrite a policy they do not own.
Final two: C beats D because pausing keeps every option open while legal counsel confirms the law, instead of the administrator interpreting it alone.
Exam cue: when law and policy seem to conflict, stop any step that cannot be undone and refer the question to legal counsel.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Laws outrank internal preference ... never interpret the law alone' (notes 1.3.2 Laws and Regulations). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A pottery studio's new payment vendor says it is certified to ISO/IEC 27002. Which response from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Accept it if the ISO/IEC certificate's scope covers the payment service
options.B: Question it, since ISO/IEC schemes certify products, not vendors
options.C: Accept it, since ISO/IEC 27002 has replaced ISO/IEC 27001
options.D: Question it, since certification is against ISO/IEC 27001 instead

questions.key_concept: Organizations certify against ISO/IEC 27001's requirements; ISO/IEC 27002 is companion control guidance that is not certified against.
questions.pre_read: Recall which of the well-known frameworks an organization can be certified against.
questions.correct_explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 sets the certifiable requirements for an information security management system; ISO/IEC 27002 is guidance on controls and is not certified against. So the analyst questions the claim and asks for the actual certificate. Checking scope, the runner-up, is a sound habit for a real ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, but no scope check can rescue a certificate that should not exist.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: checking that a certificate's scope covers the service is good practice. But accredited certification is against ISO/IEC 27001, so this claim fails first.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because some security certifications do cover products. But ISO/IEC 27001 certifies an organization's management system, so a vendor can hold one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both standards were updated in 2022. But they are companions, not versions: 27001 holds the certifiable requirements and 27002 the control guidance.

tips: Eliminate: B wrongly says ISO/IEC certification is only for products, and C treats 27002 as a newer version of 27001 rather than its companion guidance.
Final two: D beats A because certification is against ISO/IEC 27001; checking the scope of a 27002 certificate misses the real problem.
Exam cue: 27001 is the certifiable standard and 27002 is its companion control guidance. A claim of certification to 27002 is a red flag.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information security management systems: Requirements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Organizations get certified against ISO/IEC 27002 (exam trap: certification is against ISO/IEC 27001's requirements; 27002 is guidance)' (notes 1.3.3 Security Frameworks and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Final fix round (4 Nov 2026): edition year dropped from C so the options match.

questions.question: Using NIST CSF 2.0, a hostel chain's security manager records the outcomes the chain achieves today and those it aims to reach within two years. What has the manager MOST accurately produced?

options.A: A current profile and a target profile
options.B: A set of CSF tiers for the hostel chain
options.C: A CIS Controls implementation group
options.D: A certification plan for NIST CSF 2.0

questions.key_concept: A CSF 2.0 Current Profile records the outcomes achieved now, and a Target Profile the outcomes chosen as goals; the gap guides plans.
questions.pre_read: Recall how NIST CSF 2.0 describes where an organization is now and where it wants to be.
questions.correct_explanation: In NIST CSF 2.0, a Current Profile records the outcomes an organization achieves now, and a Target Profile records the outcomes it has chosen to reach; comparing them shows the gaps to plan for. CSF Tiers, the runner-up, are also part of CSF 2.0, but they describe how rigorous the organization's risk governance and management are, not which outcomes it achieves.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Tiers are part of NIST CSF 2.0. But they rate the rigor of risk governance and management, not the specific outcomes achieved now and planned.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because implementation groups also set a path. But they belong to the CIS Controls, which rank safeguards, not CSF outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a two-year goal sounds like preparing for an audit. But NIST CSF 2.0 is voluntary and has no certification.

tips: Eliminate: C comes from the CIS Controls, not CSF 2.0, and D assumes CSF 2.0 offers a certification it does not have.
Final two: A beats B because profiles record which outcomes are achieved now and targeted later, while tiers describe how rigorous risk management is.
Exam cue: CSF 2.0 profiles answer 'which outcomes now, and which next?'; tiers answer 'how rigorous is our approach?'
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (CSF Profiles: Organizational Profiles are used to understand, tailor, assess, prioritize and communicate outcomes); NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.2 (CSF Tiers: Tiers characterize the rigor of an organization's cybersecurity risk governance and management practices)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'In CSF 2.0, a Current Profile records the outcomes achieved now and a Target Profile the outcomes sought; Tiers rate how rigorous risk governance and management are' (notes 1.3.3 Security Frameworks and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A dance academy's leaders want one document setting out the academy's security objectives, who is responsible for what, and its commitment to meet legal duties. Which document BEST fits what they want?

options.A: The acceptable use policy for staff and students
options.B: The top-level information security policy
options.C: A standard listing approved security settings
options.D: A guideline of good everyday security habits

questions.key_concept: The top-level information security policy states objectives, scope, responsibilities and commitments; topic policies, standards and guidelines sit beneath it.
questions.pre_read: Match each document's breadth and authority to what the leaders want it to cover.
questions.correct_explanation: The top-level information security policy sets the organization's security objectives, scope and responsibilities, and commits it to meeting legal and other requirements; senior management approves it. An acceptable use policy, the runner-up, is a real policy too, but a topic policy covering one area, how people may use systems, rather than the academy's overall objectives and responsibilities.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an acceptable use policy is mandatory and approved by leaders. But it is a topic policy for one area, not the document setting overall objectives and duties.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because standards are mandatory. But a standard gives specific settings under a policy; it does not set objectives or assign responsibilities.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because guidelines spread good habits. But they are optional advice, so they cannot set mandatory objectives and duties.

tips: Eliminate: C holds specific settings that sit under policy, and D is optional advice that cannot set mandatory duties.
Final two: B beats A because the leaders want the academy's overall objectives and responsibilities; an acceptable use policy covers one topic only.
Exam cue: overall direction, scope and responsibilities belong in the top-level policy; single areas get topic policies beneath it.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.1 (Policies for information security); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (cybersecurity policy is established, communicated and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A top-level information security policy sets objectives, scope and responsibilities' (notes 1.3.4 Security Policies). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An escape room company's help desk technician finds a faster order for the steps in the documented new-laptop setup procedure, which the IT manager owns. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Follow the procedure and suggest the faster order to its owner
options.B: Use the faster order, since procedures are recommended steps
options.C: Use the faster order, since the finished laptop ends up the same
options.D: Rewrite the procedure document, then tell its owner

questions.key_concept: Procedures are mandatory steps; improvements go to the procedure's owner, who approves changes, rather than being applied on one's own.
questions.pre_read: Recall which document types are mandatory, and who approves changes to each.
questions.correct_explanation: Procedures are mandatory: they list the exact steps for a task, often in an order that matters for reasons a technician may not see. The technician follows the current steps and suggests the faster order to the IT manager, who approves changes. Using the faster order because the result looks the same, the runner-up, skips that check; a step order can carry controls, such as encrypting a laptop before it joins the network.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because some documents are only advice. But that describes guidelines; procedures are mandatory steps that staff follow as written.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the outcome seems unchanged. But the technician cannot confirm the order does not matter; the owner checks before the procedure changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the owner hears about it. But the owner approves changes first; editing the procedure and telling them afterward bypasses that approval.

tips: Eliminate: B describes guidelines rather than procedures, and D changes a document before its owner has approved the change.
Final two: A beats C because the order of steps may carry controls the technician cannot see; the owner confirms before anything changes.
Exam cue: mandatory documents are followed as written. Improvements go to the document's owner; they are not applied on your own.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Standards, Guidelines, and Procedures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Procedures list the exact steps for a task, such as setting up a new user' (notes 1.3.5 Standards, Procedures and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A student-housing company plans four new uses of AI. Which use should its security analyst flag to legal counsel for review FIRST?

options.A: Deciding which tenants must pay a larger security deposit
options.B: Summarizing internal meeting notes for the staff team
options.C: Suggesting the best times to clean each shared kitchen
options.D: Drafting social media posts for marketing to review

questions.key_concept: AI that makes decisions about people draws consumer, privacy and AI-specific law, so it goes to legal review before use.
questions.pre_read: Ask which use decides something about people outside the company.
questions.correct_explanation: AI that decides something about people, such as who must pay a larger deposit, falls under consumer, privacy and anti-discrimination law, and AI laws such as the EU AI Act add duties for some decisions about people. It goes to legal counsel first. Summarizing meeting notes, the runner-up, may touch personal data, but it informs staff rather than deciding anything about tenants.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: meeting notes can mention people, so privacy rules apply. But the summaries inform staff and decide nothing about tenants, so the deposit tool comes first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it uses AI on company data. But scheduling cleaning uses kitchen-use patterns and makes no decision about any person.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because public posts carry reputational risk. But a person in marketing reviews each draft, and no decision about anyone is made.

tips: Eliminate: C schedules cleaning without deciding anything about people, and D has a person review every draft before it goes out.
Final two: A beats B because deciding who pays a larger deposit is a decision about customers, which consumer, privacy and AI laws regulate most closely.
Exam cue: when AI decides something about people, such as money, jobs or housing, bring in legal counsel before it goes live.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.1 (legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed and documented); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Employment and consumer laws also reach AI decisions about people' (notes 1.3.6 Laws and Rules That Apply to AI). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bridal shop loses about $4,000 a year in stolen sample veils and jewelry, and its owner wants a control. Which proposal from the security analyst is BEST?

options.A: An extra floor assistant at $20,000 a year, stopping most thefts
options.B: Security tags at $1,500 a year, stopping most thefts
options.C: Locked cases at $4,500 a year, stopping almost every theft
options.D: Staff training at $500 a year, stopping about a tenth of thefts

questions.key_concept: A control is worth it when the yearly loss it prevents exceeds its yearly cost; neither the strongest nor the cheapest option wins by default.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each proposal would save each year with what it would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: A control is worth buying when the loss it prevents each year is more than it costs. Tags stop most of the $4,000 yearly loss, so they save more than $2,000 a year, above their $1,500 cost. Staff training, the runner-up, is the cheapest option, but stopping a tenth of thefts saves about $400 a year, less than its $500 cost.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a watchful assistant stops most thefts. But at $20,000 a year it costs five times the whole $4,000 loss.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because locked cases stop almost every theft. But at $4,500 a year they cost more than the entire $4,000 loss they protect.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it is the cheapest proposal. But stopping a tenth of $4,000 saves about $400 a year, less than its $500 cost.

tips: Eliminate: A costs five times the $4,000 yearly loss, and C costs more than all of it, however well each stops theft.
Final two: B beats D because the cheapest option is not the best value; training saves about $400 for $500, while tags save over $2,000 for $1,500.
Exam cue: compare what a control saves each year with what it costs. Neither the strongest nor the cheapest control wins on that alone.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: quantitative assessments support cost-benefit analysis of risk responses); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-7 (Risk Response)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Its yearly cost should not exceed the loss it is expected to prevent' (notes 1.4.1 What a Security Control Is). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Final fix round (4 Nov 2026): savings claims limited to what 'most thefts' supports.

questions.question: After a change to a bowling alley chain's firewall, which the network manager owns, the change procedure has the network technician confirm the new blocks work. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the network manager to confirm that the new blocks work
options.B: Try the blocked connections from outside and record the results
options.C: Check that the console shows the change without errors, and record it
options.D: Watch intrusion detection alerts for any traffic that gets through

questions.key_concept: A technical control is proven by testing what it does; when the procedure assigns the test, the practitioner runs it.
questions.pre_read: Note what the change procedure assigns to the technician, and how a block is best shown to work.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure gives the technician the job of confirming the blocks, and the reliable way is to test them: attempt the blocked connections from outside and record what happens. Asking the network manager to confirm, the runner-up, routes the task to the owner, but the procedure assigned this check to the technician, and the owner would still need a test to know.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the network manager owns the firewall. But the procedure assigns the check to the technician, and the owner's view is no substitute for a test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it looks at the change itself. But a change can apply without errors and still block the wrong thing; only a test shows the effect.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because detection would reveal leaks. But waiting for alerts leaves attackers to test the rules, and the detection system may not flag everything.

tips: Eliminate: C shows the change was applied, not that it blocks anything, and D waits for real traffic to reveal gaps instead of testing.
Final two: B beats A because the procedure assigns the check to the technician; a named owner does not take back a task the procedure gives you.
Exam cue: prove a technical control by testing its effect. When the procedure assigns the test to you, run it rather than passing it upward.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3(2) (Configuration Change Control | Testing, Validation, and Documentation of Changes); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'All depend on correct configuration; a wrong firewall rule opens the path it should close' (notes 1.4.2 Technical Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Outside cleaners work overnight at a boatbuilder's design office, where engineers leave printed hull drawings on their desks. Which administrative control should the security manager propose as BEST?

options.A: A clean-desk rule that engineers lock drawings away each night
options.B: Cameras recording the design office throughout the night
options.C: A sign-in sheet for the cleaners at the front desk
options.D: Encryption of the hull drawing files on the design server

questions.key_concept: Administrative controls are rules and practices people follow, such as a clean-desk rule; cameras are physical and encryption is technical.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option by control type first, then ask whether it protects the printed drawings.
questions.correct_explanation: A clean-desk rule is an administrative control: a rule people follow, here putting printed drawings away each night so overnight visitors cannot see them. A sign-in sheet, the runner-up, is also administrative, but it only records who was in the building; it does nothing to keep the drawings out of view while the cleaners work.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because cameras watch the office overnight. But they are a physical control that records events; they would not stop anyone reading the drawings.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a sign-in sheet is an administrative control too. But it only shows who came in; the drawings stay on desks in plain view.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects drawing files. But it is a technical control for stored files; the risk here is printed copies left on desks.

tips: Eliminate: B is a physical control that only records, and D is a technical control that protects files, not paper.
Final two: A beats C because both are administrative, but only the clean-desk rule keeps the printed drawings out of sight.
Exam cue: sort the options by control type first, then ask which one actually treats the stated risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Administrative controls, also called managerial controls, are the policies, procedures, training and people practices that direct how security is handled' (notes 1.4.3 Administrative Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A mountain observatory's data servers crash during brief power cuts, and its standby generator takes about a minute to start. Which physical control should the facilities team add as BEST?

options.A: A second standby generator that starts up at the same moment
options.B: A surge protector on the power feed to each of the servers
options.C: A gas fire suppression system for the server room
options.D: A battery-backed uninterruptible power supply for the servers

questions.key_concept: An uninterruptible power supply bridges the gap between a power cut and backup power; a generator alone needs time to start.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to the servers in the seconds before the generator is running.
questions.correct_explanation: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) switches to battery the instant mains power fails, so the servers keep running through brief cuts and until the generator takes over, or can shut down cleanly. A surge protector, the runner-up, guards against voltage spikes, but it stores no energy, so the servers still lose power the moment the mains drops.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it adds backup power. But a second generator needs the same start-up time, so the servers still crash in the gap.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a surge protector does guard equipment from power problems. But it only blocks spikes; it supplies no power when the mains cuts out.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because server rooms need fire protection. But fire suppression does nothing for crashes caused by power cuts.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the same start-up gap, and C answers fire rather than power loss.
Final two: D beats B because a surge protector stops voltage spikes but holds no energy; only a UPS keeps the servers powered through the gap.
Exam cue: brief outages and generator start-up gaps call for a UPS, spikes call for surge protection, and long outages call for a generator.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-11 (Emergency Power)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Backup power has two parts: an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) carries equipment on battery the instant power fails, and a generator takes over once it starts' (notes 1.4.4 Physical Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: After a spice importer's antivirus flags malware on a sales laptop, the help desk technician removes the malware from it. Which control function does the removal MOST accurately serve?

options.A: Detective, because the malware was found on the laptop
options.B: Recovery, because the laptop can be used for work again
options.C: Corrective, because it takes away the cause of the problem
options.D: Deterrent, because it discourages attackers from trying again

questions.key_concept: Corrective controls fix the cause of a problem; recovery controls restore normal operations; detective controls find the problem.
questions.pre_read: Separate what found the problem, what fixed it and what would bring service back.
questions.correct_explanation: Corrective controls fix the problem itself; removing the malware takes away the cause of the harm on this laptop. Recovery, the runner-up, restores normal operations after an incident, such as rebuilding a system or restoring files from backup. The removal may let the laptop return to work, but its function is fixing the cause; recovery covers what is needed beyond that.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because detection happened. But the antivirus alert did the detecting; the removal that followed is what this question asks about.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the laptop does return to use. But recovery restores operations, such as files from backup; removing the malware fixes the cause, which is corrective.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removal makes the laptop a harder target. But deterrents discourage attacks before they happen, like warning signs; removal does not.

tips: Eliminate: A describes the antivirus alert rather than the removal, and D describes controls that discourage attacks before they happen.
Final two: C beats B because removing malware fixes the cause; recovery is restoring normal operations, such as data from backup, when more is needed.
Exam cue: found it is detective, fixed the cause is corrective, and brought service back is recovery.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MI-02 (incidents are eradicated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'corrective fixes the problem; recovery restores normal operations' (notes 1.4.5 Control Functions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An immigration advice service's standard requires full-disk encryption, but six old laptops cannot support it, and the standard's owner will consider a compensating control. Which proposal fits BEST?

options.A: Install antivirus scanning on the six old laptops
options.B: Require longer sign-in passwords on the six old laptops
options.C: Keep client files on the central server, not the laptops
options.D: Remind staff each year to keep the old laptops with them

questions.key_concept: A compensating control must reduce the same risk as the missing control, by another means; unrelated safeguards do not compensate.
questions.pre_read: Name the risk full-disk encryption treats, then test each option against that risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Full-disk encryption protects client data on a lost or stolen laptop. Keeping client files off those laptops, on the central server, removes that exposure by another means, so it compensates for the same risk. Longer passwords, the runner-up, protect the sign-in, but a thief who removes the disk can read unencrypted files without ever signing in, so the risk remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because antivirus is a sound control. But it treats malware, not data exposed on a stolen laptop, so it does not stand in for encryption.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: stronger passwords protect the sign-in. But a thief can remove the disk and read unencrypted files without signing in.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because careful staff lose fewer laptops. But a yearly reminder still leaves readable files on any laptop that is lost or stolen.

tips: Eliminate: A treats malware rather than stolen data, and D relies on a yearly reminder while the laptops still hold readable files.
Final two: C beats B because removing the disk bypasses a password; keeping files off the laptops removes the exposure encryption was meant to cover.
Exam cue: a compensating control must reduce the same risk as the missing one. Name that risk, then test each substitute against it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Appendix A Glossary (compensating controls); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'When a required control is impossible, a compensating control reduces the same risk another way' (notes 1.4.6 Layering and Compensating Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.4 Security controls. Controls for AI tools
questions.question: A greeting card maker's AI image tool checks each image it generates and blocks any showing a real person's likeness before staff can download it. Which control function does this check MOST accurately perform?

options.A: Detective, because it spots images showing a real person
options.B: Preventive, because it stops those images being released
options.C: Corrective, because it fixes images after they go out
options.D: Deterrent, because it discourages staff from requesting them

questions.key_concept: A control that stops an unwanted event before it happens is preventive, even if it must spot the problem first, like an AI output filter.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each control function does, then match it to what this check does to each image.
questions.correct_explanation: A preventive control stops an unwanted event before it happens. The check blocks look-alike images before anyone can download them, so none reach a printed card. Detective, the runner-up, is tempting because the check must first spot each image, but a detective control reports a problem after it occurs; this one stops the release.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the check does spot look-alike images. But it then blocks them before release, and stopping the event is what makes a control preventive.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the check deals with bad images. But corrective controls fix a problem after it happens; nothing has gone out yet.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because blocked requests may discourage staff. But deterrents work by discouraging, like warning notices; this check stops the images whatever staff intend.

tips: Eliminate: C acts after images go out, which this check never allows, and D works by discouraging people rather than blocking anything.
Final two: B beats A because the check stops look-alike images before release; a detective control would only report them afterward.
Exam cue: classify a control by its effect. If it stops the event before harm, it is preventive, even when it has to detect something first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.8 (Information Integrity: deepfakes and content that impersonates others)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Technical: limit who can change models and training data, filter inputs and outputs, and log prompts with the model version used' (notes 1.4.7 Controls for AI Tools). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: During a tender for new laptops, a bidding vendor offers a quarry company's security analyst two concert tickets, and the company's code of conduct bans gifts from bidders. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the tickets but leave the bid scoring to colleagues
options.B: Decline the tickets and report the offer to their manager
options.C: Accept the tickets and report them once the tender closes
options.D: Decline the tickets and keep the offer to themselves

questions.key_concept: A code of conduct protects fair dealing: decline a banned gift and tell your manager, so the offer itself can be handled.
questions.pre_read: Note what the code says about gifts, then ask who else needs to know about the offer.
questions.correct_explanation: The code bans gifts from bidders, so the analyst declines the tickets, and reporting the offer lets the manager judge whether the vendor's approach affects the tender. Declining quietly, the runner-up, keeps the analyst within the rule, but it hides an improper approach during a live tender from the people responsible for running it fairly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because stepping back from scoring seems to remove the bias. But the code bans the gift itself, whoever scores the bids.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reporting gifts is common practice. But the code bans gifts from bidders, and reporting one later does not make accepting it allowed.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: declining keeps to the rule. But the manager needs to know a bidder offered a gift, since it may affect how the tender is run.

tips: Eliminate: A and C both accept a gift the code bans, whatever happens to the scoring or the report afterward.
Final two: B beats D because declining keeps the analyst within the code, but the manager needs to know a bidder offered gifts during the tender.
Exam cue: in conduct questions, follow the rule and make the issue visible to the right person. Quiet compliance can leave others unaware.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior); ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Common themes are honesty, avoiding conflicts of interest and protecting confidential information' (notes 1.5.1 Professional Code of Conduct). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A roller rink's security analyst plans a conference talk using the rink's internal phishing statistics and screenshots of its email security console. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Use them, since they contain no customers' personal data
options.B: Use them after blurring the rink's logo in each screenshot
options.C: Ask their manager to approve showing the rink's material
options.D: Ask the conference organizers to approve the material first

questions.key_concept: Confidentiality duties cover an employer's internal business information, not just personal data; using it outside work needs approval.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the material, and whether anyone has approved its use outside work.
questions.correct_explanation: Codes of conduct protect an employer's confidential information, which includes internal statistics and views of its security tools, not only personal data. Screenshots of a security console can also reveal settings attackers could use. So the analyst asks their manager to approve the material first. No personal data, the runner-up, removes one concern but still shares the rink's business information without permission.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: no personal data makes it less sensitive. But internal statistics and console views are the rink's confidential information, which needs approval to share.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it hides whose slides they are. But the settings and statistics stay visible, and the analyst still lacks permission to share them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because organizers vet every talk. But they do not own the rink's information; only the rink can approve sharing its confidential material.

tips: Eliminate: B blurs the logo but leaves the internal details visible, and D seeks approval from organizers who do not own the material.
Final two: C beats A because confidential information includes the employer's own business data, not only customers' personal data.
Exam cue: before using work material outside work, ask who owns it and get their approval. Confidential is wider than personal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior); ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons (service to principals)

questions.subtopic: 1.5 Professional conduct. Due care and due diligence
questions.question: An e-bike maker's penetration test six months ago found an exposed admin page, but nobody acted on the report, and attackers have now broken in through it. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: It failed due care, since a known flaw was left unfixed
options.B: It failed due diligence, since the flaw was used in the break-in
options.C: It met its duties, since the attackers caused the break-in
options.D: It met due care, since it paid for a full penetration test

questions.key_concept: Due diligence finds the problem; due care acts on it. Knowing about a flaw and leaving it unfixed is a failure of due care.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the company found out from what it did about it.
questions.correct_explanation: Due diligence is finding out, and the company did that: the penetration test found the exposed page. Due care is acting on what is known, as a prudent organization would, and nobody did, so a break-in through a reported flaw is a due care failure. Failed due diligence, the runner-up, would mean the company never looked; here it looked and found the flaw, then failed to act.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: something in the company's duties clearly failed. But diligence was done when the test found the flaw; the failure was in acting on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the attackers are to blame for attacking. But duties are judged by the company's own conduct, and it left a known flaw open.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the test was money well spent. But a test is diligence; care requires acting on its results, which nobody did.

tips: Eliminate: C shifts the judgment to the attackers instead of the company's conduct, and D counts a test as care when care means acting on it.
Final two: A beats B because the company did find the flaw; the gap was in acting on it, which is due care.
Exam cue: found it but did nothing is a due care failure. Never looked is a due diligence failure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-8 (Penetration Testing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Knowing about a risk is enough to show due care (exam trap: knowledge without action is what negligence claims target)' (notes 1.5.2 Due Care and Due Diligence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A certified freelance analyst rushes a dog-grooming chain's firewall review, skipping steps their own method requires, and misses serious flaws. Which canon does this MOST directly breach?

options.A: Protect society, the common good and the infrastructure
options.B: Provide diligent and competent service to principals
options.C: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
options.D: Advance and protect the profession

questions.key_concept: Careless, incomplete work for a client fails the canon on diligent and competent service to principals.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the analyst was working for, and what kind of failure the stem describes.
questions.correct_explanation: The canon on diligent and competent service covers the quality of work done for principals, the employers and clients a member serves. Skipping steps and missing serious flaws in a client's review is a direct failure of that duty. Advancing and protecting the profession, the runner-up, can suffer from poor work, but only indirectly; the breach falls first on the client.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missed flaws could later hurt the public. But nothing in the stem describes harm to society; the failure is in work done for a client.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it covers responsible conduct. But nothing dishonest or illegal is described; the problem is careless work, which another canon names directly.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: shoddy work can harm the profession's reputation. But that harm is indirect; the direct breach is the incomplete service given to the client.

tips: Eliminate: A needs harm to the public, and C needs dishonest or illegal conduct; the stem describes neither.
Final two: B beats D because the careless review directly fails the client, the principal served; harm to the profession's reputation follows only indirectly.
Exam cue: match a breach to a canon by what went wrong: public harm, dishonesty or illegality, poor service to a client, or harm to the profession.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons (service to principals)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The canons below are in ISC2's order, quoted word for word, each with a plain-words gloss' (notes 1.5.3 The ISC2 Code of Ethics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: After customer data is stolen from an online board-game retailer, a manager asks the security analyst to break into the attacker's server and delete the copy. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Break in, since the stolen data belongs to the retailer
options.B: Break in just to delete the stolen files, touching nothing else
options.C: Decline, and ask the attacker's hosting provider to shut the server
options.D: Decline, and hand what they know to the incident response lead

questions.key_concept: Hacking back is illegal whatever the motive; an ethical practitioner declines and routes evidence through the incident response process.
questions.pre_read: Test each option for legality first, then for whether it uses the proper channel.
questions.correct_explanation: Breaking into the attacker's server is unauthorized access, which is illegal however good the motive, so the analyst declines. Handing what they know to the incident response lead keeps evidence and decisions in the proper channel, where the lead can involve legal counsel and law enforcement. Contacting the hosting provider directly, the runner-up, is legal, but outside contact during an incident is the lead's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the data is the retailer's. But owning the stolen data gives no right to enter someone else's server; that is still unauthorized access.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it limits the intrusion. But any unauthorized access is illegal, however narrow, and it can destroy evidence investigators need.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: asking a provider to act is lawful. But outside contact during an incident goes through the incident response lead, who coordinates with legal counsel.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both break into a system without authorization, which is illegal however the access is limited or justified.
Final two: D beats C because contacting outside parties during an incident is the incident response lead's call, made with legal counsel.
Exam cue: never hack back. Decline illegal requests, even from your employer, and route the matter through the incident process.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons; NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MA-04 (incidents are escalated or elevated as needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Stay within your authority: test only with the system owner's written permission, whoever is paying, and never hack back' (notes 1.5.4 Applying the Canons to Dilemmas). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A certified consultant did careless work for a local martial arts school, and the consultant's neighbor, who is not a security professional, wants to file an ethics complaint about it. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The neighbor may complain under any canon, as a public member
options.B: Only the certifying body itself may start an ethics complaint
options.C: The neighbor may complain under canon 4 about harm to the profession
options.D: Only the school, the principal served, may complain under canon 3

questions.key_concept: Standing depends on the canon: anyone under canons 1 and 2, principals under canon 3, fellow professionals under canon 4.
questions.pre_read: Name the canon that careless client work falls under, then recall who may complain under it.
questions.correct_explanation: Complaint standing depends on the canon. Careless work for a client falls under the canon on diligent and competent service, where only principals, such as the school that hired the consultant, may complain. Canon 4, the runner-up, does cover harm to the profession, but complaints under it may come only from fellow certified or licensed professionals who follow an ethics code, which the neighbor is not.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because anyone may complain under canons 1 and 2. But standing narrows for canons 3 and 4; not every canon is open to the public.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the certifying body enforces the code. But complaints come from people who claim injury and have standing; its committee reviews them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: canon 4 does concern the profession. But only fellow certified or licensed professionals who follow an ethics code may complain under it.

tips: Eliminate: A opens every canon to the public, and B wrongly limits complaints to the certifying body itself.
Final two: D beats C because canon 4 complaints come only from fellow professionals bound by an ethics code, and the neighbor is not one.
Exam cue: for standing, name the canon first: anyone for canons 1 and 2, principals for canon 3, fellow professionals for canon 4.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (standing of complainant and form of complaints)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Anyone may complain under canons 1 and 2; only principals, such as employers or clients, under canon 3' (notes 1.5.5 Ethics Complaints and Enforcement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A pet insurer's awareness lead wants an AI clone of the CEO's voice to narrate a staff video about phone scams, and the CEO has not been asked. What should the awareness lead do FIRST?

options.A: Use the clone, since the video protects staff from scams
options.B: Use the clone, built from the CEO's public talks and interviews
options.C: Label the voice as AI-generated, without asking the CEO
options.D: Ask the CEO's consent and label the voice as AI-generated

questions.key_concept: Using AI to imitate a real person needs that person's consent and an honest label; a good purpose or public recordings are not permission.
questions.pre_read: Note whose voice the video would imitate and who will hear it.
questions.correct_explanation: Imitating a real person with AI is honest only when that person agrees and the audience knows the voice is synthetic. The CEO has not been asked, so the lead asks for the CEO's consent and labels the narration as AI-generated. Labeling without asking, the runner-up, is honest with staff, but it still puts words in the CEO's voice without the CEO's permission.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the video teaches staff to resist scams. But a good purpose is not permission to imitate a real person, and staff are not told the voice is AI.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because public recordings seem fair to use. But being able to copy someone's voice is not permission to imitate it; the CEO still has not agreed.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a label keeps staff from being misled. But it does not give permission; imitating the CEO's voice still needs the CEO's consent.

tips: Eliminate: A and B use a real person's voice with no consent and no label; a good purpose or public recordings authorize neither.
Final two: D beats C because a label is honest with staff, but imitating the CEO still needs the CEO's consent.
Exam cue: using AI to imitate a real person needs that person's consent and an honest label, unless it is part of an authorized test.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons; NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.8 (Information Integrity: deepfakes and content that impersonates others)

questions.question: Customers queuing at a pawn shop's counter can read other customers' ID details on the clerk's screen. Which control should the security analyst propose to BEST protect this data?

options.A: Fit privacy filters to the counter screens facing the queue
options.B: Encrypt the database server that stores the customers' ID details
options.C: Hash each ID record so that any change can be detected
options.D: Log each customer record that the clerks open on screen

questions.key_concept: Confidentiality covers data on screen as well as stored data; screen filters stop onlookers, while encryption at rest does nothing for displayed data.
questions.pre_read: Note where the data is when the wrong people see it.
questions.correct_explanation: The exposure happens while the data is in use on screen, so the fix must stop onlookers from reading it there. Privacy filters narrow the viewing angle so only the clerk sees the screen. Encrypting the database, the runner-up, protects stored data, but the application decrypts records for the clerk, so people in the queue could still read the screen.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: encryption is a strong confidentiality control for stored data. But the screen shows decrypted records, so encryption at rest does nothing about onlookers in the queue.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hashing is a familiar security control. But a hash helps detect changes, an integrity goal; it does not stop anyone reading the screen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logging tracks who opens records. But it records the clerk's own lookups; it cannot stop customers in the queue from reading the screen.

tips: Eliminate: C protects integrity, not secrecy, and D records the clerk's lookups without stopping anyone in the queue from seeing the screen.
Final two: A beats B because the data leaks while displayed; encryption at rest protects storage, and the screen still shows decrypted records.
Exam cue: match the confidentiality control to where the data is exposed; stored, sent and on-screen data each need their own protection.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-5 (Access Control for Output Devices: monitor or screen filters); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Confidentiality covers data stored, sent or in use; encryption does not replace controls on displayed data' (notes 1.1.2 Confidentiality). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A subtitling firm encrypts each file it sends a streaming client, whose project lead says this also proves no file was altered in transit. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agreed, since nobody can alter data they are unable to read
options.B: Agreed, since encryption protects all three security goals at once
options.C: Not quite; it does if the files use the client's public key
options.D: Not quite; altered files can go unnoticed without an integrity check

questions.key_concept: Encryption hides content; detecting alteration needs an integrity check, such as a keyed hash, a signature or the built-in check of authenticated encryption.
questions.pre_read: Recall what encryption protects, and against what.
questions.correct_explanation: Encryption keeps the files secret, but an attacker can change ciphertext without reading it, and the change may go unnoticed. Detecting alteration needs an integrity check, such as a keyed hash or a digital signature; authenticated encryption modes build such a check in, and it is the check, not the secrecy, that reveals changes. Encrypting with the client's public key, the runner-up, proves nothing about changes, because anyone can encrypt with a public key.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because unreadable data feels untouchable. But attackers can change ciphertext blindly; without an integrity check, the change may go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption is the best-known security control. But it mainly serves confidentiality; it does not prove integrity or keep files available.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: public-key cryptography sounds like proof. But anyone can encrypt with the client's public key, so it shows neither who sent a file nor that it is unchanged.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes unreadable data cannot be changed, and B credits encryption with all three goals; encryption mainly protects confidentiality.
Final two: D beats C because anyone can encrypt with a public key, so only an integrity check, such as a signature, reveals an altered file.
Exam cue: encryption answers who can read it; integrity checks answer whether it changed. Never let one stand in for the other.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.1 (Data Encryption)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'If data is encrypted, nobody could have changed it (exam trap): attackers can alter encrypted data without reading it' (notes 1.1.3 Integrity and Authenticity). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A karaoke chain's booking app locks accounts for 24 hours after three failed sign-ins, so an attacker locked out every manager on a Saturday. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Swap the long lockout for waits that grow after each failure
options.B: Remove the failed sign-in limit so managers cannot be locked out
options.C: Lengthen the lockout to a week so that attackers stop guessing
options.D: Require every manager to set a longer, more complex password

questions.key_concept: A security control can become an availability weakness; short waits that grow after failed sign-ins slow guessing without letting attackers lock users out.
questions.pre_read: Ask which security goal the attacker actually harmed.
questions.correct_explanation: The attacker never needed the right password: three wrong guesses locked each manager out for a day, an availability attack. Waits that grow after each failure still slow guessing, but an attacker cannot shut users out for long. Longer passwords, the runner-up, make correct guesses harder, yet failed guesses would still trigger the same 24-hour lockouts.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because no limit means no lockouts. But unlimited attempts let attackers guess passwords freely, trading an availability problem for a confidentiality one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a harsher penalty sounds stronger. But it makes the attack worse: each burst of wrong guesses now shuts a manager out for a week.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: strong passwords resist guessing. But the attacker did not need to guess right; wrong guesses alone triggered the lockouts.

tips: Eliminate: B opens the door to unlimited password guessing, and C lengthens the very lockout the attacker is abusing, so availability gets worse.
Final two: A beats D because the harm came from failed guesses triggering lockouts; stronger passwords leave those lockouts in place.
Exam cue: when a protective control is turned against users, keep the protection but blunt its effect, such as delays instead of long lockouts.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.2 (Rate Limiting (Throttling): waits that grow after failed attempts reduce the chance an attacker locks out the legitimate user); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts: lockouts are usually temporary because of the potential for denial of service)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Availability is one of the three security goals; denial of service attacks it directly' (notes 1.1.4 Availability). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A hot-air balloon operator's staff portal asks for a password and then the answer to a security question. How should the security analyst MOST accurately describe this sign-in?

options.A: Multifactor, because it asks for two separate secrets
options.B: Single-factor, because both answers are something you know
options.C: Multifactor, because the answer is stored apart from the password
options.D: Single-factor, because neither check uses a fingerprint or face

questions.key_concept: Factors are counted by type, not by number of checks; a password plus a security answer is still one factor, something you know.
questions.pre_read: Recall the three authentication factor types.
questions.correct_explanation: Multifactor authentication needs two or more different factor types. A password and a security answer are both something the user knows, so the portal uses one factor twice. The runner-up reaches the same verdict for the wrong reason: a biometric is not required, since a password plus a code from an enrolled phone, something you have, would already be multifactor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because two checks feel like two factors. But factors count by type; two secrets the user knows are one factor.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because separate storage sounds like separation. But where answers are stored does not change their type; both are still something you know.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it reaches the right verdict. But multifactor does not need a biometric; a password plus a phone-held code would already be two factors.

tips: Eliminate: A and C count two checks as two factors, but both answers are something the user knows, so the type is the same.
Final two: B beats D because the verdict rests on both checks being one type; multifactor needs different types, not a biometric.
Exam cue: count authentication factors by type: know, have, are. Repeating a type never adds a factor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: multi-factor authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A password plus a security question is single-factor (exam trap): MFA needs two different factor types' (notes 1.1.5 Authentication). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A toy library's volunteer coordinator signs in with a passkey without trouble, then sees 'access denied' when opening the payroll folder. Which AAA function MOST accurately produced the denial?

options.A: Authentication, because it confirmed the coordinator's identity
options.B: Identification, because the coordinator claimed an account name
options.C: Accounting, because the refusal was written to the access log
options.D: Authorization, because it grants or refuses each user's access

questions.key_concept: An access denied message after a successful sign-in is authorization at work: it decides, resource by resource, what a proven identity may open.
questions.pre_read: Picture the three AAA questions: who are you, what may you do, what did you do.
questions.correct_explanation: The coordinator passed authentication, since the passkey proved their identity. The refusal came next, when the system checked whether that identity may open the payroll folder: authorization, which follows the owner's rules and least privilege. Accounting, the runner-up, may well record the refusal in a log, but recording a decision is not making it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the passkey check is the visible security step. But it succeeded; proving identity says nothing about which folders that identity may open.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a username comes first. But identification only makes a claim; it neither proves it nor decides access to folders.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the log may well record the refusal. But accounting tracks what happened; the decision to refuse came from authorization.

tips: Eliminate: A succeeded, since the passkey proved identity, and B only claims an identity; neither decides which folders the user may open.
Final two: D beats C because authorization makes the allow-or-deny decision; accounting just records what happened.
Exam cue: after a successful sign-in, an 'access denied' message is authorization at work; the log that shows it is accounting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Authentication proves identity only; authorization is a separate decision for each resource' (notes 1.1.6 Authorization and Accounting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.1 Cybersecurity concepts. Privacy and personal data
questions.question: A laser tag arena plans to let members enter by fingerprint, storing a template of each print instead of the image. How should the security analyst MOST accurately classify the templates?

options.A: Personal data only once they are stored with members' names
options.B: Sensitive personal data, since biometrics identify a person directly
options.C: Not personal data, since a template is only a set of numbers
options.D: Ordinary personal data, protected just like an email address

questions.key_concept: Biometric data, templates included, is personal data in a sensitive category, with stricter handling than ordinary contact details.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the data could single out a person, and how much harm its misuse would do.
questions.correct_explanation: A fingerprint template still singles out one person, so it is personal data, and biometrics sit in the sensitive categories that carry stricter rules, partly because nobody can change their fingerprints after a leak. Treating the templates as ordinary data, the runner-up, gets the first half right but would protect them only as well as an email address.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because names feel like what makes data personal. But a fingerprint template identifies a person on its own, with or without a name.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because templates are stored as numbers. But NIST lists biometric template data as personal information; its format does not change what it identifies.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the templates are personal data. But biometrics are a sensitive category; unlike an email address, a leaked fingerprint cannot be replaced.

tips: Eliminate: A and C treat the templates as anonymous, but biometric templates identify a person on their own, whatever their format.
Final two: B beats D because biometrics belong to the sensitive categories, with stricter rules than ordinary contact details.
Exam cue: health and biometric data are sensitive personal data; expect them to need more justification and protection than names or emails.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-122 Section 2.2 (Examples of PII Data: fingerprints and other biometric image or template data); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.34 (Privacy and protection of PII)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Sensitive categories, such as health and biometric data, carry stricter rules' (notes 1.1.8 Privacy and Personal Data). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.1 Cybersecurity concepts. AI and the CIA triad
questions.question: A scrap metal yard's AI fraud checker tested as accurate, yet it approves every sale whose notes contain one rare word, however suspicious the sale. What should the security analyst conclude is MOST likely?

options.A: Model drift, as sales patterns have shifted since the model trained
options.B: Poisoned training data that planted a hidden trigger in the model
options.C: An overload, as too many sales reach the checker at once
options.D: A privacy leak, as the model exposes sellers' details in its notes

questions.key_concept: A model that behaves normally except when one specific trigger appears points to backdoor poisoning, an integrity attack on its training data.
questions.pre_read: Compare the pattern of the fault with the AI risks you know.
questions.correct_explanation: Poisoning can teach a model hidden behavior: it works normally, so it passes testing, but a planted trigger flips its decision. Approving any sale carrying one rare word, however suspicious, fits that backdoor pattern and is an integrity attack. Drift, the runner-up, also makes models go wrong, but it wears down accuracy broadly as data changes; it does not obey one trigger word.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: drift is a real cause of AI errors. But drift wears down accuracy across many cases; it would not approve every sale carrying one specific word.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because heavy load can break services. But overload hurts availability, slowing or stopping answers; it does not make the checker approve particular sales.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI models can leak personal data. But nothing here is exposed; the fault is a wrong decision, which is an integrity problem.

tips: Eliminate: C would slow or stop the checker, an availability harm, and D describes exposed data, but here the harm is wrong decisions.
Final two: B beats A because drift degrades accuracy broadly, while one trigger word that flips decisions is the mark of a planted backdoor.
Exam cue: normal behavior plus one input that reliably flips the result suggests poisoning; a gradual, wide decline suggests drift.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 2.3.3 (Backdoor Poisoning: a model learns to misclassify inputs containing a trigger pattern)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Poisoning corrupts training data so a model learns wrong or hidden behavior: an integrity attack' (notes 1.1.9 AI and the Core Security Concepts). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bookbinding workshop's new risk analyst is filling in its first risk register for the order system. Which item MOST accurately belongs in the threat column?

options.A: Missing backups for the order system's database
options.B: The cost of losing a week of customer orders
options.C: The chance that order data is lost this year
options.D: Staff deleting order files by mistake

questions.key_concept: A threat is anything that could cause harm, including human error and nature, not only attackers; the weakness it uses is a vulnerability.
questions.pre_read: Recall how threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact differ.
questions.correct_explanation: A threat is a possible cause of harm, and it need not be an attacker: honest mistakes, storms and equipment faults count too. A staff member deleting files by mistake is an accidental threat. Missing backups, the runner-up, are the weakness that lets that mistake become a lasting loss, so they belong in the vulnerability column.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: missing backups are a real problem worth recording. But they are a weakness a threat can exploit, so they belong in the vulnerability column.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because lost orders are the harm being prevented. But a week of lost orders is the impact if a threat succeeds, not the threat.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a chance of loss sounds like the danger itself. But how likely harm is forms part of the risk rating, not the threat.

tips: Eliminate: B is the impact if something goes wrong, and C is the likelihood that feeds the risk rating; neither is a cause of harm.
Final two: D beats A because a deletion by mistake is a cause of harm, while missing backups are the weakness that makes it costly.
Exam cue: threats are causes of harm, including mistakes and nature; vulnerabilities are weaknesses; risk combines likelihood and impact.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix D Table D-2 (Taxonomy of Threat Sources: adversarial, accidental, structural and environmental); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A threat is anything that could cause harm, such as an attacker, an error or a storm' (notes 1.2.1 Threats, Vulnerabilities and Risk). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A vending machine operator's IT manager wants to buy an expensive card-skimming detector for every machine, though nobody has yet rated the skimming risk. What should the risk analyst propose FIRST?

options.A: Buy the detectors, since any added control lowers the risk
options.B: Accept the skimming risk, since the detectors cost too much
options.C: Assess the risk's likelihood and impact before choosing a fix
options.D: Fit detectors on half the machines as a trial, then decide

questions.key_concept: Treatment comes after assessment: rate a risk's likelihood and impact first, so the chosen response and its cost fit the risk.
questions.pre_read: Locate where the organization is in the identify, assess, treat, monitor cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: The lifecycle runs identify, assess, treat, monitor. Skimming has been identified but not rated, so nobody knows whether costly detectors fit its likelihood and impact. Assessing first lets the risk owner weigh the treatment's cost against the risk.
