questions.key_concept: Physical controls include environmental protection; removing a single point of failure, such as one cooling unit, keeps systems available.
questions.pre_read: Find the single point of failure, then ask which option removes it.
questions.correct_explanation: The failure is a single cooling unit, so the fix that keeps servers running is redundancy: a second unit that starts automatically when the first fails. A temperature alarm, the runner-up, is a useful detective control, but at night someone must wake, travel and act before the servers overheat, which has already happened twice.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an alarm warns someone fast. But it only detects; at night a person must still respond in time, while a backup unit keeps cooling on its own.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because battery backup protects servers. But the problem is heat from a failed air conditioner, not lost power.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because closets should be locked. But limiting entry does nothing when the cooling fails.

tips: Eliminate: C covers power cuts, not cooling, and D controls entry, which has nothing to do with heat.
Final two: B beats A because automatic backup cooling keeps the servers running without waiting for a person to respond at night.
Exam cue: for availability, remove the single point of failure; an alarm that needs a person to respond detects but does not keep things running.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-14(1) (Environmental Controls | Automatic Controls); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Fire suppression, cooling and backup power protect equipment' (notes 1.4.4 Physical Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Clearing disk space, a resort's system administrator accidentally deleted a week of guest-booking logs that the security team uses for investigations. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Say nothing to the security team, as one week is minor
options.B: Rebuild the missing entries by hand from other records
options.C: Restore the deleted logs from backup and carry on with the cleanup
options.D: Tell the security team what was deleted and when

questions.key_concept: Professional conduct means owning mistakes openly: tell the people who rely on the affected records rather than fixing things quietly.
questions.pre_read: Ask who relies on the deleted logs and what they need to know.
questions.correct_explanation: Honesty about your own mistakes is a core professional duty, and the security team relies on these logs for investigations, so they need to know about the gap and can check whether any restore is complete. Restoring quietly, the runner-up, is a sensible repair but not a substitute for telling them: a quiet fix hides the gap from the people who rely on those records.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a week of logs sounds minor. But investigators rely on those logs, and hiding an error breaches the honesty every code of conduct expects.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it fills the gap. But hand-made entries are not genuine logs; presenting them as real would damage the records' integrity.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: restoring is a sensible repair. But a quiet fix hides the gap from the team that relies on the logs, who must also confirm the restore is complete.

tips: Eliminate: A conceals the error, and B creates entries that are not genuine; both breach honesty and the logs' integrity.
Final two: D beats C because the people who rely on the logs must know about the gap; repairing quietly hides the mistake from them.
Exam cue: own your mistakes: tell the people who rely on what you affected, then help fix it through the proper process.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-5 (Response to Audit Logging Process Failures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Common themes are honesty, avoiding conflicts of interest and protecting confidential information' (notes 1.5.1 Professional Code of Conduct). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.5 Professional conduct. Due care and due diligence
questions.question: Before a legal aid charity adopts an AI transcription service, its security analyst checks where recordings are stored and whether the vendor trains models on them. What is this check MOST accurately?

options.A: Due diligence, researching the vendor's risks
options.B: Due care, acting to protect the clients' recordings
options.C: Risk acceptance, taking on the vendor's remaining risks
options.D: Risk transfer, moving the recordings' risks to the vendor

questions.key_concept: Researching an AI vendor's data handling before adoption is due diligence; acting on the findings, such as changing settings, is due care.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the check finds things out or acts on them.
questions.correct_explanation: Researching a vendor before adoption, here how it stores recordings and whether it trains on them, is due diligence: finding out what a prudent organization should know. Due care, the runner-up, is acting on what was found, such as switching off model training on recordings or choosing another service. The check informs that action; it is not yet the action.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the check does aim to protect clients. But it gathers facts; due care is what the charity then does, such as changing settings or choosing another service.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because using a vendor means living with some risk. But acceptance is an owner's decision on assessed risk; this check comes before any decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outsourcing sounds like handing risk over. But checking the vendor transfers nothing, and the charity stays accountable for clients' data.

tips: Eliminate: C and D are risk decisions, and this check makes no decision; it gathers facts before one.
Final two: A beats B because investigating the vendor is finding out; due care is acting on the findings.
Exam cue: researching, assessing and verifying are due diligence; implementing, enforcing and fixing are due care.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 3.1 (AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Due diligence investigates: researching a vendor, assessing risks, testing controls' (notes 1.5.2 Due Care and Due Diligence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A certified analyst spends weekends mentoring students who want security careers and helping a local chapter build free training. Which canon does this work MOST directly support?

options.A: Advance and protect the profession
options.B: Protect society, the common good and the infrastructure
options.C: Provide diligent and competent service to principals
options.D: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally

questions.key_concept: Mentoring and teaching newcomers advances the profession, the focus of the fourth canon; principals are those served under an agreement.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the work serves directly: the public, a client or the field.
questions.correct_explanation: Mentoring newcomers and building training grows the security field and its standing, which is what the canon on advancing and protecting the profession covers. Protecting society, the runner-up, is a fair secondary benefit, since better-trained people make systems safer, but the work's direct aim is developing the profession. The other canons concern honest conduct and service to principals, and no principal is served here.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a stronger workforce does help protect society in the end. But the work directly develops people entering the field, which is the profession canon's focus.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst gives skilled service. But principals are employers or clients served under an agreement, and the students are neither.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because volunteering is honorable. But that canon is about conducting oneself honestly and legally, not about growing the field.

tips: Eliminate: C needs a principal, which the students are not, and D concerns honest, lawful conduct rather than growing the field.
Final two: A beats B because the work directly develops the security profession; any benefit to society comes through that.
Exam cue: match the action to each canon's focus: the public, honest conduct, principals or the profession; the listed order is not a ranking.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Canon 4 asks members to support the security field and its good name' (notes 1.5.3 The ISC2 Code of Ethics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Testing a client's network under contract, a certified tester finds a serious flaw in a router model used by many organizations. What is the tester's BEST response?

options.A: Tell the client, and with the client's consent, alert the maker
options.B: Report it in the client's findings only, as the contract is private
options.C: Post the details online so every organization can protect itself
options.D: Scan other networks for the router to show how widespread it is

questions.key_concept: When a flaw affects many organizations, report it through proper channels, client first and then the maker, rather than hiding or publishing it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option does for the client, for other router owners and for attackers.
questions.correct_explanation: The flaw threatens many organizations, so keeping it to one report fails the public, yet publishing it before a fix hands attackers a way in. The tester serves the client first: tell the client and, with its consent, report the flaw to the router's maker so it can be fixed for everyone. Keeping it in the client's report only, the runner-up, honors confidentiality but leaves every other owner of that router exposed.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: client confidentiality matters. But the flaw is in a product many others use; with the client's consent, telling the maker protects them without exposing the client.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it warns everyone fast. But publishing before a fix gives attackers a ready way in, and it may breach the client contract.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it would measure the risk. But scanning networks nobody authorized is illegal and unethical, whatever the motive.

tips: Eliminate: C publishes before a fix exists, helping attackers, and D tests networks without authorization, which is illegal.
Final two: A beats B because the flaw endangers many organizations; going to the maker, with the client's consent, protects them while honoring the contract.
Exam cue: in dilemmas, look for the option that serves the client and protects the public through proper channels, such as telling the vendor.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Preamble and Canons
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Report flaws to the owner first; publishing before a fix hands attackers a way in' (notes 1.5.4 Applying the Canons to Dilemmas). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A cyber cafe owner wants to file an ethics complaint against a certified consultant but fears the consultant will learn who complained. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: Their name is never shared with the consultant, at any stage
options.B: Their name may be published along with the board's final decision
options.C: Their name is kept from the public but may reach the consultant
options.D: Their name can be left off, as complaints may be filed anonymously

questions.key_concept: Ethics complaints are kept confidential from the public, but the respondent may learn who complained so they can answer fairly.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the complainant's privacy against the respondent's right to answer.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedures keep the identities of both parties confidential from the general public, but filing a complaint implies consent to share the complainant's identity with the respondent where due process needs it, since the consultant may see the complaint and answer it. Never sharing it, the runner-up, would leave the consultant unable to answer specific allegations from a known source.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: identities are protected from the public. But the respondent may see the complaint and answer it, so the complainant's name can be shared for due process.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because board actions may be published. But the parties' identities are kept confidential from the general public.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because anonymity feels safer. But a complaint must be a sworn written statement, so the complainant is named and stands behind it.

tips: Eliminate: B contradicts the confidentiality the procedures give both parties, and D overlooks that complaints are sworn statements by a named person.
Final two: C beats A because filing implies consent to share the complainant's identity with the respondent where due process needs it.
Exam cue: ethics procedures balance privacy with fairness: hidden from the public, but the accused can see and answer the case.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (confidentiality: identities are kept from the general public, and filing implies consent to disclose the complainant's identity to the respondent for due process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The member complained about sees the complaint and evidence and may reply in a sworn statement' (notes 1.5.5 Ethics Complaints and Enforcement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A junior analyst submitted a firewall rule an approved AI assistant wrote, without checking it; the change board approved it, and it caused an outage. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The analyst stays accountable for the rule they chose to submit
options.B: The tool's approver is accountable, having approved the AI assistant
options.C: The change board alone is accountable, having approved it
options.D: The firewall's system owner is accountable for every rule on it

questions.key_concept: Professionals stay accountable for AI output they rely on; reviewers' approval adds a check but does not remove the submitter's responsibility.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chose to rely on the AI's rule, and what approval does and does not change.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever relies on AI output owns the result: the analyst chose to submit the AI's rule without checking it, so they remain accountable for it. The change board's approval, the runner-up, is a real second check, but approval does not move the submitter's responsibility onto the reviewers; both share in the outcome, and the analyst cannot point to the board or the tool.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because someone approved the assistant for use. But approving a tool is not approving each output it produces; the analyst who submitted the rule still had to check it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the board did approve the change. But approval adds a second check; it does not remove the submitter's responsibility for what they submitted.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the system owner holds the firewall's risk. But owning a system does not take over the submitter's duty to check their own work before submitting it.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses approving a tool with approving each output, and D lets system ownership absorb the submitter's duty to check their work.
Final two: A beats C because review by others adds a check but does not take over the submitter's responsibility for unchecked work.
Exam cue: AI is a tool; the professional who relies on its output stays accountable, so verify before you submit.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 3.4 (Accountable and Transparent); ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons (service to principals)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI is a tool; the professional stays accountable' (notes 1.5.6 Ethical Use of AI at Work). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ticket reseller's security analyst suspects, without proof, that a coworker sells customer data; the code of conduct sends such concerns to the ethics hotline. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Confront the coworker privately to hear their side first
options.B: Search the coworker's mailbox for proof before calling the ethics hotline
options.C: Warn customers that their data may have been sold
options.D: Use the ethics hotline to raise the possible data sale

questions.key_concept: Raise suspected misconduct through the channel the code of conduct names; using your own access to investigate misuses it.
questions.pre_read: Note what the code of conduct says about raising concerns, and what the analyst is assigned to do.
questions.correct_explanation: A suspicion of data theft is serious, but the analyst has no proof and no assignment to investigate. The code of conduct names the ethics hotline for such concerns, so the analyst raises it there, letting authorized people investigate properly. Searching the coworker's mailbox, the runner-up, feels thorough, but it uses access for work nobody assigned and could breach privacy and spoil any investigation.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because hearing both sides seems fair. But a confrontation can tip off someone who may be stealing data, letting them hide evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: evidence would make the concern stronger. But searching a coworker's mailbox uses access for work nobody assigned and can spoil a proper investigation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because customers may be harmed. But nothing is confirmed yet, and notices to customers are a decision for the organization, not one analyst.

tips: Eliminate: A risks tipping off a possible thief, and C alarms customers about something nobody has confirmed.
Final two: D beats B because the code sends concerns to the hotline; investigating a coworker with your own access is not your assigned work.
Exam cue: raise concerns through the channel your code of conduct names, and never use your access to investigate on your own.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(2) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Insider Threat); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Use access only for assigned work, and raise concerns through proper channels' (notes 1.5.1 Professional Code of Conduct). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A certified analyst at a payment app sees that a draft breach notice tells customers no sensitive data was taken, though card numbers were. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Challenge the wording with the incident response lead and legal counsel
options.B: Defer to management, since breach notices are management's decision
options.C: Post the true details on social media so customers learn the facts
options.D: Email affected customers the correct details from a personal account

questions.key_concept: When an employer's message would mislead the public, raise the inaccuracy through official channels before it goes out; silence makes you party to it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what customers would do differently if the notice were accurate.
questions.correct_explanation: A notice saying no sensitive data was taken, when card numbers were, misleads customers who need to protect themselves, so staying silent would make the analyst party to a dishonest statement. The right channel is to raise the inaccuracy with the incident response lead and legal counsel before it goes out. Deferring to management, the runner-up, respects their authority over notices, but that authority does not make a false statement acceptable.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: management does decide what the notice says. But the analyst knows it is false; raising that through proper channels comes before deferring.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because customers deserve the truth. But going public skips the internal channels that can still correct the notice, and may breach confidentiality.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns customers directly. But it bypasses the organization's process, and a personal account has no authority, so customers may not trust it.

tips: Eliminate: C and D bypass the internal channels that can still correct the notice before it goes out.
Final two: A beats B because management's authority over notices does not make a false statement acceptable; the analyst must raise the inaccuracy.
Exam cue: when an employer's statement would mislead the public, raise it through official channels first; neither silence nor going public comes first.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons; NIST CSF 2.0 RS.CO-03 (information is shared with designated internal and external stakeholders)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Reject any illegal or deceptive option, even if an employer asks for it' (notes 1.5.4 Applying the Canons to Dilemmas). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sawmill pays log suppliers by the weights in its weighbridge records, and its manager worries that staff could quietly edit a weight. Which control should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Require a second person to sign off each weight change
options.B: Encrypt the weight records where they are stored on the server
options.C: Add a standby server so the weighbridge system stays running
options.D: Back up the weight records nightly to a separate server

questions.key_concept: Name the goal a threat targets, then choose a control built for that goal; quiet edits threaten integrity, so control who can change data.
questions.pre_read: Ask which security goal a quiet edit to a record would harm.
questions.correct_explanation: A quiet, unauthorized change to a weight is an integrity threat, so the control should govern changes: a second person signing off each edit stops one person altering a record alone. Nightly backups, the runner-up, help restore lost data, but they do nothing to stop an edit, and a quietly edited weight is copied into the next backup as if it were correct.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption is a strong control. But it keeps records secret from outsiders; staff who can open the system can still change a weight.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the weighbridge must keep working. But a standby server protects availability; it does nothing to stop a weight being edited.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: backups help restore damaged data. But they do nothing to stop an edit, and an edited weight is backed up as if correct.

tips: Eliminate: B protects confidentiality and C protects availability; neither stops someone changing a weight.
Final two: A beats D because a second sign-off stops a quiet change, while a backup simply copies the edited weight.
Exam cue: name the goal at stake first; for unauthorized changes, pick a control over who can change data, such as approval or change control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Name the goal first: was secrecy, correctness or access harmed? Then pick a control built for that goal' (notes 1.1.1 The CIA Triad). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A shipping broker's chartering assistant will share their screen on a video call with one client, while other clients' contracts are open on the same desktop. Which step should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Turn on the meeting tool's end-to-end encryption
options.B: Label every open contract Confidential before the call
options.C: Ask the client not to record the call
options.D: Share only the window holding this client's contract

questions.key_concept: Confidentiality covers data in use: limit what is shown to the people present, because encryption cannot hide what an intended viewer sees.
questions.pre_read: Ask who will see the screen and what encryption can and cannot hide.
questions.correct_explanation: Confidentiality covers data while it is displayed, not only stored or sent. The client is a legitimate participant who will see whatever is shared, so sharing only this client's contract window keeps other clients' contracts off their screen. End-to-end encryption, the runner-up, keeps outsiders out of the call, but it delivers the shared screen intact to the client, including any other contract on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: encryption protects the call in transit. But the client is an intended viewer, and encryption shows them everything shared.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because labels mark sensitive data. But a label hides nothing; a contract on screen is still readable.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recordings spread data. But the client still sees the other contracts live, recorded or not.

tips: Eliminate: B only labels what is on screen, and C stops a recording but not live viewing.
Final two: D beats A because encryption protects the call from outsiders, while the client, an intended viewer, still sees everything shared.
Exam cue: for data in use, limit what is displayed; encryption protects data stored or sent, not what an authorized viewer sees.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Confidentiality means keeping information away from people, processes and devices not authorized to see it, whether stored, sent or in use' (notes 1.1.2 Confidentiality). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A hot spring spa's system administrator downloads an update for its booking kiosks, and the file's hash does not match the value the vendor publishes. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Install it, since it came from the vendor's own website
options.B: Scan it for viruses and install it if the scan is clean
options.C: Set the file aside unused and report it to the security team
options.D: Delete the file and keep the kiosks on the current version

questions.key_concept: A hash that does not match the trusted published value means the data changed; stop using it and report the mismatch.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a mismatched hash tells you about the file.
questions.correct_explanation: A hash that does not match the published value means the file is not the one the vendor released: it was corrupted or tampered with. A file that fails an integrity check should not be used, and the mismatch should be reported so the security team can investigate. Deleting it, the runner-up, also keeps it off the kiosks, but a failed check may point to a tampered download site, and deleting loses the evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor's site is a trusted source. But the mismatch shows the file differs from what the vendor published, wherever it came from.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a clean scan feels like proof of safety. But a scan finds only known malware; it cannot show the file is the one the vendor released.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: not installing it is right. But a failed check may mean a tampered download site; the security team needs to know, and deleting the file loses the evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts the download site over the failed check, and B lets a virus scan stand in for the failed integrity check.
Final two: C beats D because a file that fails its integrity check is kept unused and reported, not just discarded; the team needs it as evidence.
Exam cue: when a hash or signature check fails, stop using the data and report it; never install it, work around the failure or quietly discard it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Compare a file's hash with the trusted published value' (notes 1.1.3 Integrity and Authenticity). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: C no longer echoes the stem's 'hash'; D (pilot install) replaced by a non-installing option (delete it), so the key is not the only cautious option.

questions.question: A wind farm's control room door opens only after a worker shows their badge and then a fingerprint. If a worker drops their badge outside, what MOST stops a finder from getting in?

options.A: The badge's photo, which the door reader checks against the holder
options.B: The fingerprint, which is a different factor type from the badge
options.C: The badge number, which only its holder is meant to know
options.D: The door camera, which records whoever uses the badge

questions.key_concept: Multifactor authentication needs factors of different types, so one lost or stolen factor alone does not open access.
questions.pre_read: Picture the finder at the door and walk through each check.
questions.correct_explanation: The badge is something the worker has, and the fingerprint is something they are. A finder holds the badge but not the worker's finger, so the second factor, of a different type, keeps the door shut. That is the point of multifactor authentication: losing one factor alone does not open access. The door camera, the runner-up, records who uses the badge, but recording is detective; it does not stop the finder.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because badges often carry a photo. But a door reader reads the badge's data, not the face printed on it; the photo helps only a person checking by eye.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the number ties the badge to its holder. But the number travels with the badge, so whoever finds the badge has it too; it is not a secret.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the camera adds a record of who entered. But recording is detective; it shows who got in afterwards rather than stopping the finder at the door.

tips: Eliminate: A expects the door reader to compare a photo with a face, and C treats a badge number as a secret, though it travels with the badge.
Final two: B beats D because the fingerprint stops the finder at the door; the camera only records them once they are in.
Exam cue: multifactor works because its factors are of different types; ask what an attacker holding one factor still lacks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: multi-factor authentication); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Multifactor authentication (MFA) needs two or more different factor types; two passwords are still one type' (notes 1.1.5 Authentication). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled from naming the factor types (taught by cc_d3_162, cc_d1_024 and cc_d1_114) to why multifactor helps when one factor is lost; key B and subtopic kept.

questions.question: A touring circus's box-office staff sign in to shared ticket tablets with their own accounts, but refunds are logged with only the time, amount and tablet. Which addition should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Encryption of the refund log so staff cannot read it
options.B: The user ID of the person who processed each refund
options.C: One login shared by supervisors to approve every refund
options.D: A rota that assigns each tablet to one person per shift

questions.key_concept: Accounting gives accountability only when each logged action names the unique identity that performed it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the log could name the person behind a disputed refund.
questions.correct_explanation: Accounting must record who did what, when and from where. Staff already have their own accounts, so adding each person's user ID to every refund entry ties each refund to a person. A rota, the runner-up, only says who was meant to use each tablet; staff can swap or share tablets, so the log still could not prove who issued a refund.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because protecting logs matters. But encryption hides entries; it adds nothing that names who issued each refund.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it adds oversight. But a login shared by supervisors cannot show which person approved a refund.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a rota links tablets to people on paper. But staff can swap tablets, so the log still cannot prove who issued a refund.

tips: Eliminate: A protects the log's secrecy without naming anyone, and C creates a shared login, which cannot show who acted.
Final two: B beats D because only the user ID in each entry proves who acted; a rota shows who should have used the tablet.
Exam cue: accountability needs each log entry tied to a unique identity; a device, location or schedule is not a person.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-3 (Content of Audit Records); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Accounting logs who did what, when and from where' (notes 1.1.6 Authorization and Accounting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A fabric supplier denies sending a kite maker a price agreement, though the file's plain hash still matches the one recorded on arrival. Which conclusion should the security analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: The file has stayed unchanged since it arrived
options.B: The supplier sent the file and cannot credibly deny it
options.C: The file has stayed unchanged since the supplier sent it
options.D: The file has stayed encrypted since it arrived

questions.key_concept: A matching hash shows data unchanged only since the hash was recorded; it proves neither earlier integrity nor who sent the data.
questions.pre_read: Separate what a hash can prove from what a signature can prove.
questions.correct_explanation: A plain hash recorded on arrival shows only that the file has not changed since that moment. It uses no key, so it says nothing about who created the file or what happened to it before it arrived. Unchanged since the supplier sent it, the runner-up, claims more than the evidence covers, and defeating the denial would need the supplier's digital signature, made with their private key.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the hash is real evidence about the file. But a plain hash uses no key and names no sender; defeating a denial needs the supplier's digital signature.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the file may well be unchanged since sending. But the hash was recorded on arrival, so it vouches for nothing before then.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because hashing is a cryptographic tool. But hashing is not encryption; it fingerprints the data and keeps nothing secret.

tips: Eliminate: B reads a sender into a hash that names no one, and D mistakes hashing for encryption.
Final two: A beats C because the hash was recorded on arrival, so it proves no change only from then; the file's journey and its sender stay unproven.
Exam cue: a hash proves no change only since it was recorded, never who created the data; a denial needs a signature to defeat.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-10 (Non-repudiation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Integrity shows data is unchanged; non-repudiation shows a specific person cannot deny creating it' (notes 1.1.7 Non-Repudiation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.1 Cybersecurity concepts. Privacy and personal data
questions.question: A podcast app's data owner says that because every listener profile is encrypted, the app's privacy duties are handled. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree, provided only the app's own staff hold the encryption keys
options.B: Agree; privacy and confidentiality are two names for one goal
options.C: Disagree; encryption has no part to play in protecting privacy
options.D: Disagree; privacy also covers what is collected, why and how long

questions.key_concept: Privacy covers what personal data is collected, why and for how long; encryption protects only its secrecy.
questions.pre_read: Ask what privacy covers beyond keeping data secret.
questions.correct_explanation: Encryption protects secrecy, but privacy is broader: it asks whether personal data should be collected at all, whether it is used only for the stated purpose and how long it is kept. A fully encrypted profile can still breach privacy if it holds data nobody needed or is reused without a lawful basis. Keeping the keys in-house, the runner-up, strengthens secrecy but answers none of those questions.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: key control does matter for encryption. But it only strengthens secrecy; it says nothing about what data is collected, why or for how long.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because both protect personal data. But confidentiality asks who can see data; privacy also asks whether its collection and use are fair and agreed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it rejects the claim. But encryption does help privacy by keeping personal data secret; it is simply not enough alone.

tips: Eliminate: B merges privacy into confidentiality, and C wrongly says encryption plays no part in privacy.
Final two: D beats A because privacy also governs collection, purpose and retention; where the keys sit only affects secrecy.
Exam cue: if an option says encryption settles privacy, check collection, purpose and retention; privacy can fail with no leak at all.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-8(33) (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles | Minimization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Encryption protects secrecy. Privacy also asks whether data should be collected, and how it is used and kept' (notes 1.1.8 Privacy and Personal Data). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.1 Cybersecurity concepts. AI and the CIA triad
questions.question: A birdwatching society will publish the photo set it trains its bird-identification model on, and many volunteers' photos carry the GPS location of rare nests. Which step should the security analyst propose FIRST?

options.A: Strip location tags from the photos before publishing
options.B: Publish the set only to the society's 400 volunteers
options.C: Add more photos to make the rare nests harder to pick out
options.D: Back up the training data before it is published

questions.key_concept: Training data can carry sensitive details, such as locations, to everyone it reaches; remove what the purpose does not need before sharing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what harm publishing the set could cause, and to whom.
questions.correct_explanation: The photos' GPS tags would tell anyone who downloads the set where rare birds nest, a confidentiality risk to the nests. Identifying birds needs the images, not the locations, so stripping the location tags before publishing removes the exposure and keeps the set useful. Sharing only with the 400 volunteers, the runner-up, narrows the audience, but the locations still reach hundreds of people who can pass them on, and the model never needed them.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a smaller audience lowers exposure. But 400 people would still hold the nest locations and could pass them on, and the model does not need them at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more data can dilute any single record. But each extra photo keeps its own GPS tag, so the nest locations still go out with the set.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because backups protect the set. But a backup supports availability; it does nothing to stop the nest locations going out with the published photos.

tips: Eliminate: C hides the locations in a bigger set that still carries them, and D protects availability, not the confidentiality of the nest locations.
Final two: A beats B because removing locations the model does not need protects the nests from everyone; a smaller audience still receives them.
Exam cue: before sharing training data, remove the sensitive details its purpose does not need; limiting who receives it comes second.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 3.3 (Secure and Resilient: security concerns include exfiltration of training data, and secure AI systems maintain confidentiality, integrity and availability); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-22 (Publicly Accessible Content)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Poisoning corrupts training data or the model so it learns wrong or hidden behavior: an integrity attack' (notes 1.1.9 AI and the Core Security Concepts). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled from training-data poisoning (taught by cc_d4_056 and cc_d1_025) to confidentiality of published training data; key letter A and subtopic kept; 'named' dropped.

questions.question: Attackers keep emailing a cider orchard's office staff fake invoices with malicious attachments. In risk terms, what role does email MOST accurately play in this case?

options.A: The threat actor that is attacking the orchard
options.B: The vulnerability that lets the attack succeed
options.C: The threat vector that the attack travels along
options.D: The exploit that takes advantage of the weakness

questions.key_concept: A threat vector is the path a threat uses to reach its target, such as email, a web application or a removable drive.
questions.pre_read: Sort the attackers, the email and the attachment into their risk terms.
questions.correct_explanation: A threat vector is the path a threat uses to reach its target, and here email is how the attackers deliver their attachments to staff. The attackers are the threat actor, and the attachment carries the attack. Calling email the vulnerability, the runner-up, confuses the path with the weakness: the weakness is whatever lets a malicious attachment succeed, such as unpatched software or untrained staff.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because email is where the attack appears. But the threat actor is the person or group behind it: the attackers sending the invoices.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: email is how harm arrives. But a vulnerability is a weakness, such as unpatched software; email is the path the attack travels.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the attachments are malicious. But an exploit is the code or technique that uses a weakness; email only carries it to staff.

tips: Eliminate: A names the people behind the attack, and D names the attack technique, not the path it travels.
Final two: C beats B because email is the route the attack takes; the vulnerability is the weakness it relies on once it arrives.
Exam cue: actor is who, vector is the path, vulnerability is the weakness, exploit is the technique; match each term to its role.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Threat vector: the path a threat uses to reach its target, such as email, a web application or a removable drive' (notes 1.2.1 Threats, Vulnerabilities and Risk). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: stem no longer says 'channel', which echoed the key's pathway wording. C reworded so the key is not the lone shortest.

questions.question: A newly formed taxi cooperative asks its first security analyst to set up risk management from scratch, following NIST's risk management process. Which step should come FIRST?

options.A: Agree on priorities, legal duties and appetite with leaders
options.B: List the cooperative's assets and the threats facing each one
options.C: Rate each risk's likelihood and impact on an agreed scale
options.D: Choose controls with leaders for the most serious risks

questions.key_concept: Risk management begins by framing the context: priorities, legal duties and risk appetite, before risks are identified.
questions.pre_read: Recall the order of the risk management lifecycle.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk management starts by framing the context: what the organization values, which legal duties apply and how much risk its leaders will take. Every later step depends on it, since ratings and treatments are judged against those priorities and that appetite. Listing assets and threats, the runner-up, begins the assessment (NIST groups identifying and rating risks under assess); it comes next, once the analyst knows what the cooperative cares about and must comply with.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: identifying assets and threats starts the assessment. But without the context first, the analyst cannot tell which assets matter most or what limits apply.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rating is central to risk work. But risks must be identified before they can be rated, and rated against an agreed context.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it acts quickly and involves leaders. But choosing controls before risks are identified and assessed spends money on guesses.

tips: Eliminate: C rates risks before any are identified, and D picks controls before anything is assessed.
Final two: A beats B because framing the context comes before identifying risks; it tells the analyst what matters and what limits apply.
Exam cue: framing comes first, then assessing (identify and rate), treating and monitoring; when a new program asks what comes first, choose setting the context.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 2.1 (Components of Risk Management: frame, assess, respond and monitor)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Frame the context: what the organization values, its legal duties and its risk appetite' (notes 1.2.2 The Risk Management Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: D also involves leaders, so owner wording is not only on the key; A lengthened so the key is not the lone shortest.

questions.question: An insurance broker's claims team uses an AI plug-in that sends claim letters to its vendor for drafting, and a security analyst logs the risk. Who should the analyst MOST appropriately propose as risk owner?

options.A: The IT manager, who installed the plug-in and still supports it
options.B: The security analyst, who found and logged the risk
options.C: The head of claims, who runs the process using the plug-in
options.D: The plug-in vendor, whose servers receive and draft the claim letters

questions.key_concept: A risk owner is accountable for the activity at risk, with authority to decide its treatment; finders and custodians are not owners.
questions.pre_read: Ask who has authority over the work the plug-in supports.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner is the person accountable for a risk, with authority to decide its treatment. The plug-in serves the claims process, so the head of claims, who decides how that work is done, should own the risk. The IT manager, the runner-up, installed and supports the tool, but that is a custodian's role; they cannot decide whether claims staff keep using it or accept what remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: IT does run the plug-in. But supporting a tool is a custodian's job; the owner needs authority over the business process that uses it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the analyst knows the risk best. But anyone can raise a risk; owning it needs authority to decide its treatment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor holds the letters. But accountability for the broker's data stays with the broker, so an outside vendor cannot own its risk.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses finding a risk with owning it, and D hands the broker's accountability to an outside vendor.
Final two: C beats A because the owner needs authority over the process the risk affects; supporting the tool is custodian work.
Exam cue: propose as risk owner the person accountable for the business activity at risk, not whoever found, built or supports it.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 6.1.3 f) (risk owners approve the risk treatment plan and accept residual risk); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Anyone can raise a risk; the owner decides what happens to it' (notes 1.2.7 Risk Register, Ownership and Reporting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A salt works' analyst built a $90,000 yearly loss figure from staff estimates with no loss history and calls it more reliable than a High rating. Which reply from the security manager is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; a dollar figure is more reliable for weighing costs
options.B: Agree; numbers are objective, so they always beat rated levels
options.C: Disagree; a loss figure should cover one outage, not a year
options.D: Disagree; a figure from weak inputs only looks more precise

questions.key_concept: Quantitative figures rest on their inputs; built on weak estimates, they look precise without being more accurate than qualitative ratings.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the figure's inputs came from.
questions.correct_explanation: Quantitative results are only as good as their inputs. Built from staff estimates with no loss history behind them, the $90,000 looks precise without being more reliable than a careful High rating. Weighing a money figure against control costs, the runner-up, is a real use of quantitative analysis, but usefulness is not reliability; it does not make estimated numbers more accurate.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a money figure does help leaders compare with control costs. But being useful is not being reliable; the figure is only as sound as the estimates behind it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because numbers feel objective. But estimates dressed as figures carry the same uncertainty as the estimates beneath them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it questions the figure. But a yearly figure is right for annualized loss expectancy; the cost of one outage is the single loss expectancy.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes numbers are always objective, and C mixes up annualized loss expectancy with the cost of one outage.
Final two: D beats A because a dollar figure is handy for comparing costs, but that does not make it reliable; weak inputs give precise-looking, uncertain results.
Exam cue: quantitative analysis needs reliable data; without it, numbers only look precise, and qualitative ratings are often the honest choice.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: quantitative assessments support cost-benefit analysis of risk responses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Quantitative numbers rest on estimates; poor inputs give precise-looking wrong results' (notes 1.2.4 Qualitative and Quantitative Analysis). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: setting moved to a salt works; stem says 'staff estimates with no loss history' and D says 'weak inputs', so no stem word sits only on the key.

questions.question: A comic shop's web store has frequent losses from bot-placed fake orders; its owner has little appetite for fraud, and its payment provider offers low-cost checkout screening. Which is the owner's BEST treatment?

options.A: Live with the risk, since each bot order costs little
options.B: Mitigate it by switching on the checkout screening
options.C: Close the web store so fake orders cannot happen
options.D: Transfer it by insuring the shop against checkout fraud

questions.key_concept: Choose a treatment by weighing the risk's rating, the owner's appetite and each option's cost; cheap, effective controls favor mitigation.
questions.pre_read: Weigh how often the losses happen, the appetite and the cost of each option.
questions.correct_explanation: The fake orders are frequent, the owner has little appetite for fraud, and a cheap control directly cuts their likelihood, so mitigation fits best. Transfer, the runner-up, shifts financial impact to an insurer, but frequent, predictable small losses are costly or impossible to insure, and the shop would still handle every fake order. Living with it ignores the low appetite, and closing the store drops the business.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because each loss is small. But the losses are frequent, the owner has little appetite for fraud, and a cheap fix exists.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because avoidance removes the risk entirely. But closing the store gives up the business when a low-cost control handles the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: transfer shifts financial impact. But frequent, predictable small losses are hard to insure cheaply, and the fake orders would keep coming.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps a frequent risk the owner has little appetite for, and C gives up the business when a cheap fix exists.
Final two: B beats D because a cheap control that cuts the fake orders beats insuring frequent, predictable losses that would continue.
Exam cue: weigh the rating, the appetite and each option's cost; a cheap control that cuts likelihood usually beats insuring frequent losses.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The rating, each option's cost and the risk appetite guide the choice' (notes 1.2.5 Risk Treatment Options). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: stem's 'cheap bot check' became a low-cost screening feature; D also names checkout, so B is not the only option echoing the stem.

questions.question: A harp maker's tolerance gives its payment system 30 days to fix any critical flaw. One found 20 days ago has a fix approved for day 25; what is the security analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Escalate it to senior management and record it as over tolerance
options.B: Track the fix until day 25, then record the flaw's closure
options.C: Ask the risk owner to sign an acceptance for the flaw
options.D: Patch the flaw tonight, ahead of the approved change window

questions.key_concept: Tolerances turn appetite into measurable limits; a treatment on track within the limit is tracked, not escalated or accepted.
questions.pre_read: Compare the fix date with the tolerance before deciding who needs to know.
questions.correct_explanation: The tolerance allows 30 days, and the approved fix lands on day 25, so the risk stays within the limit leaders set. Nothing needs escalating or accepting; the analyst tracks the planned fix and records its closure. Asking the risk owner to sign an acceptance, the runner-up, would suit a flaw left unfixed, but this one is being treated on time, so there is no decision to make.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the flaw is still open. But day 25 is inside the 30-day limit, so the risk is within tolerance and nothing needs senior management.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: risk owners do accept residual risk. But this flaw is being fixed within tolerance, so there is no remaining risk to accept.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because sooner feels safer. But the fix is on track within tolerance, and bypassing the approved window risks an unplanned outage.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an on-time fix as beyond tolerance, and D bypasses the approved change window without need.
Final two: B beats C because a flaw being fixed within tolerance needs tracking, not an acceptance; acceptance is for risk left in place.
Exam cue: compare the plan with the tolerance before escalating; within the limit, track the treatment, and escalate only what will breach it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Tolerances make appetite measurable, such as at most four hours of downtime a month' (notes 1.2.6 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and Acceptance). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: setting moved to a harp maker; key B now says 'until' (an honest 'until' key).

questions.question: A cosmetics maker's High risk, owned by its head of logistics, has a treatment three months overdue; procedure has analysts raise such delays through regular risk reporting. What should the security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the overdue treatment privately to the head of logistics
options.B: Carry out the overdue treatment on the logistics system
options.C: Close the register entry, since its due date has already passed
options.D: Add the overdue treatment to this month's risk report

questions.key_concept: Risk reporting shows leaders top risks and overdue actions; use the agreed channel for overdue treatments rather than a private word.
questions.pre_read: Check what the procedure says to do with overdue treatments.
questions.correct_explanation: Registers exist so leaders can see top risks and overdue actions, and the procedure gives the analyst a set step: raise such delays through regular risk reporting. Adding this one to this month's report puts the delay before people who can act on it. A private report to the head of logistics, the runner-up, looks respectful of ownership, but it keeps a High risk's delay out of sight.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner does decide the treatment. But the procedure sends overdue treatments to leaders through risk reporting; a private report hides the delay.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it gets the fix done. But changing a system you do not own bypasses its owner and may break it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the date has passed. But an overdue treatment means the risk is still open; closing it would hide an untreated High risk.

tips: Eliminate: B changes a system the analyst does not own, and C closes a risk that is still untreated.
Final two: D beats A because the procedure routes overdue treatments to leaders through risk reporting; a private report keeps the delay hidden.
Exam cue: when the procedure names a channel for overdue or unowned risks, use it, even if a quieter route to the owner seems kinder.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Leaders see top risks and overdue actions; 2.4 covers indicators and dashboards' (notes 1.2.7 Risk Register, Ownership and Reporting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A solar installer's security manager has compared ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF 2.0 and recommends one for the company's security program. Who should MOST appropriately make the final choice?

options.A: The security manager, who will run the program day to day
options.B: Senior management, which sets the program's direction
options.C: The IT team, which will configure most of the controls
options.D: A certification body, which audits against standards

questions.key_concept: Senior management sets security direction, including which frameworks to follow; the security manager recommends and runs the program.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether choosing a framework is direction-setting or daily operations.
questions.correct_explanation: Choosing a framework sets the direction of the whole security program, which is a governance decision for senior management, who stay accountable for security risk. The security manager, the runner-up, rightly researches the options, recommends one and will run the program day to day, but managing the program follows the direction leaders set rather than setting it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the security manager knows the frameworks best. But they recommend; setting the program's direction is senior management's governance decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IT will do much of the work. But configuring controls is daily operations, not deciding the program's direction.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it knows the standards well. But a certification body audits independently; choosing for the client would compromise that.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses doing the work with setting direction, and D asks an independent auditor to make the client's decision.
Final two: B beats A because choosing a framework sets program direction, a governance call; the security manager researches and recommends.
Exam cue: leaders set direction and approve; management and practitioners recommend and carry out. Match the decision to the level that owns it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Leaders choose frameworks and approve policies; standards, procedures and guidelines sit beneath (see 1.3.5)' (notes 1.3.1 Security Governance and Its Roles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A tram operator's system administrator, who runs backups for timetable data its planning director owns, wants to cut backup retention from 90 to 30 days to save storage. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Propose the change to the planning director for a decision
options.B: Make the change, since the administrator runs the backups
options.C: Ask the security manager to approve the new retention period
options.D: Cut retention on a test copy, then show the planning director

questions.key_concept: A data custodian looks after data as the owner directs; decisions that change how the data is protected belong to the data owner.
questions.pre_read: Separate who runs the backups from who owns the data.
questions.correct_explanation: A data custodian looks after data day to day, such as running backups, as the data owner directs. Cutting retention changes how well the owner's data is protected, so the planning director, who owns it, decides. Asking the security manager, the runner-up, is a sensible check on standards, but the security manager does not own the timetable data, so their approval cannot replace the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the administrator runs the backups. But a custodian carries out the owner's direction; changing how long the data is protected is the owner's call.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the security manager knows backup standards. But they do not own the timetable data, so they cannot decide its protection for the owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testing changes is good practice. But a test shows how to make a change, not whether the owner wants the data protected for less time.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the custodian decide the owner's protection level, and D tests how to cut retention before anyone decides whether to.
Final two: A beats C because the data owner decides how their data is protected; the security manager does not own the timetable data.
Exam cue: custodians run the work and owners make the decisions about their data; route any change in protection level to the data owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Senior management is accountable; owners decide for their assets; custodians and users follow the rules' (notes 1.3.1 Security Governance and Its Roles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A software vendor tells a community land trust that NIST CSF 2.0 describes outcomes to reach, not the products or settings to use. Which reply from the trust's security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disagree; each outcome names the product that meets it
options.B: Disagree; Tier 4 requires the settings the CSF lists
options.C: Agree; each sector's regulator picks the methods to use
options.D: Agree; each organization picks its own way to reach them

questions.key_concept: NIST CSF 2.0 sets outcomes, not methods; each organization chooses the controls and products that achieve them.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the CSF Core contains and what it leaves to its users.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST CSF 2.0 describes outcomes, such as having assets inventoried, and does not prescribe how to reach them; separate online resources suggest practices and controls, and each organization chooses its own. Saying each sector's regulator picks the methods, the runner-up, treats the CSF as a regulation. It is voluntary guidance, so no regulator assigns methods under it, although a regulator may set its own rules separately.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because every outcome needs some product or process to meet it. But the CSF is technology-neutral; it names no products, and the choice stays with each organization.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Tiers sound like levels with set requirements. But Tiers describe how rigorous risk governance and management are; the CSF lists no settings for any Tier.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the CSF does leave methods open. But it is voluntary guidance, not a regulation, so the organization using it chooses how to reach each outcome, not a regulator.

tips: Eliminate: A says outcomes name products, and B treats Tiers as settings to meet; the CSF is technology-neutral and lists neither.
Final two: D beats C because the CSF is voluntary guidance, not law; the organization using it, not a regulator, chooses how to reach each outcome.
Exam cue: NIST CSF 2.0 says what to achieve, not how; the controls and products that achieve each outcome are the organization's choice.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 1 (CSF Overview); NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.2 (CSF Tiers: Tiers characterize the rigor of an organization's cybersecurity risk governance and management practices)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'CSF is voluntary and has no certification. Organizations needing one usually turn to ISO/IEC 27001' (notes 1.3.3 Security Frameworks and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled from 'CSF has no certification' (taught by cc_d1_011 and cc_d1_093) to CSF being outcome-based; key D kept, the speaker stays right.

questions.question: A shipyard's data-handling policy, owned by its operations director, cites a replaced privacy law; counsel has listed the new law's duties, and procedure has the security analyst draft updates. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the operations director if the new law needs a policy review
options.B: Keep applying the policy as written until it is reviewed
options.C: Draft an update for the new law for the director's approval
options.D: Publish a revised policy once the security team approves it

questions.key_concept: Policies are reviewed after major changes; the security team drafts updates, and the senior leader who owns the policy approves them.
questions.pre_read: Note who the procedure says drafts updates and who approves them.
questions.correct_explanation: Policies need review after major changes, like a replaced law. The procedure gives drafting to the security analyst, counsel has already set out the new duties, and approval stays with the operations director, the senior leader who owns the policy. So the analyst drafts the update and sends it for approval. Asking the director whether a review is needed, the runner-up, re-asks what the replaced law already answers and delays the work the procedure assigns.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the director owns the policy and will decide. But the law has plainly changed, and the procedure assigns drafting to the analyst; asking first only delays it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the policy is still approved. But it points to a law that no longer applies, so applying it unchanged leaves the new duties unmet.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the security team drafts policies. But approval belongs to the senior leader who owns the policy, which gives the update its authority.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps applying a policy built on a replaced law, and D has the security team approve its own policy update.
Final two: C beats A because the procedure assigns drafting to the analyst and the change is plain; the director's role is to approve the draft.
Exam cue: after a change in laws, technology or ways of working, policies need review; the security team drafts and the senior owner approves.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-02 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated and enforced to reflect changes in requirements, threats, technology and organizational mission); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.1 (Policies for information security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Policies are reviewed on a schedule and after major changes, such as new technology, laws or ways of working' (notes 1.3.4 Security Policies). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: A now names the law too, so 'law' is not only on the key; approver described as the senior leader who owns the policy, matching cc_d1_036 and notes 1.3.4.

questions.question: An animation studio's AI standard limits its approved tool to Public data, but a newer prompt guideline suggests pasting Internal scripts. A producer asks which to follow; what is the security analyst's BEST answer?

options.A: The standard, with the clash reported to the guideline's owner
options.B: The guideline, since it is the newer and more specific advice
options.C: Either one, since both documents were properly approved
options.D: Neither, until the two documents' owners agree which applies

questions.key_concept: A guideline cannot override a mandatory standard; follow the standard and report the conflict to the owner of the document that strays.
questions.pre_read: Identify which document is mandatory and which is advice.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards are mandatory and guidelines are advice, so a guideline cannot widen what the standard allows. The producer keeps to Public data, and the analyst reports the clash to the guideline's owner so the advice is corrected. Waiting until the owners agree, the runner-up, looks careful, but the standard already gives a clear, mandatory answer, so work can go on under it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because newer, specific advice feels current. But a guideline is advisory and cannot override a mandatory standard.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both were published. But a standard binds and a guideline advises; they do not carry equal weight.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: waiting for the owners avoids a wrong step. But the mandatory standard already answers the question, so work continues under it while the clash is fixed.

tips: Eliminate: B lets advisory text override a mandatory standard, and C treats a guideline and a standard as equal.
Final two: A beats D because the mandatory standard still applies, so work goes on under it while the guideline's owner fixes the clash.
Exam cue: when documents conflict, follow the mandatory, higher one and report the clash to the owner of the document that strays.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Standards, Guidelines, and Procedures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Each document must agree with the one above it; if they conflict, follow the higher one where your role allows and report the conflict to the lower document's owner' (notes 1.3.5 Standards, Procedures and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bus depot's IT team writes numbered steps that staff must follow to cancel a leaver's building badge on their last day. What kind of document is this MOST accurately?

options.A: A guideline for badge cancellation
options.B: A standard for badge cancellation
options.C: A procedure for badge cancellation
options.D: A policy for badge cancellation

questions.key_concept: A procedure gives mandatory, step-by-step instructions for a task; a standard sets the specific requirement the steps must meet.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the document says what must be true or how to do a task.
questions.correct_explanation: A procedure lists the exact steps for a task, such as cancelling a leaver's badge, and staff must follow it. A standard, the runner-up, is also specific and mandatory, but it states what must be true, such as which badge system or settings to use, not the step-by-step way to do the task. Policies stay high-level, and guidelines are optional advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the steps show a way to work. But guidelines are optional; these steps are mandatory instructions for a task.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: standards are specific and mandatory. But a standard sets requirements, such as which settings to use; step-by-step instructions are a procedure.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff must follow it. But a policy is a high-level statement of what and why, not numbered steps for one task.

tips: Eliminate: A calls mandatory steps optional advice, and D files task-level steps as a high-level policy.
Final two: C beats B because numbered steps for doing a task are a procedure; a standard states what must be true, not how to do it.
Exam cue: a policy says what and why, a standard sets the specific requirement, a procedure says how step by step, and a guideline suggests.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Standards, Guidelines, and Procedures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Procedures list the exact steps for a task, such as setting up a new user' (notes 1.3.5 Standards, Procedures and Guidelines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: setting moved to a bus depot; every option ends 'for badge cancellation', so the stem's verb is no longer echoed only by the key.

questions.question: An AI vendor tells a Portuguese estate agency that its lead-scoring model needs no privacy review because it learned only from people's public social media posts. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; posts people make public fall outside privacy law
options.B: Agree, once the tool passes a review under the EU AI Act
options.C: Disagree; only signed consent makes AI training lawful
options.D: Disagree; personal data is still personal data when public

questions.key_concept: Personal data stays covered by privacy law even when posted publicly, and AI-specific laws add to privacy law rather than replace it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether public data can still be personal data.
questions.correct_explanation: Personal data stays personal data when people post it publicly, so privacy law, such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), still governs collecting and using it to score leads; legal counsel should confirm the duties. The EU AI Act review, the runner-up, may also apply, but AI-specific law adds duties on top of privacy law rather than replacing it, so it cannot remove the need for a privacy review.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the posts are visible to anyone. But privacy law covers personal data however it was obtained, including what people post publicly.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: AI-specific law may apply too. But it adds duties on top of privacy law; it cannot replace the privacy review.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because consent is a common lawful basis. But it is not the only one; legitimate interests or another lawful basis may also apply.

tips: Eliminate: A treats public posts as outside privacy law, and C makes consent the only lawful basis.
Final two: D beats B because AI-specific law adds to privacy law rather than replacing it; public personal data still needs a privacy review.
