Exam cue: new technology gets no exemption; when AI touches personal data from any source, privacy law applies alongside any AI-specific law.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.1 (legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed and documented); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Privacy law still covers personal data in prompts, training data and outputs' (notes 1.3.6 Laws and Rules That Apply to AI). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An orchid nursery protects its breeding records with a written access policy and folder permissions on its file server. Which addition BEST layers that protection with a control of a different type?

options.A: Encryption of the breeding records folder on the server
options.B: Yearly staff training on the written access policy
options.C: A locked room for the file server, keyed to IT staff
options.D: A second set of folder permissions on a backup copy

questions.key_concept: Layering mixes control types and functions, so one failure does not expose the asset; add the type that is missing.
questions.pre_read: Classify each existing control by type before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Layering works best when controls differ in type, so one failure does not open the way. The records already have an administrative control, the policy, and a technical one, the permissions; a locked server room adds the missing physical layer. Encryption, the runner-up, is a strong addition that protects data even if permissions fail, but it is another technical control, so it adds no new type.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: encryption adds real protection. But it is technical, like the folder permissions, so it does not add a new type of control.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training supports the policy. But training is administrative, the same type as the written policy already in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it adds more permissions. But that is another technical control of the same kind, which tends to fail the same way.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats the administrative type of the policy, and D repeats the technical type of the permissions.
Final two: C beats A because a locked room adds the missing physical type; encryption, though strong, is another technical control.
Exam cue: to layer, list the types already protecting an asset, then add the type that is missing: administrative, technical or physical.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Appendix A Glossary (defense in depth); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cover each important risk with several types: a policy, a technical block, a physical lock' (notes 1.4.6 Layering and Compensating Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A carpet maker wants a technical control on its stock system that detects password-guessing attempts rather than preventing them. Which control should the system administrator propose as BEST?

options.A: Alerts to the security team on bursts of failed sign-ins
options.B: An account lockout after five failed sign-ins in a row
options.C: A policy clause forbidding staff from guessing passwords
options.D: A longer minimum password length for all accounts

questions.key_concept: Technical controls are built into systems; some prevent, such as lockouts, and some detect, such as alerts that flag activity.
questions.pre_read: Decide both the control type and the function the stem needs.
questions.correct_explanation: The company wants to detect password guessing, not prevent it, so it needs a detective control, and it must be technical. Alerts generated by the system do both: they watch sign-ins and notify the team automatically. An account lockout, the runner-up, is also technical and reacts to failed sign-ins, but it is preventive: it stops further guesses by blocking the account.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a lockout is a technical response to failed sign-ins. But it blocks further attempts, a preventive function, not the detective one the company asked for.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets password guessing. But a written rule is administrative, and it notices nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is a technical control against password guessing. But it only makes guessing harder; it notices nothing and alerts no one.

tips: Eliminate: C is a written rule, so administrative, and D only makes guessing harder; it notices no failed sign-ins.
Final two: A beats B because the company wants to detect guessing, a detective function; a lockout is preventive, since it blocks further attempts.
Exam cue: classify by type and function together: technical or not, then prevent, detect or correct; match both to what the stem asks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-4(5) (System Monitoring | System-generated Alerts); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts: lockouts are usually temporary because of the potential for denial of service)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Some detect activity, such as intrusion detection raising alerts' (notes 1.4.2 Technical Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A timber merchant is moving a yard worker, whose background was checked only for yard work, into its cash office to handle supplier refunds. Which administrative control should the finance manager require as BEST?

options.A: Install a camera above the cash office counter before the move
options.B: Encrypt the refunds database before the worker gains access
options.C: Have the worker sign the cash office's conduct rules
options.D: Screen the worker for the cash role before granting access

questions.key_concept: Personnel screening is an administrative control; screen people again when they move into a more sensitive role.
questions.pre_read: Compare the checks done at hiring with the risk of the new role.
questions.correct_explanation: Personnel screening is an administrative control, and sensitive roles warrant checks suited to their risk. The worker's background was checked only for yard work, so before they handle refunds, the merchant should screen them for the cash role. Signing the cash office's rules, the runner-up, is also administrative and sets expectations, but it verifies nothing about the person who will now handle money.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because cameras watch cash handling. But a camera is a physical control, and it says nothing about whether the worker suits the role.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because refunds data is sensitive. But encryption is technical, and the system decrypts data for the worker once access is granted.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: signed rules are an administrative control too. But they set expectations; they do not check the background of someone moving into a cash role.

tips: Eliminate: A is physical and B technical, though the finance manager needs an administrative control.
Final two: D beats C because screening checks that the person suits a cash role; signed rules only set expectations.
Exam cue: when someone moves into a more sensitive role, check whether the screening done at hiring still fits the new access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-3 (Personnel Screening)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Hiring practices include background checks and prompt access removal when people leave' (notes 1.4.3 Administrative Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A film post-production house is adding gas fire suppression to its equipment room, where editors often work late. Which feature should the security analyst insist on FIRST?

options.A: A warning alarm and delay so people can leave before release
options.B: Doors that lock during release to hold the gas in the room
options.C: Release at the first sign of smoke to save the equipment
options.D: A camera feed of the room for the security desk

questions.key_concept: Physical controls must protect people first; suppression in occupied rooms needs warnings and time to leave before release.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the gas could do to someone still in the room.
questions.correct_explanation: Life safety comes first. A gas system that fills an occupied room can harm the people inside, so a warning alarm and a short delay before release let them leave first. Releasing at the first sign of smoke, the runner-up, saves equipment a little sooner, but it could flood the room while editors are still in it, putting property ahead of people.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it keeps the gas where it works. But locking doors during release could trap people inside; escape routes must always let people out.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: fast release protects equipment best. But it could release gas while editors are still inside; people must get out first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the desk could see who is inside. But watching the room does not get anyone out before the gas is released.

tips: Eliminate: B could trap people behind locked doors, and D watches the room without getting anyone out.
Final two: A beats C because people must be able to leave before release; saving equipment a little sooner never outranks their safety.
Exam cue: when a physical control could harm people, choose the option that protects life first, even at some cost to equipment.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-13 (Fire Protection); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2.8 (Occupant Emergency Plan (OEP))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Life safety comes first: escape-route doors must let people out, even when that weakens security' (notes 1.4.4 Physical Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: role sweep: 'security technician' became 'security analyst'.

questions.question: A sail loft's till software automatically undoes any unapproved change to its settings within minutes, returning them to the approved baseline. Which control function does this MOST accurately serve?

options.A: Preventive, because it stops unapproved changes being made
options.B: Deterrent, because staff know their changes will not last
options.C: Directive, as it tells staff which settings to use
options.D: Corrective, because it reverses the unapproved change

questions.key_concept: A corrective control fixes a problem after it occurs; a preventive control stops it before it takes effect.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the change happens before the control acts.
questions.correct_explanation: A corrective control fixes a problem after it happens. The till software lets the change happen, then undoes it, returning the settings to the approved baseline, which is correction. Preventive, the runner-up, would block the change before it took effect; here the unapproved settings exist for a few minutes, so the control does not stop the change, it reverses it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the end result resembles prevention. But the change does happen and runs for minutes; a preventive control would block it before it took effect.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because staff may give up making changes. But any discouragement is a side effect; the control's job is to undo changes once made.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it enforces approved settings. But directive controls tell people what to do, such as a policy; this software acts on the system itself.

tips: Eliminate: B names a side effect, not the control's job, and C confuses software that acts with a rule that instructs people.
Final two: D beats A because the change happens and is then undone; preventive controls stop it before it takes effect.
Exam cue: ask when the control acts: before an event to stop it (prevent), to notice it (detect), or after it to fix it (correct).
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Appendix A Glossary (security: protective measures may combine deterrence, avoidance, prevention, detection, recovery and correction); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-01 (configuration management practices are established and applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Corrective: fixes the problem, such as removing malware' (notes 1.4.5 Control Functions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: setting moved to a sail loft (ski settings overused).

questions.question: A paint maker's endpoint standard requires antivirus on every PC, but the vendor of its color-matching PC forbids installing any. Which compensating control should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the PC's disk so stolen color data stays unreadable
options.B: Record the malware risk as accepted, as the vendor forbids changes
options.C: Scan the other office PCs twice as often instead
options.D: Isolate the PC on its own network without internet or email

questions.key_concept: A compensating control lowers the same risk as the missing control by another means; a control aimed at a different risk does not compensate.
questions.pre_read: Name the risk the missing antivirus was meant to reduce.
questions.correct_explanation: A compensating control must lower the same risk another way. Antivirus is there to stop malware, so isolating the PC from the internet and email cuts off the usual ways malware arrives. Disk encryption, the runner-up, is a sound control, but it protects data on a stolen PC, a different risk; malware could still reach and run on it. Any exception still needs the standard owner's approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: encryption is a strong control. But it protects data if the PC is stolen; it does nothing against the malware antivirus was meant to stop.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor's rule cannot change. But an analyst cannot accept risk, and compensating controls come before any acceptance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it adds scanning. But scanning other PCs does nothing for the one PC that cannot run antivirus.

tips: Eliminate: B has the analyst accept risk, and C adds protection to the wrong PCs.
Final two: D beats A because isolation lowers the same malware risk antivirus covers; encryption addresses theft, a different risk.
Exam cue: a compensating control must address the same risk as the missing control; first name what the missing control was for.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Appendix A Glossary (compensating controls)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'When a required control is impossible, a compensating control reduces the same risk another way' (notes 1.4.6 Layering and Compensating Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.4 Security controls. Controls for AI tools
questions.question: A football club's press office uses an AI tool to draft public statements. Which of its safeguards is MOST accurately an administrative control?

options.A: A filter that blocks drafts naming injured players
options.B: A badge lock on the press office door
options.C: A rule that a press officer signs off each draft
options.D: A log that records each prompt and the model version used

questions.key_concept: Classify safeguards by how they work: a human sign-off rule is administrative, and a log the system writes itself is technical, even for oversight.
questions.pre_read: Sort each safeguard by how it works, not by what it protects.
questions.correct_explanation: Administrative controls are the policies, procedures and people practices that direct how work is done. A rule requiring a press officer to sign off each AI draft is a human-review procedure, so it is administrative. The prompt log, the runner-up, can feel like paperwork, but the system records it automatically, which makes it a technical control that supports accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it shapes what the tool may produce. But a filter built into software is a technical control.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it guards the office where the tool is used. But a door lock is a tangible barrier, which makes it physical.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: logs feel like records kept for oversight. But the system writes them automatically, so the log is a technical control.

tips: Eliminate: A is a software filter, so technical, and B is a door lock, so physical.
Final two: C beats D because a sign-off rule is a people procedure; a log the system writes automatically is technical.
Exam cue: sort by mechanism, not purpose; a rule people follow is administrative, even for an AI tool, and a record software writes is technical.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Administrative: an AI use policy, a risk review before launch and human review of high-impact outputs' (notes 1.4.7 Controls for AI Tools). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A mattress maker's new security analyst kept detection rules they wrote as part of their job at their former employer, on a personal USB drive, and wants to reuse them. Which action is BEST?

options.A: Use the rules, since the analyst wrote them personally
options.B: Strip the former employer's name, then reuse the rules
options.C: Ask the new manager to approve reusing the former employer's rules
options.D: Delete the copies and write new rules for this employer

questions.key_concept: The duty to protect an employer's confidential information continues after leaving; work done for them belongs to them.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns work done for an employer.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules written as part of a job belong to the employer they were written for, and the duty to protect its confidential information continues after leaving. The analyst should delete the copies and build new rules for the new employer from their own skills. Asking the new manager, the runner-up, sounds transparent, but the new manager has no authority over another company's confidential material, so even a yes would not make reuse right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the analyst did the work. But work done for an employer belongs to that employer, so the rules are its confidential property.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it hides where the rules came from. But removing the name does not change who owns them; it only disguises the misuse.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: raising concerns with a manager is usually wise. But the rules belong to the former employer, and the new manager cannot authorize use of another company's confidential material.

tips: Eliminate: A treats work done for an employer as personal property, and B disguises the rules' origin instead of respecting it.
Final two: D beats C because the new manager cannot authorize using another firm's confidential work; the analyst should not keep it at all.
Exam cue: confidentiality duties to a former employer outlast the job; bring your skills to a new role, never their materials.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons; NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Common themes are honesty, avoiding conflicts of interest and protecting confidential information' (notes 1.5.1 Professional Code of Conduct). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: stem now says the rules were written as part of the job, so the former employer's ownership is explicit; C names the former employer's rules; PL-4 replaced by PS-4 (exit interviews remind leavers of the constraints of being former employees).

questions.subtopic: 1.5 Professional conduct. Due care and due diligence
questions.question: A coffee roaster's security analyst reviews the payroll share's access list monthly and finds a former employee still listed; the help desk technician then removes the entry. How are these steps MOST accurately described?

options.A: The review is due care, and the removal is due diligence
options.B: The review is due diligence, and the removal is due care
options.C: Both are due care, as both protect the payroll share
options.D: Both are due diligence, as both follow from the review

questions.key_concept: Due diligence investigates and verifies; due care acts on what was found, as a prudent person would.
questions.pre_read: Ask which step finds things out and which acts on them.
questions.correct_explanation: Due diligence is finding out: checking whether safeguards still hold, as the analyst does by reviewing the access list each month. Due care is acting on what was found, as the help desk technician does by removing the former employee's entry. The reversed pairing, the runner-up, is the common mix-up; remember that diligence discovers and care carries it out.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it names both ideas. But it reverses them: reviewing and checking is diligence, and acting on the finding is care.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both steps protect the payroll share. But reviewing the list finds things out, which is diligence; only the removal acts on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the removal came from the review. But fixing what was found is action, which is due care, not diligence.

tips: Eliminate: C and D give both steps one label, though one step finds out and the other acts.
Final two: B beats A because reviewing the access list is diligence and removing the entry is care; A reverses them.
Exam cue: diligence discovers, care carries it out; researching, assessing or verifying is diligence, and fixing or enforcing is care.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Both are ongoing: diligence keeps checking, care keeps acting on the results' (notes 1.5.2 Due Care and Due Diligence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: re-set from vendor patches (cc_d1_017, cc_d1_184) to a monthly access review and removal; lesson and key B kept.

questions.question: A certified analyst works weekdays for a managed security provider and, with the provider's approval, also holds their own weekend contract to monitor a rowing club's network. Who are the analyst's principals MOST accurately?

options.A: Only the provider, which employs the analyst full time
options.B: The provider's leadership team, which directs the work
options.C: The provider and the club, each under its own agreement
options.D: The provider and club members whose data they guard

questions.key_concept: Principals are those a member serves under an employment or contract relationship: each employer and each client they hold a contract with.
questions.pre_read: List every employment or contract relationship the analyst holds.
questions.correct_explanation: Principals are those a member serves under an employment or contract relationship. The analyst is employed by the provider and holds their own contract with the rowing club, so both are principals owed diligent, competent service. Naming only the provider, the runner-up, overlooks the club, which the analyst serves under their own contract.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the employer is a principal. But the analyst also serves the club under their own contract, which makes the club a principal too.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because leaders direct the work. But principals are the parties served under an employment or contract relationship, not a group of leaders inside one of them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the analyst protects members' data. But the members have no agreement with the analyst; the club holds the contract, and protecting members falls under the duty to society.

tips: Eliminate: B narrows principals to a leadership team, and D swaps the club for its members, who have no agreement with the analyst.
Final two: C beats A because the analyst's own contract with the club makes it a principal alongside the employer.
Exam cue: list every employment or contract relationship you hold; each employer and client on that list is a principal.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons (service to principals); ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (standing of complainant and form of complaints)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Principals are those you serve under an employment or contract relationship, such as employers and clients' (notes 1.5.3 The ISC2 Code of Ethics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: B no longer opens 'Only'; C no longer opens 'Both' or echoes 'separate'; D also pairs the provider with a second party, so the key is not the only two-party option.

questions.question: A crane hire firm's manager asks a certified analyst to secretly read an operator's personal webmail, sometimes opened on a work laptop, to learn whether they plan to quit. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Read it only after the manager confirms the request in writing
options.B: Read only the subject lines, to keep the intrusion small
options.C: Refuse, and point the manager to HR and legal counsel instead
options.D: Decline, and report the manager to the police at once

questions.key_concept: Reject illegal or deceptive tasks even when a manager asks, and route the concern to proper channels such as HR and legal counsel.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether any approval could make this action lawful.
questions.correct_explanation: Reading someone's personal webmail without a lawful basis is likely illegal and plainly dishonest, whoever asks. The analyst should refuse and point the manager to HR and legal counsel, who handle staff concerns lawfully. A written request, the runner-up, documents the order, but a manager's signature cannot make an unlawful intrusion legal, so it does not change the answer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: written authorization matters for many security tasks. But a manager cannot authorize reading private mail unlawfully; paperwork does not make it legal.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems a smaller step. But reading subject lines is still reading private mail without a lawful basis.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it refuses firmly. But going straight to the police skips internal channels such as HR and legal, which can still stop this properly.

tips: Eliminate: B still reads private mail, and D skips the internal channels that can handle the request.
Final two: C beats A because a manager's signature cannot make reading private mail lawful; HR and legal handle the concern lawfully.
Exam cue: an employer's request never makes an illegal or deceptive act acceptable; decline it and route the matter through proper internal channels.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Reject any illegal or deceptive option, even if an employer asks for it' (notes 1.5.4 Applying the Canons to Dilemmas). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A certified consultant falsely tells a radio show that a town's water system is fully secure, and a listener with no security role wants to complain. Which statement about the listener's standing is MOST accurate?

options.A: No; complaints about a consultant must come from their clients
options.B: No; complaints must come from other certified professionals
options.C: Yes, but only after the town's water company complains
options.D: Yes, as anyone may complain about dishonest public conduct

questions.key_concept: Anyone may complain under the canons on society and honest conduct; principals and fellow professionals have standing for the other two.
questions.pre_read: Match the misconduct to a canon before deciding who may complain.
questions.correct_explanation: Standing depends on the canon. Complaints under the canons on protecting society and acting honestly may come from anyone, so a listener with no security role may complain about a false public statement. Limiting complaints to clients, the runner-up, applies only to the canon on service to principals; a dishonest statement to the public falls under canons anyone can invoke.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: some complaints are limited to principals. But that applies to the canon on service to principals; anyone may complain about dishonesty.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fellow professionals do have special standing. But that covers the canon on the profession; dishonesty complaints are open to anyone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the water company is most affected. But nothing requires another party to complain first; the listener has standing in their own right.

tips: Eliminate: B limits all complaints to fellow professionals, and C invents a rule that another party must complain first.
Final two: D beats A because anyone may complain about dishonesty or harm to the public; only service-to-principals complaints need a principal.
Exam cue: match the concern to the canon, then check standing: anyone for society and honesty, principals for service, professionals for the profession.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (standing of complainant and form of complaints)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Anyone may complain under canons 1 and 2; principals, such as employers or clients, under canon 3' (notes 1.5.5 Ethics Complaints and Enforcement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Final fix round, 12 Nov 2026: C drops 'once' (a losing word); D lengthened so the key is not the lone shortest.

questions.question: At a lighthouse museum, a colleague says using an AI tool to write a convincing phishing email for coworkers is fine because it is only practice. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; practice phishing needs no approval if nobody is harmed
options.B: It is acceptable only inside an authorized, scoped test
options.C: It is acceptable if sent from a personal email account
options.D: Disagree; AI-written lures are never allowed, even in tests

questions.key_concept: Using AI to create attack content, such as phishing lures, is acceptable only inside an authorized, scoped test.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes a phishing email a test rather than an attack.
questions.correct_explanation: Attack content such as a phishing lure is acceptable only inside an authorized, scoped test, where the owner has approved the targets and limits; otherwise it can cause real harm and deceives coworkers. Saying AI-written lures are never allowed, the runner-up, overcorrects: an authorized phishing simulation may use AI-drafted emails, because the authorization and scope, not the tool, make it acceptable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the intent is training. But without authorization, a convincing lure can cause real harm and deceives coworkers who never agreed to a test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it keeps company systems out of it. But sending an unauthorized lure from a personal account makes it more deceptive, not less.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: caution with AI lures is wise. But authorized, scoped phishing tests may use AI-drafted emails; the authorization, not the tool, decides.

tips: Eliminate: A treats good intent as authorization, and C makes an unauthorized lure harder to trace.
Final two: B beats D because authorized, scoped tests may use AI-written lures; it is the missing authorization that makes this wrong.
Exam cue: for attack-style work, ask whether it is authorized and scoped; the same act is a test with permission and misconduct without it.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons; NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(1) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Practical Exercises)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Attack content is acceptable only inside an authorized, scoped test. Otherwise it risks real harm' (notes 1.5.6 Ethical Use of AI at Work). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An online grocer's order system stayed online at month-end, but pages took minutes, so staff stopped taking orders. Its IT manager calls this an availability failure; which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disagree; the system stayed online, so availability held
options.B: Agree; it was not usable when staff needed it
options.C: Disagree; slow pages are an integrity problem, not availability
options.D: Agree, but only if an attacker caused the slowdown

questions.key_concept: Availability means authorized users can use systems and data when needed; a system that is online but unusable has failed it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether staff could actually use the system when they needed it.
questions.correct_explanation: Availability means authorized users can reach systems and data in a usable state when they need them. Pages taking minutes stopped staff taking orders, so availability failed even though the system never went offline. Agreeing only if an attacker caused it, the runner-up, mistakes the cause for the goal: availability is harmed by overload and faults as well as by attacks.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing crashed. But availability means usable when needed, not just switched on; staff could not take orders.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because something went wrong. But integrity is about data staying correct, and no order data was changed here.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: attacks such as denial of service do harm availability. But overload and faults harm it too; the goal is judged by the effect, not the cause.

tips: Eliminate: A equates availability with being switched on, and C calls slowness an integrity problem though no data changed.
Final two: B beats D because availability is judged by whether users can work, whatever the cause; overload harms it as surely as an attack.
Exam cue: availability means usable when needed; a system that is up but too slow to use has still failed it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-04 (adequate resource capacity to ensure availability is maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Availability means authorized users can reach the systems, data and services they need, in a usable state, when they need them' (notes 1.1.4 Availability). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A flooring wholesaler plans to treat emailed orders as binding when they arrive unsigned from a customer's usual address over an encrypted connection. What should the security analyst MOST accurately conclude?

options.A: Such orders would not prove which of its customers sent them
options.B: The encrypted connection would prove the customer sent each one
options.C: The usual sender address would stop a customer denying one
options.D: A disputed order could not be checked, as it has no signature

questions.key_concept: Non-repudiation needs evidence tied to something only the sender controls; an unsigned email from a familiar address over an encrypted link does not provide it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what, if anything, would tie each order to one specific person.
questions.correct_explanation: Non-repudiation needs proof tied to something only the sender controls, such as a digital signature made with their own private key. These orders would carry no signature, and a familiar address can be spoofed or used by someone else on the account. Treating the usual address as undeniable, the runner-up, mistakes where a message seems to come from for proof of who created it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption sounds like strong proof. But it protects each order on the link; it does not show who wrote it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a known address looks convincing. But addresses can be spoofed or misused, and nothing only the customer controls would tie an order to them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the strongest proof, a signature, would be missing. But mail headers and server logs could still be examined; they help an inquiry though they fall short of non-repudiation.

tips: Eliminate: B treats link encryption as proof of authorship, and D assumes an unsigned order could not be checked, though headers and logs could still be examined.
Final two: A beats C because a familiar address is not something only the customer controls; without a signature, a customer could credibly deny an order.
Exam cue: for non-repudiation, look for something only one person holds, such as their private key; addresses and encrypted links do not qualify.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-10 (Non-repudiation); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.3 (Electronic Signatures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Non-repudiation is evidence strong enough that a person cannot credibly deny sending a message, signing a document or performing an action' (notes 1.1.7 Non-Repudiation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An arcade chain's customer chatbot can add game credits to accounts, granting any amount a user asks for with no limit or staff check. How should the security analyst MOST accurately label this missing check?

options.A: A vulnerability, since a weakness need not be a coding bug
options.B: A vulnerability only once a customer has abused it
options.C: Not a vulnerability, since the chatbot works as it was built
options.D: A threat, since it could cost the chain money

questions.key_concept: A missing limit or human check is a vulnerability even when the tool works exactly as built and before anyone abuses it.
questions.pre_read: Think about what has to be true for something to count as a vulnerability.
questions.correct_explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness a threat could use. A design that lets a chatbot grant any amount with no limit or staff check is one, even though no code is faulty. The weakness exists now, before anyone abuses it; the people who might ask for huge credits are the threat. Saying it is not a vulnerability because the chatbot works as built, the runner-up, mistakes 'no bug' for 'no weakness'.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing has gone wrong yet. But a weakness exists before it is used; abuse would turn it into an incident, not make it a vulnerability.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the chatbot works exactly as built. But a design granting unlimited value with no check is itself the weakness; working as built does not mean safe.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the gap could cost the chain money. But a threat is a cause of harm, such as whoever might abuse the chatbot, not the chatbot's own missing check.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for abuse before calling it a weakness, though a vulnerability exists before anyone uses it, and D calls the gap a threat, though the threat is whoever abuses it.
Final two: A beats C because a design with no limit or human check is a weakness even when no code is faulty; working as built does not mean safe.
Exam cue: a vulnerability need not be a bug or already abused; a tool, AI included, that can act with no limit or human check has a weakness built into its design.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use, such as unpatched software' (notes 1.2.1 Threats, Vulnerabilities and Risk). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A dog-walking app's security analyst maintains its risk ratings and briefs risk owners on changes; a law passed today will fine leaks of clients' location data from next year. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Schedule the location-data re-rating for next year, when fines start
options.B: Keep last quarter's ratings, as no location data has leaked
options.C: Re-rate the location-data risks to reflect the coming fines
options.D: Buy insurance to cover fines for location-data leaks

questions.key_concept: A new law sends affected risks back to assessment when it is passed, not when it takes effect, so owners have time to treat them.
questions.pre_read: Think about when a coming law starts to change a risk's rating.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk lifecycle loops back to assessment whenever something important changes, and a law that will fine leaks raises their impact. Re-rating now, then briefing the owners, gives them time to choose and put in place any new treatment before the fines start. Waiting until the law takes effect, the runner-up, leaves owners deciding on old ratings until it is too late to prepare.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the fines do not apply yet. But treatments take time, and owners can only plan them once the ratings show the coming impact.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing has gone wrong yet. But the fines raise the impact of any future leak, and the old ratings no longer fit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because insurance is a real treatment. But treatment comes after the risk is re-rated, and owners, not the analyst, choose it.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps ratings that a change in the law has made outdated, and D picks a treatment before the risk is reassessed.
Final two: C beats A because reassessing when the law passes gives owners time to treat the risk before the fines start.
Exam cue: reassess when a new law, threat or system appears, not when it starts to bite; early ratings give owners time to act.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk management never finishes. After a big change, an incident or a new threat, go back to identifying and assessing' (notes 1.2.2 The Risk Management Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An event caterer's finance team canceled the database replica listed as the control for a booking-loss risk that the operations director owns. What should the security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask finance to fund a cheaper replacement for the replica
options.B: Tell the operations director the replica was canceled
options.C: Restart the replica under the IT budget, then tell the operations director
options.D: Make finance the risk's owner, as it chose to drop the control

questions.key_concept: When a control behind a risk disappears, the risk owner must hear first, because the owner, or senior management beyond tolerance, decides the new treatment.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decides what happens to a risk once its control is gone.
questions.correct_explanation: Each register entry has an owner who decides how the risk is treated. Finance's cut removed the director's control, so the risk is larger than the director believes; the analyst tells them first, and they decide whether to replace the control, accept the larger risk within tolerance or take it to senior management. Asking finance to fund a cheaper replacement, the runner-up, picks a treatment before the owner has decided one is needed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a replacement may well be the answer. But choosing the treatment is the director's decision; finance holds the budget, not the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it restores protection and still informs the owner. But the replica's budget is not the analyst's call; acting first hands the director a treatment already chosen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because finance's cut changed the risk. But management assigns ownership, not whoever cuts a budget; the analyst cannot reassign it, and the director keeps the risk.

tips: Eliminate: C reverses a decision the analyst does not own before the director hears of it, and D hands the risk to finance, though management assigns ownership and a budget cut does not move it.
Final two: B beats A because the owner decides the new treatment; asking finance for a replacement settles a decision that is neither finance's nor the analyst's.
Exam cue: when a control behind a risk disappears, tell the risk owner first; the owner, not the budget holder, decides what happens next.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A risk register is the shared record of known risks, each with a rating, an owner, a treatment and a status' (notes 1.2.7 Risk Register, Ownership and Reporting). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A stadium operator's new board member says that once the board approves the security budget, it needs no security reports until next year. Which reply from the security manager is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; approving the budget completes the board's security role
options.B: Disagree; the board must keep reviewing security results regularly
options.C: Agree; the security manager answers for results once funded
options.D: Disagree; the board must also approve each security change

questions.key_concept: Board oversight is ongoing: the board keeps checking security results through regular reports, while management runs daily work such as approving changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a board still owes once it has funded the security program.
questions.correct_explanation: Governance does not end with funding. The board sets direction and stays accountable, so it keeps reviewing security results through regular reports and adjusts course when they fall short; management runs the daily work. Saying the board must also approve each security change, the runner-up, rightly rejects the claim but for the wrong reason: approving single changes is management's job, not oversight.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approving the budget is a real board decision. But governance also means checking whether the money delivers results, and that review continues all year.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the security manager runs the program day to day. But the board stays accountable for security results, and funding a manager does not hand that duty over.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it rightly disagrees with the board member. But oversight means reviewing results, not approving each change; single changes are management's daily work.

tips: Eliminate: A treats budget approval as the board's whole role, though governance keeps reviewing results, and C moves accountability to the manager, though it stays with the board.
Final two: B beats D because oversight means reviewing results through regular reports; approving each security change is management's daily work, not the board's.
Exam cue: governance sets direction and keeps reviewing results; it does not run daily work, and funding a program does not end its oversight.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-03 (organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Governance sets direction and checks results within legal duties; management runs the daily work' (notes 1.3.1 Security Governance and Its Roles). questions.question: A chess app's IT manager says the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which applies to it, requires adopting a framework such as NIST CSF 2.0. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; the GDPR names NIST CSF 2.0 as the framework to adopt
options.B: Agree; the GDPR requires the app to adopt some recognized security framework
options.C: Disagree; the GDPR covers privacy rights, not security duties
options.D: Disagree; the GDPR requires security fit to the risk, not a framework

questions.key_concept: Laws such as the GDPR require security appropriate to the risk but name no framework; adopting one is a voluntary way to meet the duty.
questions.pre_read: Separate what a law requires from how an organization chooses to meet it.
questions.correct_explanation: The GDPR requires organizations it covers to protect personal data with measures appropriate to the risk, but it does not name a framework or make adopting one a duty. NIST CSF 2.0 is a voluntary framework the app may choose to organize that work. Agreeing that the law requires some recognized framework, the runner-up, turns one way of meeting the duty into the duty itself.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because NIST CSF 2.0 is widely used. But the GDPR is an EU law and names no framework, NIST's or any other.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a framework is a common way to show security is managed. But the GDPR sets an outcome, security fit to the risk, and leaves the method open.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the GDPR is best known for privacy rights. But it also requires appropriate security for personal data, so it does set security duties.

tips: Eliminate: A claims an EU law names a US framework, and C limits the GDPR to privacy rights, though it also requires security appropriate to the risk.
Final two: D beats B because the law requires the outcome, security fit to the risk, while adopting a framework stays a voluntary choice of method.
Exam cue: laws usually require an outcome, such as security fit to the risk, and leave the method open; a framework is one way to reach it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 1 (CSF Overview); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Laws are rules passed by governments, and regulations are detailed rules agencies issue under those laws; both are mandatory' (notes 1.3.2 Laws and Regulations). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A research firm's contracts bar sharing clients' survey answers with third parties without consent; staff want them summarized by a cloud AI tool approved for internal documents. What should the security analyst raise FIRST?

options.A: Whether AI-specific law treats survey answers as high risk
options.B: Whether the contracts let the AI vendor see survey answers
options.C: Whether its summaries are as accurate as staff ones
options.D: Whether the AI vendor's certification satisfies the contracts

questions.key_concept: Contracts and laws that already bind an organization apply to AI tools too; an AI vendor is a third party for data-sharing limits.
questions.pre_read: List the rules that already govern this data before looking at the tool.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules that already bind an organization still apply when AI arrives, and contracts are among them. These contracts forbid passing survey answers to third parties without consent, and a cloud AI vendor is a third party, whatever approval the tool has for internal work. Asking whether the vendor's certification satisfies the contracts, the runner-up, misses that a security certificate cannot stand in for the clients' consent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI-specific laws are new and visible. But obligations the firm already has, such as these contracts, apply first and are clear here.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because quality matters to clients. But accuracy is a business question; it does not decide whether the answers may leave the firm.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: vendor security does matter. But the contracts require client consent, and a certification shows controls, not the clients' permission.

tips: Eliminate: A looks only at AI-specific law though contracts already bind the firm, and C raises output quality, which settles nothing about sharing.
Final two: B beats D because the contracts ask for client consent; a vendor's security certificate cannot give that permission.
Exam cue: before data goes to an AI service, check what laws and contracts already say about sharing it; approving the tool internally does not override them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.1 (legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI governance applies the laws and internal rules that already bind an organization, plus new AI-specific laws, to the AI tools it builds or uses' (notes 1.3.6 Laws and Rules That Apply to AI). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1.4 Security controls. What a control is
questions.question: A garden center's register lists email link scanning as its phishing control, but the security analyst finds the feature was bought and never switched on. What should the analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: The control is in place, as the company paid for the license
options.B: The risk is not lowered, since the feature is not running
options.C: The risk is accepted, as nobody turned the feature on
options.D: The risk is not the center's, as a vendor sold the feature

questions.key_concept: A control lowers risk only when it operates; a purchased feature left switched off is not a working control.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the feature is doing today to the chance or impact of phishing.
questions.correct_explanation: A security control is a measure that lowers risk by reducing the likelihood or the impact of harm. A feature that was bought but never switched on does neither, so the phishing risk is no lower than before and the register overstates protection. Treating the purchase as a control in place, the runner-up, confuses owning a product with operating a safeguard.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the purchase shows intent to treat the risk. But a control counts only when it operates, and this one has never run.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because nobody acted. But acceptance is a deliberate decision by the risk owner, recorded as such, not the result of a feature left off.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a vendor supplied the feature. But buying a product does not transfer risk; the garden center still owns its phishing risk.

tips: Eliminate: C mistakes inaction for acceptance, which needs a deliberate owner decision, and D mistakes buying a product for transferring the risk.
Final two: B beats A because a control must operate to lower risk; a license on file changes nothing while the feature stays off.
Exam cue: judge a control by whether it is working, not by whether it was bought or written down.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Appendix A Glossary (security control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A security control, or safeguard, is any measure that lowers risk by reducing the likelihood of a harmful event or the damage it causes' (notes 1.4.1 What a Security Control Is). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A science center's visitor kiosk should show only an exhibit guide, but visitors keep closing the guide and browsing the PC's files. Which technical control should the system administrator apply as BEST?

options.A: Full-disk encryption on the drive that holds the exhibit guide files
options.B: Antivirus software that scans and cleans the kiosk PC daily
options.C: A kiosk mode that keeps the screen locked to the exhibit guide
options.D: A standard user account with no administrator rights on the PC

questions.key_concept: Technical controls should limit a single-purpose device to its one function; least functionality closes paths that limited accounts leave open.
questions.pre_read: Ask what visitors are doing and which setting would stop them doing it.
questions.correct_explanation: The kiosk exists for one task, so the best technical control limits it to that task: a kiosk mode that keeps the screen locked to the exhibit guide removes the path to the PC's files. A standard user account, the runner-up, is sound least privilege, but visitors could still leave the guide and browse whatever that account can read.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects stored files. But it protects a drive that is off or removed; a running, signed-in kiosk still shows files to its users.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is a familiar technical control. But visitors browsing files is not malware, and scanning does not stop it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: removing administrator rights limits damage. But visitors could still close the guide and open any files the account can read.

tips: Eliminate: A protects data on a drive that is off, not on a running kiosk, and B looks for malware, which is not the problem here.
Final two: C beats D because the kiosk needs only one function; locking it to the guide removes the path to files, while a limited account leaves it open.
Exam cue: for single-purpose devices, the strongest technical control removes every function the device does not need.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-7 (Least Functionality); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-01 (configuration management practices are established and applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Technical controls, also called logical controls, are safeguards built into hardware, software or firmware, such as firewalls, encryption and access permissions' (notes 1.4.2 Technical Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An ice cream maker will let an outside food-safety consultant read its secret recipes, and the consultant's firm already screens its staff. Which administrative control should the security manager require as BEST before access?

options.A: A second background check run by the ice cream maker
options.B: Phishing awareness training for the consultant before the visit
options.C: A clean-desk rule for staff who handle the recipes
options.D: A signed non-disclosure agreement covering the recipes

questions.key_concept: Non-disclosure agreements are administrative controls that bind outsiders to keep confidential information secret before they are given access.
questions.pre_read: Name the risk that remains once a screened person is trusted to read the recipes.
questions.correct_explanation: The consultant will be trusted with the recipes, so the remaining risk is that they disclose them later. A signed non-disclosure agreement is an administrative control that sets that duty before access and gives the company recourse if it is broken. A second background check, the runner-up, is also administrative, but the consultant's firm already screens staff, so repeating it adds little against disclosure.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: screening is a real administrative control. But the firm already screens its staff; the open risk is disclosure, which an agreement addresses.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training is administrative too. But phishing lessons target a different risk from a trusted reader passing recipes on.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it guards printed recipes. But it governs the maker's own staff, not what an authorized consultant does with what they read.

tips: Eliminate: B trains for a different risk, and C governs the maker's own staff rather than the outside reader.
Final two: D beats A because the firm already screens its people; the remaining risk is disclosure, and a signed agreement binds the consultant against it.
Exam cue: when outsiders get trusted access to confidential information, a signed agreement setting their duties comes before access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-6 (Access Agreements); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-7 (External Personnel Security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Administrative controls, also called managerial controls, are the policies, procedures, training and people practices that direct how security is handled' (notes 1.4.3 Administrative Controls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A certified analyst volunteers with a group that helps small towns' water utilities find and fix exposed control systems, without pay or any contract. Which canon does this work MOST directly support?

options.A: Protect society, public trust and the infrastructure
options.B: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
options.C: Provide diligent and competent service to principals
options.D: Advance and protect the profession

questions.key_concept: The first canon covers protecting society, public trust and infrastructure; securing systems a community depends on serves it most directly.
questions.pre_read: Ask who benefits most directly from this work.
questions.correct_explanation: The first canon asks members to protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure. Water utilities are infrastructure whole towns depend on, so helping them close exposed control systems most directly serves it. Advancing the profession, the runner-up, fits sharing knowledge and supporting fellow professionals; this work protects the public's water rather than the profession itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the work is honorable. But this canon concerns the member's own honest, legal conduct, which is not what this work is mainly about.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst gives careful service. But principals are employers or clients under an agreement, and here there is no contract.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: unpaid security work can raise the profession's standing. But this canon covers the profession and its members; protecting towns' water serves the public.

tips: Eliminate: B is about the member's own honest and legal conduct, and C needs a principal, such as an employer or client, which this unpaid work lacks.
Final two: A beats D because the work protects infrastructure the public relies on; the profession canon covers helping the profession and its members.
Exam cue: match the canon to who benefits: the public and infrastructure, the member's own conduct, the principals served, or the profession.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The ISC2 Code of Ethics is the set of mandatory principles every ISC2-certified member agrees to follow: a preamble and four canons' (notes 1.5.3 The ISC2 Code of Ethics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At a traveling fair, a certified analyst finds a ride's speed limits were changed overnight by an unknown account, and the operations director wants the ride opened on time. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Support the opening, as the director owns the ride's operation
options.B: Warn the public on social media to avoid the ride today
options.C: Reset the limits, alert the incident response lead, and open the ride
options.D: Urge keeping the ride shut, and alert the incident response lead

questions.key_concept: When an unexplained change could injure people, the ethical response puts their safety first and escalates through proper channels.
questions.pre_read: Weigh who could be harmed if the ride opens before anyone knows what changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Where people's safety is at stake, protecting them comes first. An unknown account changing a ride's speed limits could injure riders, and nobody yet knows what else was altered, so the analyst presses to keep the ride shut and brings in the incident response lead. Resetting the limits, alerting the lead and opening anyway, the runner-up, trusts a quick fix on a system an unknown party has touched.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the director owns the ride. But loyalty to an employer never means exposing riders to a ride an unknown account has altered.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns people. But a public post bypasses the owner and the incident process, and could alert whoever made the change.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: restoring known settings and alerting the team sounds responsible. But other settings may be altered too, and opening before the team has checked puts riders at risk.

tips: Eliminate: A puts the schedule ahead of riders' safety, and B goes public before the owner and the incident team have acted.
Final two: D beats C because riders stay off until the incident team has checked; alerting the team while opening the ride still puts people at risk.
Exam cue: when an employer's schedule conflicts with people's safety, protect the people first and raise it through proper channels, not by going public.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Preamble and Canons; NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 2 (GV.RM-03: incident decisions are informed by other risks, such as safety, not just cybersecurity risks in isolation); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MA-04 (incidents are escalated or elevated as needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Where people's safety is at stake, protecting them comes first' (notes 1.5.4 Applying the Canons to Dilemmas). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A kayak outfitter swore in a complaint that its certified consultant lied about finishing a review; the consultant swore they finished it, and no records settle it. What will the ethics committee MOST likely conclude?

options.A: The consultant breached the code, as they cannot prove the work
options.B: The committee will investigate the outfitter's records to find the facts
options.C: The doubt goes to the consultant, so no breach is found
options.D: The committee drops it, as the outfitter lacks standing to complain

questions.key_concept: When disputed facts cannot be settled, the ethics complaint process gives the benefit of the doubt to the member complained about.
questions.pre_read: Think about who must prove the facts when both sides swear different stories.
questions.correct_explanation: When the two sides dispute the facts and the committee cannot reach a conclusion, the complaint procedure gives the benefit of the doubt to the member complained about; the burden of proof sits with the complainant. With sworn statements on both sides and nothing to settle them, no breach is found. Finding a breach because the consultant cannot prove the work, the runner-up, puts the burden on the wrong side.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the consultant has no proof either. But when facts stay disputed, the burden of proof sits with the complainant, not the member.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because someone must check the facts. But the committee is not an investigative body; it weighs only the evidence the parties submit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because standing rules exist. But a client is a principal, and anyone may complain about dishonesty, so the outfitter has standing.

tips: Eliminate: B gives the committee investigative powers it does not have, and D denies standing to a client complaining about dishonesty.
Final two: C beats A because the complainant carries the burden of proof; when disputed facts cannot be settled, the doubt favors the member.
Exam cue: the complaint process weighs only submitted evidence, and a complaint whose facts cannot be proved does not lead to a finding.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (disagreement on the facts: where the committee cannot reach a conclusion, the benefit of all doubt goes to the respondent); ISC2 Ethical Complaint Procedures (standing of complainant and form of complaints)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ISC2 enforces its code through a formal process: a written, sworn complaint is reviewed by an ethics committee and may lead to sanctions' (notes 1.5.5 Ethics Complaints and Enforcement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A baby-monitor maker's marketing manager asks a certified analyst to use an approved AI tool to write glowing customer reviews of its app, posted under invented names. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Refuse, since fake reviews mislead the people who read them
options.B: Write the reviews, adding a note that an AI tool drafted them
options.C: Pass the request to the security team to review the tool's use
options.D: Write them, since marketing decides how the app is promoted

questions.key_concept: Using AI to create deceptive content, such as reviews from invented customers, breaks the duty to act honestly, whatever the label.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether readers of these reviews would be misled about who wrote them.
questions.correct_explanation: Reviews written by AI and posted under invented names tell readers that real customers said things nobody said, which is deception whatever tool produced them. Acting honestly is part of the code a member agrees to, so the analyst refuses and can offer to gather genuine reviews instead. Adding a note that AI drafted them, the runner-up, still presents invented people as real customers.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: honesty about AI's role often matters. But a note about drafting does not fix the deception: the customers behind the reviews do not exist.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI use often goes to the security team for review. But the tool is already approved; the problem is the deception, which no tool review fixes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the marketing manager does own promotion. But authority over marketing cannot make deceiving readers honest; the analyst's duty to act honestly does not bend to a manager's request.

tips: Eliminate: C asks for a tool review, though the tool is approved and the problem is deception, and D defers to marketing's authority, which cannot make deceiving readers acceptable.
Final two: A beats B because labeling the drafting tool does not make invented customers real; the reviews would still mislead readers.
Exam cue: AI changes how work is produced, not the duty to be honest; content that deceives people stays unethical whoever or whatever wrote it.
questions.framework_ref: ISC2 Code of Ethics, Canons; NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.8 (Information Integrity: generative AI can ease the deliberate production of false or misleading content at scale)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Ethical AI use means bringing the same honesty, care and respect for people's data to AI tools as to any other work, with a person answerable for results' (notes 1.5.6 Ethical Use of AI at Work). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D1 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.
